=== NOTES 1:11 | Ivc Art and Craft – Dancing Girl, Priest-king, Terracotta, Beads, Pottery
## SUB 0 | Sculpture – Dancing Girl, Priest-King, Torso
[11:0:0] TABLE head: Sculpture | Site | Material
  [11:0:0.0] Dancing Girl (~10.5 cm / 4 inches; found 1926; National Museum, New Delhi) | Mohenjodaro | Bronze (lost-wax) – not clay, gold or carnelian (UPSC 2025)
  [11:0:0.1] Priest-King (bearded man in trefoil shawl, half-closed eyes) | Mohenjodaro | Steatite
  [11:0:0.2] Male torso | Harappa | Red sandstone / jasper
  [11:0:0.3] Daimabad man (chariot) | Daimabad | Bronze
[11:0:1] - The IVC gives the **first cities**, the **first script** (right to left) and the **earliest stone sculpture** (three-dimensional) in the subcontinent – but **not iron** sculpture; iron was unknown (CDS 2017).
[11:0:2] - Lifelike bronze and stone figures → **advanced metallurgy** and **craft specialisation**.
[11:0:3] - **18 Jun 2026:** **NCERT** to restore the original Dancing Girl image in the new **Class 9 Art** textbook.
[11:0:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.97-99, p.112 (CDS 2017); NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.8; old app notes row 11
## SUB 1 | Pottery
[11:1:0] - **Wheel-made**, sturdy, glossy; typical **red pottery** (red slip) **with black painted designs**; **plain red** ware the most common → colour = **red** (BPSC 1995).
[11:1:1] - Motifs: **geometric, floral, pipal leaf, fish-scale**, animals.
[11:1:2] - **Perforated jars**: large hole at the base, small holes in the wall – probably for **straining liquor**.
[11:1:3] - **Kalibangan** = six types of pottery; **Lothal** = painted jar (cunning fox story); big storage jars reached Oman.
[11:1:4] - Only evidence of painting is on pottery (no wall paintings).
[11:1:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.99; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.8, p.12; old app notes row 11
## SUB 2 | Lost-wax (Cire Perdue) and Metal Crafts
[11:2:0] - 1. Wax model coated with clay. 2. Heated: wax melts out. 3. Molten metal poured into the hollow mould. 4. Clay removed.
[11:2:1] - Lost-wax objects: **Dancing Girl**, **copper dog and bird of Lothal**, **bronze bull of Kalibangan**, buffalo and goat figures; continued in Late Harappan and Chalcolithic cultures (Daimabad bronzes) and later in **Chola** bronzes such as the **Nataraja**.
[11:2:2] TABLE head: Object | Site | Metal
  [11:2:2.0] Dog chasing a deer | Harappa | Bronze
  [11:2:2.1] Dog and bird | Lothal | Copper
  [11:2:2.2] Bull / ox | Kalibangan | Bronze
  [11:2:2.3] Chariot group, buffalo, rhinoceros, elephant | Daimabad | Bronze / copper
  [11:2:2.4] Gold foundry, active furnace | Rakhigarhi | Gold
  [11:2:2.5] Gold and silver necklaces | Allahdino | Gold, silver
[11:2:3] - Tools: chisels, needles, fishhooks, razors, mirrors, axes; vessels of copper, bronze, **silver**.
[11:2:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.72, p.88, p.97; old app notes row 11
## SUB 3 | Terracotta Figurines
[11:3:0] TABLE head: Type | Examples
  [11:3:0.0] Mother Goddess | Heavily jewelled female figurines (Harappa) – the most important terracottas
  [11:3:0.1] Toys | Toy carts with seated drivers (Chanhudaro), whistles, rattles, birds, gamesmen
  [11:3:0.2] Animals | Bulls (humpless bull prominent), birds, dogs, monkeys
  [11:3:0.3] Horned god | Clay mask of a horned god (Gujarat, Kalibangan)
[11:3:1] - Terracottas are crude, used by common people as toys or cult objects; seals and metal images were for the upper class.
[11:3:2] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.97-99; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.7; old app notes row 11
## SUB 4 | Beads, Faience and Shell
[11:4:0] TABLE head: Centre | Evidence
  [11:4:0.0] Chanhudaro | Bead-making factory, furnace, shell-working, bangles (APPSC G1 2022); lipsticks, ink pot; only city without a citadel
  [11:4:0.1] Lothal | Bead workshops; carnelian beads for export
  [11:4:0.2] Rakhigarhi | Gemstone factory – 3,000+ semi-precious stones
[11:4:1] - Materials: **carnelian** (from **Saurashtra**/Bharuch), agate, jasper, **steatite**, lapis lazuli, **faience**, **gold**; beads exported to **Mesopotamia** and the **Persian Gulf**.
[11:4:2] - **Faience** (ground sand/silica, glazed blue-green): beads, bangles, tiny vessels – called the **world's first glazed ware**; tie with **mosaic glass** = early clue to glass-making.
[11:4:3] - Shell work: Chanhudaro shell-ornament factory; Nageshwar, Balakot, Lothal.
[11:4:4] - Seal carving (steatite; unicorn commonest motif) and carnelian working = new techniques of the period.
[11:4:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.88, p.100; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.7-8, p.13; old app notes row 11

=== NOTES 1:12 | Ivc Religion – Pashupati Seal, Mother Goddess, Tree and Animal Worship, Fire Altars
## SUB 0 | Mother Goddess, Pashupati and Male Deities
[12:0:0] # Mother Goddess – the chief female deity
[12:0:1] - **Mother Goddess (Devi Mata):** terracotta female figurines, heavily jewelled, with fan-shaped head-dresses → **fertility cult**; probably the chief female deity (RAS 1993; SSC 2012: Devi Mata = **Indus Valley Civilisation**).
[12:0:2] - **Sites:** Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Kot Diji, Kalibangan, Banawali (with toy plough) and Gujarat sites; not a feature of Ropar (known for the dog burial).
[12:0:3] - **Continuity:** the Mother Goddess cult survives in later **Shakti cults**.
[12:0:4] - **⚠ Trap:** "Spirit and Brahma", "ritual" and "sacrificial system" are Vedic ideas – the Indus answer is **Mother Goddess**.
[12:0:5] # Pashupati seal – the chief male deity
[12:0:6] TABLE head: Feature | Detail
  [12:0:6.0] Site | Mohenjodaro (steatite seal)
  [12:0:6.1] Figure | Three-faced, horned head-dress, seated in a yogic posture
  [12:0:6.2] Animals around | Elephant, tiger, rhinoceros, buffalo; two deer below the seat – no lion
  [12:0:6.3] Identification | Proto-Shiva / Pashupati ("lord of animals") – John Marshall
  [12:0:6.4] Caution | Script undeciphered, so the reading is an inference from later Shiva worship
[12:0:7] - **Indus people worshipped Shiva** (proto-Shiva, UKPSC 2006) – Indra and Varuna are Rig Vedic gods; Brahma and Vishnu are later.
[12:0:8] - **Both male and female deities** were worshipped (Mother Goddess + Pashupati) – the only correct statement in UPSC 2013 (no palaces or temples, no horse-drawn chariots) → **"only 2"**.
[12:0:9] # Idol worship
[12:0:10] - **Idol worship began in the pre-Aryan (Harappan) period:** no temple has been found, yet idolatry was practised through figurines and seals (UPPCS 1992). The Rig Vedic Aryans had **no idols or temples**.
[12:0:11] > Exam angle: "people of the Indus Valley believed in …" → Mother Goddess; "beginning of idol worship" → pre-Aryan; "Shiva / Rudra" → Pashupati.
[12:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 1 p.7; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.99-101; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.108-109; app notes 1:12 (sub 0, 1)
## SUB 1 | Tree, Animal and Bird Worship; Fertility Symbols
[12:1:0] # Sacred trees, animals and birds
[12:1:1] - **Pipal:** the tree most often depicted on Indus seals (a deity standing among pipal branches) – MPPSC 2021; the pipal motif goes back to the **Early Harappan** phase and is still worshipped.
[12:1:2] - **Pigeon (dove):** listed by NextGen among sacred symbols – the bird "worshipped" by the Harappans (APPSC Group-II 2011); the peacock is only a pottery motif.
[12:1:3] - **Sacred animals:** the **unicorn** (mythical one-horned animal, the commonest seal motif), the **humped bull** (next in importance), elephant, tiger, buffalo, rhinoceros; cobras and horned deities also appear.
[12:1:4] - **Animals round Pashupati** were probably worshipped too.
[12:1:5] # Fertility and phallic symbols
[12:1:6] - **Linga and yoni:** conical stones (lingas) and **round pierced stones** (yoni) – fertility objects, possibly early Shaivite elements; found at Harappa.
[12:1:7] - **Swastika:** a seal motif, later an auspicious Hindu symbol – it has nothing to do with the Vedic yajna.
[12:1:8] - **Seals:** mostly of **steatite**, mostly **square** – some with a hole used as **amulets**.
[12:1:9] > Exam angle: "shape of which tree on Indus seals" → **pipal**; "bird worshipped" → **pigeon**; "mythical sacred animal" → **unicorn**.
[12:1:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 1 p.2, p.7; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.100; app notes 1:12 (sub 2)
## SUB 2 | Fire Altars, Great Bath and Ritual Practices
[12:2:0] # Fire altars
[12:2:1] TABLE head: Site | Evidence
  [12:2:1.0] Kalibangan (Rajasthan) | A row of seven fire altars on a mud-brick platform; triangular terracotta cake with a horned deity on one side and a human pulling a goat by a rope (animal sacrifice) on the other
  [12:2:1.1] Lothal (Gujarat) | Fire altar
  [12:2:1.2] Banawali, Rakhigarhi | Small pits with terracotta cakes regarded as fire altars
[12:2:2] - **Horned deity on a terracotta cake** → **Kalibangan** (State PSC) – not Banawali, Lothal or Surkotada.
[12:2:3] - **⚠ Caution:** Harappan fire altars are **not conclusive proof of the later Vedic yajna**.
[12:2:4] # Other ritual evidence
[12:2:5] - **Great Bath (Mohenjodaro):** probably for **ritual purification** (bathing).
[12:2:6] - **Amulets:** holed seals and amulets suggest belief in **ghosts and evil forces**; deities shown in **yogic poses** → practice of yoga and meditation.
[12:2:7] - **Burials with grave goods** point to a belief in life after death (details: burial row).
[12:2:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 1 p.7, p.12-13; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.101; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.20-21; app notes 1:12 (sub 1, 3)
## SUB 3 | Nature of Harappan Religion and Continuities
[12:3:0] - **Character:** predominantly **secular** civilisation – religion present but not dominant; nature- and **fertility-oriented** worship.
[12:3:1] - **No temple** has been identified anywhere; worship was domestic or open-air (under trees).
[12:3:2] - **Undeciphered script:** every reading of Harappan religion (proto-Shiva, Mother Goddess) is inferred from later traditions.
[12:3:3] - **Continuities into Hinduism:** Shiva/Pashupati, Shakti (Mother Goddess), linga-yoni, pipal and animal veneration, yoga.
[12:3:4] - **Contrast with the Rig Veda:** Vedic religion = **male nature gods and open-air yajnas**, no idols; Harappan = Mother Goddess, idols, animal and tree worship.
[12:3:5] - **Significance:** the earliest material evidence of a Shiva-like deity, a Mother Goddess and fertility cults in India.
[12:3:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.100-101; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 1 p.7, p.28; app notes 1:12 (sub 0, 5)

=== NOTES 1:13 | Decline of the Ivc – Competing Theories; Late Harappan Cultures
## SUB 0 | Late Harappan Phase – Features and Sites
[13:0:0] # Features (c. 1900–1300 BCE, post-urban phase)
[13:0:1] - **Chalcolithic:** tools of **stone and copper**; **no metal objects requiring complicated casting**; people lived in **villages** (agriculture, stock-raising, hunting, fishing).
[13:0:2] - **Lost:** the extraordinary **uniformity** of the Mature phase (pottery, seals, bricks, weights), writing, long-distance trade, large public buildings and craft specialisation; pottery became **regionally varied**.
[13:0:3] - **Bhagwanpura (Kurukshetra, Haryana):** Late Harappan houses of **burnt brick** (so "no burnt bricks at Bhagwanpura" is **false**); Late Harappan pottery overlaps with **PGW**; a 13-roomed house (excavated by **J.P. Joshi**).
[13:0:4] - **APPSC Group-1 statements:** I chalcolithic ✓, II no complicated casting ✓, III villages ✓, IV no burnt bricks at Bhagwanpura ✗ → **I, II and III**.
[13:0:5] - **Astt. Comm. 2018:** uniformity of artefacts ✓ (Mature phase); "Late sites kept the same construction techniques" ✗ → **only I**.
[13:0:6] - **Iron** was absent in the Mature phase and came only later (PGW, Later Vedic).
[13:0:7] # Regional Late Harappan cultures
[13:0:8] TABLE head: Culture / site | Region
  [13:0:8.0] Cemetery H | Harappa region, Punjab (Pakistan)
  [13:0:8.1] Jhukar, Jhangar | Sindh
  [13:0:8.2] Rangpur | Kutch, Saurashtra and mainland Gujarat
  [13:0:8.3] Late Siswal, Bhagwanpura | Haryana
  [13:0:8.4] Bara, Dadheri | Punjab (India)
  [13:0:8.5] Alamgirpur | Uttar Pradesh (Meerut)
  [13:0:8.6] Daimabad | Maharashtra – southernmost Late Harappan site
  [13:0:8.7] Swat | Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
[13:0:9] - **Movement:** settlements shifted **eastward** to the Ganga–Yamuna Doab and **southward** to Gujarat and the Deccan.
[13:0:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.101, p.105, p.107; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.8; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 1 p.2, p.28; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.25; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhagwanpura,_Haryana; app notes 1:13 (sub 3, 4)
## SUB 1 | Decline Theories – Proponents
[13:1:0] TABLE head: Theory | Proponent(s)
  [13:1:0.0] Aryan invasion | Ramaprasad Chanda (1926), elaborated by Mortimer Wheeler (1947) – Indra "Purandara", huddled skeletons
  [13:1:0.1] Floods | Marshall, Mackay, S.R. Rao; floods + tectonic uplift – M.R. Sahni
  [13:1:0.2] Shift of the Indus course | H.T. Lambrick – Mohenjodaro abandoned
  [13:1:0.3] Climate change / aridity | Aurel Stein, A.N. Ghosh
  [13:1:0.4] Drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra (Sarasvati) | D.P. Agrawal and Sood – Kalibangan, Banawali abandoned
  [13:1:0.5] Ecological imbalance | W.A. Fairservis
  [13:1:0.6] Decline of trade with Mesopotamia (c. 1900 BCE) | trade-decline school
[13:1:1] - **Other stresses:** **soil salinity**, deforestation, malaria at **Mohenjodaro**; **Chanhudaro** was flooded several times.
[13:1:2] - **⚠ Trap:** Aurel Stein = climate, **not** Aryan invasion.
[13:1:3] - **Consensus:** decline was **gradual and multi-causal** – urban collapse over about **200 years** (c. 1900–1700 BCE) and a long tail to c. 1300 BCE; climate change and the drying of the Sarasvati are the most widely accepted causes.
[13:1:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.105-106; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 1 p.13; app notes 1:13 (sub 0)
## SUB 2 | Climate and the 4.2 ka Event
[13:2:0] - **4.2 ka event:** sharp weakening of the monsoon about **4,200 years ago**; the same aridity is linked to the fall of **Akkad** and Old Kingdom Egypt.
[13:2:1] - **Deoria Tal (Uttarakhand):** pollen record – the **oak-to-pine ratio** shift shows the monsoon **weakened sharply**.
[13:2:2] - **IIT Kharagpur study:** continuous low rainfall for about **900 years** drove the decline and migration.
[13:2:3] - **Ghaggar-Hakra:** the densest cluster of Harappan sites; its drying ended cities like Kalibangan.
[13:2:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.105; app notes 1:13 (sub 2)
## SUB 3 | Invasion Theory and Its Rejection
[13:3:0] - **Wheeler's case:** the Rig Veda's fort-breaking Indra (Purandara) and the huddled skeletons of Mohenjodaro.
[13:3:1] - **Rejected because:** the Rig Veda postdates the decline; the skeletons belong to different levels (multiple burials, not a massacre); there is no evidence of large-scale conflict between Late Harappans and Indo-Aryans.
[13:3:2] - **Rakhigarhi DNA (female, c. 4,600 years ago):** no **steppe pastoralist** component → challenges invasion theories, supports **indigenous continuity**; migration (not invasion) is still argued from other DNA studies.
[13:3:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.105-107; app notes 1:13 (sub 1)
## SUB 4 | OCP, Copper Hoards and Harappan–Vedic Continuity
[13:4:0] - **Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP):** the Ganga–Yamuna Doab Late Harappan phase; **Copper Hoards** often found with OCP in the **Doab**.
[13:4:1] - **Continuity view:** identification of the Ghaggar-Hakra with the Rigvedic **Sarasvati**; Bhagwanpura's **Late Harappan + PGW** overlap.
[13:4:2] - **Traits that continued:** crafts, pottery, beads, weights, agriculture – **not iron tools**, which are post-Harappan.
[13:4:3] - **Rakhigarhi:** the only Harappan site so far to yield **ancient DNA**.
[13:4:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.8; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 1 p.28; app notes 1:13 (sub 5)

=== NOTES 1:18 | Later Vedic Period – Eastward Expansion, Iron (krishna Ayas), Painted Grey Ware
## SUB 0 | Eastward Expansion – Kuru-Panchala, Videgha Madhava, Agastya
[18:0:0] # Period and spread
[18:0:1] - **Later Vedic (post-Rigvedic) period = 1000–600 BC (BCE).** Texts composed in the upper Gangetic basin.
[18:0:2] - **Course:** **Punjab → Ganga-Yamuna Doab** (Kurukshetra, Delhi, upper Doab) → **Kosala** (eastern UP), **Kashi** (Varanasi), **Videha** (north Bihar), reached by about 600 BCE.
[18:0:3] - **Kurus** = union of the **Bharatas and Purus**; first between the Sarasvati and Drishadvati, then Delhi and the upper Doab (Kurukshetra). **Panchalas** = middle Doab (Bareilly, Badaun, Farrukhabad).
[18:0:4] - **Kuru-Panchala** = **centre / axis of Aryan culture** in the post-Vedic period: the Vedic texts were compiled here (not Anga-Magadha, Kosala-Videha or Matsya-Shurasena).
[18:0:5] TABLE head: Place | Capital of
  [18:0:5.0] Hastinapur (Meerut district) | Kuru kingdom (Kauravas)
  [18:0:5.1] Indraprastha (Purana Qila, Delhi) | Kuru kingdom (Pandavas)
  [18:0:5.2] Ahichchhatra (Ramnagar, Bareilly) | Panchala
[18:0:6] # Videgha Madhava legend (Shatapatha Brahmana)
[18:0:7] - **Videgha Madhava** (Mathava), king of Videha, lived on the **Sarasvati**; with his priest **Gautama Rahugana** he followed **Agni Vaishvanara** (sacrificial fire) as it burnt the forests eastward.
[18:0:8] - They crossed the **Sadanira (Gandak)**; the land beyond was settled as **Videha**.
[18:0:9] - Read as the eastward movement and agricultural colonisation by **burning and clearing forests** (fire and iron axes).
[18:0:10] # Aryanisation of the South
[18:0:11] - **Agastya** = the sage said to have **Aryanised South India** (crossed the Vindhyas); not Vishvamitra, Vasishtha or Apastamba.
[18:0:12] > Axis of Aryan culture = Kuru-Panchala; Videgha Madhava's priest = Gautama Rahugana; river crossed = Sadanira (Gandak).
[18:0:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.30; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.131, p.139, p.148; old app notes 1:18
## SUB 1 | Iron – Krishna Ayas, Dates and Earliest Sites
[18:1:0] # Vedic metal terms
[18:1:1] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [18:1:1.0] Ayas (Rigveda) | Copper or bronze
  [18:1:1.1] Krishna ayas / Shyama ayas ("black metal") | Iron (Later Vedic texts; first in the Yajurveda)
  [18:1:1.2] Lohita ayas | Copper
  [18:1:1.3] Hiranya | Gold
  [18:1:1.4] Nishka | Gold ornament; later a unit of value
[18:1:2] # Iron in North India
[18:1:3] - Iron technology about **1000–800 BCE**; common at most **PGW sites** of the Doab; iron weapons (arrowheads, spearheads) common in western UP from about 800 BCE.
[18:1:4] - Iron axes and fire cleared Gangetic forests; knowledge of iron reached Kosala and Videha by the end of the period.
[18:1:5] - **Earliest iron among the classic northern sites = Atranjikhera** (Etah, UP; excavated by R.C. Gaur) – not Taxila, Kaushambi or Hastinapur. Other early sites: Hastinapur, Kaushambi, Taxila (Gandhara, c. 1000 BC).
[18:1:6] - **Jakhera** (UP): iron in the **Black and Red Ware phase, before 1200 BCE**; iron in Dharwar (Karnataka) c. 1000 BCE.
[18:1:7] # Earliest iron – Tamil Nadu dates (2025)
[18:1:8] TABLE head: Site | District (TN) | Finding
  [18:1:8.0] Sivagalai | Thoothukudi | Iron dated to about 2953 BCE (to 3345 BCE) – now the oldest (TN report, Jan 2025)
  [18:1:8.1] Mayiladumparai | Krishnagiri | Iron AMS-dated to 2172 BCE; earliest claim before Sivagalai
  [18:1:8.2] Thirumalapuram | Tenkasi | Iron Age urn chamber
  [18:1:8.3] Adichanallur | Thoothukudi | Urn burials; not a PGW or northern iron site
[18:1:9] - These dates push iron use far earlier than the Gangetic 1000 BCE; they say **nothing about where PGW began**.
[18:1:10] - **First metal used in India = copper** (Chalcolithic = "copper-stone" age, Greek *khalkos* + *lithos*); iron came later.
[18:1:11] > Krishna ayas = iron, not copper; Sivagalai (2953 BCE) is older than Mayiladumparai (2172 BCE).
[18:1:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.30, p.32; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.132; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.7; old app notes 1:18
## SUB 2 | Pottery Sequence and Painted Grey Ware
[18:2:0] # Sequence of protohistoric pottery (Ganga-Yamuna Doab)
[18:2:1] TABLE head: Order | Pottery | Date | Phase
  [18:2:1.0] 1 | Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP) | 2000–1500 BCE | Chalcolithic
  [18:2:1.1] 2 | Black and Red Ware (BRW) | 1450–1200 BCE | Chalcolithic; also Later Vedic; Megalithic south
  [18:2:1.2] 3 | Painted Grey Ware (PGW) | 1200–500 BCE | Early Iron Age / Later Vedic
  [18:2:1.3] 4 | Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) | 700–100 BCE (from c. 600 BCE in the Ganga valley) | Mahajanapadas, second urbanisation
[18:2:2] - **OCP** is an ill-fired red ware that leaves an **ochre colour on the fingers**; **christened (named) at Hastinapur by B.B. Lal (1950–52)**, not Ahichchhatra, Noh or Red Fort.
[18:2:3] - **Four wares known to the Later Vedic people:** **Red Ware** (most popular), **Black-slipped Ware**, **Black-and-Red Ware**, **Painted Grey Ware** (most distinctive) = I, II, III, IV. **NBPW is NOT** Later Vedic (post-Vedic, shiny black).
[18:2:4] # Painted Grey Ware culture
[18:2:5] - **Grey pottery with black linear / geometric painted designs**; mainly **bowls and dishes**; deluxe tableware of the upper strata; not polished black.
[18:2:6] - **Pottery of 1000–600 BC in the Gangetic plain = PGW.**
[18:2:7] - About **700 sites**, mainly in the **upper Ganga basin** and the Indo-Gangetic divide (Punjab, Haryana, western UP) – not the lower Indus basin.
[18:2:8] - First found at **Ahichchhatra** (excavations 1940–44); **Hastinapur** excavation (1950–52, **B.B. Lal**) established it as a culture.
[18:2:9] - Finds: **iron weapons**, copper objects (copper possibly from **Khetri**, Rajasthan), glass, bone, semi-precious beads (trade, barter; no coins).
[18:2:10] TABLE head: Site | Region
  [18:2:10.0] Hastinapur | Meerut, western UP (Kuru capital)
  [18:2:10.1] Atranjikhera | Etah, western UP (Doab)
  [18:2:10.2] Ahichchhatra | Bareilly, UP
  [18:2:10.3] Bhagwanpura | Haryana – 13-roomed mud house; pre-iron PGW with late Harappan pottery
  [18:2:10.4] Noh | Rajasthan (OCP–BRW–PGW sequence)
[18:2:11] - Early PGW (Ghaggar-Hakra, Bhagwanpura) has **no iron**; later Doab PGW is iron-using.
[18:2:12] > Later Vedic wares exclude NBPW; PGW = upper Ganga basin, 1000–600 BC; OCP named at Hastinapur.
[18:2:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.30, p.32; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.133; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.6-9; old app notes 1:18
## SUB 3 | Agriculture, Settlements and Crafts
[18:3:0] - **Agriculture** became the main livelihood; wooden ploughshare common; ploughs drawn by **6, 8, 12 and even 24 oxen**.
[18:3:1] TABLE head: Crop | Later Vedic term
  [18:3:1.0] Rice | Vrihi (ritual use; rice remains of 8th c. BCE at Hastinapur, Atranjikhera)
  [18:3:1.1] Wheat | Godhuma
  [18:3:1.2] Barley | Yava (continued)
  [18:3:1.3] Sugarcane | Ikshu
[18:3:2] - **Settlements:** mainly **villages** of mud-brick and wattle-and-daub houses; **burnt bricks not common**; Hastinapur and Kaushambi only proto-urban; **true towns** came in the **NBPW phase** (second urbanisation: Shravasti, Kausambi, Hastinapur).
[18:3:3] - **Crafts:** carpentry (chariots), leather, pottery, weaving (by women), copper-bronze-iron smiths; **Shresthins** = merchant groups; units of value **nishka, satamana, krishnala**; barter still main.
[18:3:4] - **AP angle:** Iron Age in Andhra = **Megalithic culture with BRW** (Brahmagiri, Nagarjunakonda, Gudivada, Jonnawada); H.D. Sankalia: rice first harvested in AP in the Iron Age (Megalithic) era.
[18:3:5] - **Sep 2026:** BHU opened 22 sealed boxes of 10,000+ **Rajghat** (Varanasi) artefacts; pre-NBPW pottery dates Varanasi's urban origins to about **800 BCE**.
[18:3:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.32; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.132-133; old app notes 1:18
## SUB 4 | Later Vedic Religion – Gods and Priests
[18:4:0] TABLE head: God | Position
  [18:4:0.0] Prajapati | Creator; became supreme
  [18:4:0.1] Vishnu | Rose as preserver (minor in the Rigveda)
  [18:4:0.2] Rudra | God of animals; later merged with Shiva
  [18:4:0.3] Pushan | Cattle god; god of the Shudras
  [18:4:0.4] Indra, Agni, Varuna | Lost importance
[18:4:1] - Prayers declined; elaborate **sacrifices** grew, raising the priests' power; Upanishadic thinkers criticised **ritualism**.
[18:4:2] TABLE head: Priest | Veda / role
  [18:4:2.0] Hotri | Recited the Rigveda
  [18:4:2.1] Adhvaryu | Yajurveda; did the practical, manual work of the sacrifice
  [18:4:2.2] Udgatri | Chanted the Samaveda
  [18:4:2.3] Brahman | Atharvaveda; supervised
[18:4:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.33; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.139; old app notes 1:18

=== NOTES 1:21 | Vedic Literature – Vedas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads, Vedangas, Sutras
## SUB 0 | Four Vedas – Content, Priests, Trayi
[21:0:0] TABLE head: Veda | Content | Priest | Upaveda
  [21:0:0.0] Rigveda | Hymns (prayers); oldest / earliest | Hotri (Hota) | Ayurveda
  [21:0:0.1] Yajurveda | Sacrificial formulas; rites and rituals of yajnas (verse + prose) | Adhvaryu | Dhanurveda
  [21:0:0.2] Samaveda | Rigvedic hymns set to melody; shortest; origin of Indian music | Udgatri | Gandharvaveda
  [21:0:0.3] Atharvaveda | Magical charms, spells, healing; latest | Brahman | Shilpaveda (architecture) / Arthashastra
[21:0:1] - **Samaveda** is **compiled from the Rigveda**: about 1,549 verses (1,875 with repeats), all but about **75** from the Rigveda (mostly Mandalas VIII and IX).
[21:0:2] - **Atharvaveda**: earliest charms and spells; **Ayurveda ("Science of Life") first appears** here (its prime origin; PMF lists Ayurveda as Upaveda of the Rigveda); term **kshetra-patni ("mistress of the field")** originates here (UPSC 2026); Sabha and Samiti = "twin daughters of **Prajapati**"; mentions Pashupati; recensions **Paippalada, Shaunaka**; reflects non-Aryan beliefs.
[21:0:3] - **Trayi / Vedatrayi** = **Rig, Yajur, Sama**; Atharvaveda excluded (recognised later).
[21:0:4] - **Yajurveda** has two branches, **Krishna (Black)** and **Shukla (White)**; first mentions Rajasuya and Vajapeya.
[21:0:5] - **Upavedas:** Ayurveda – medicine; Dhanurveda – warfare; Gandharvaveda – music; **Shilpaveda – architecture** (not astronomy).
[21:0:6] - Vedic people were skilled in **astronomy** (Vedanga Jyotisha), **mathematics** (Sulbasutra geometry) and **medicine** (Atharvaveda) – **not chemistry**.
[21:0:7] > Hotri-Adhvaryu-Udgatri-Brahman = Rig-Yajur-Sama-Atharva; Trayi excludes Atharva.
[21:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.21-23, p.29; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.147-148; old app notes 1:21; UPSC CSE Prelims 2026 key (Vajiram & Ravi)
## SUB 1 | Layers of Vedic Literature – Shruti
[21:1:0] - Order: **Samhitas → Brahmanas → Aranyakas → Upanishads**; Vedangas, Sutras, Smritis come later.
[21:1:1] - All are **Shruti** ("heard"), **apaurusheya** (not of human origin); Smriti = remembered (Dharmashastras, epics, Puranas).
[21:1:2] - **Samhitas + Brahmanas = Karma-kanda**; **Aranyakas + Upanishads = Jnana-kanda**.
[21:1:3] - **Brahmanas**: prose commentaries that **explain the Vedic hymns** and the meaning of sacrifices (karma-marga; "liturgies").
[21:1:4] - **Aranyakas**: "**forest texts**", concluding parts of the Brahmanas; symbolic / secret meaning of ritual; bridge karma-marga → jnana-marga. **Atharvaveda has no Aranyaka**.
[21:1:5] - **Veda Vyasa (Krishna Dvaipayana)** compiled and classified the Vedas. Veda from *vid* = to know.
[21:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.21-24; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.143, p.149, p.152; old app notes 1:21
## SUB 2 | Rigveda – Mandalas, Hymns, Gayatri
[21:2:0] - **10 mandalas, 1,028 hymns (suktas)** = 1,017 + 11 Valakhilya; 10,552 mantras; a **collection of hymns** to nature deities; similar to the Iranian **Avesta**; "First Testament of Mankind".
[21:2:1] TABLE head: Mandala | Content
  [21:2:1.0] II–VII | Family books, oldest core (Gritsamada, Vishvamitra, Vamadeva, Atri, Bharadvaja, Vasishtha)
  [21:2:1.1] III | Gayatri Mantra – composed by Vishvamitra, deity Savitri
  [21:2:1.2] VII | Battle of Ten Kings (Vasishtha)
  [21:2:1.3] IX | Wholly Soma (Soma Pavamana, 114 hymns)
  [21:2:1.4] X | Purusha Sukta (four varnas, origin of caste – first use of "varna" for the four orders), Nasadiya Sukta (creation), Surya Sukta (marriage, X.85)
[21:2:2] - Word **gotra** first occurs in the **Rigveda**, meaning cow shelter / herd of cows.
[21:2:3] - **Memory of the World (2007):** **30 Rigveda manuscripts** at the **Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune** on UNESCO's register; Vedic chanting = UNESCO intangible heritage (2008).
[21:2:4] - **Script:** the Rigveda was composed and transmitted **orally**; exam keys give **Brahmi** as its basic script (surviving manuscripts are much later, in Devanagari / Sharada).
[21:2:5] > Gayatri = Mandala III, Vishvamitra; Soma = Mandala IX; Purusha Sukta = Mandala X.
[21:2:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.22-23, p.29; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.145-147; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.1; old app notes 1:21
## SUB 3 | Yajurveda Branches and the Brahmanas
[21:3:0] TABLE head: Branch | Nature | Samhitas | Brahmana
  [21:3:0.0] Shukla (White) | Mantras only, clearly arranged | Vajasaneyi (Madhyandina, Kanva) | Shatapatha
  [21:3:0.1] Krishna (Black) | Mantras + prose mixed | Taittiriya, Maitrayani, Kathaka, Kapishthala | Taittiriya
  [21:3:0.2] Veda | Brahmanas | Aranyakas | Upanishads
  [21:3:0.3] Rig | Aitareya, Kaushitaki | Aitareya, Kaushitaki | Aitareya, Kaushitaki
  [21:3:0.4] Sama | Panchavimsha (Tandya), Jaiminiya, Shadvimsha, Chandogya | Jaiminiya, Chandogya | Chandogya, Kena
  [21:3:0.5] Yajur | Taittiriya, Shatapatha | Taittiriya, Brihadaranyaka | Brihadaranyaka, Isha, Katha, Taittiriya (Krishna YV), Shvetashvatara
  [21:3:0.6] Atharva | Gopatha (only one) | None | Mundaka, Mandukya, Prashna
[21:3:1] - **Shatapatha Brahmana**: largest; Videgha Madhava's eastward journey; **Great Flood**; **first reference to money-lending** (kusidin); full **upanayana**; "wife is half her husband"; **Purushamedha** (described with the Vajasaneyi Samhita of the Shukla Yajurveda).
[21:3:2] - **Aitareya Brahmana**: origin of kingship, ten forms of government, Shudra as servant, first mention of the **Andhras** (Sunahshepa story).
[21:3:3] > Gopatha = Atharva; Jaiminiya = Sama; Purushamedha = Shatapatha.
[21:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.23-24, p.29; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.144, p.147-148; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.117; old app notes 1:21
## SUB 4 | Upanishads and Vedanta
[21:4:0] - **108** (Muktika list), about **13 principal**; c. 800–600 BCE; **anti-ritualistic**; **Atman = Brahman**; karma, samsara, moksha; called **Vedanta** ("end of the Vedas").
[21:4:1] - **Prasthanatrayi** = **Upanishads, Brahma Sutra** (Badarayana), **Bhagavad Gita**; the **Bhagavata is not** included. **Shankaracharya** wrote bhashyas on these three – **not on the Rigveda**.
[21:4:2] TABLE head: Saying / story | Upanishad
  [21:4:2.0] Satyameva Jayate (national motto, adopted 26 Jan 1950, below the State Emblem) | Mundaka
  [21:4:2.1] Asato ma sadgamaya; Yajnavalkya with Gargi and Maitreyi; first statement of transmigration | Brihadaranyaka
  [21:4:2.2] Tat tvam asi; Satyakama Jabala (son of the unmarried Jabala); Uddalaka–Shvetaketu; Krishna, son of Devaki (first mention) | Chandogya
  [21:4:2.3] Nachiketa–Yama dialogue on death | Katha (Kathopanishad)
  [21:4:2.4] Trimurti | Maitrayani
  [21:4:2.5] Name means "white horse"; introduces bhakti | Shvetashvatara
  [21:4:2.6] Taittiriya Upanishad | Krishna Yajurveda
[21:4:3] > Satyameva Jayate = Mundaka (not Mandukya); Jabala Upanishad is a different, later text.
[21:4:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.24-25; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.149-152; old app notes 1:21
## SUB 5 | Vedangas, Sutras and Grammarians
[21:5:0] TABLE head: Vedanga | Subject
  [21:5:0.0] Shiksha | Phonetics
  [21:5:0.1] Kalpa | Rituals (Sutras)
  [21:5:0.2] Vyakarana | Grammar (Panini)
  [21:5:0.3] Nirukta | Etymology (Yaska)
  [21:5:0.4] Chandas | Metrics (Pingala)
  [21:5:0.5] Jyotisha | Astronomy
[21:5:1] - Mimamsa is a darshana, **not** a Vedanga.
[21:5:2] TABLE head: Sutra | Subject
  [21:5:2.0] Shrauta | Public, large sacrifices
  [21:5:2.1] Grihya | Domestic rites
  [21:5:2.2] Dharma | Law, social practice
  [21:5:2.3] Sulba | Measurement and construction of altars (geometry)
[21:5:3] - Sulba authors: **Baudhayana, Apastamba, Katyayana**, Manava. **Baudhayana theorem** = lengths of the sides of a right-angled triangle = the **Pythagoras theorem**.
[21:5:4] TABLE head: Author | Work
  [21:5:4.0] Panini (c. 500 BCE) | Ashtadhyayi (Sanskrit grammar)
  [21:5:4.1] Yaska | Nirukta
  [21:5:4.2] Katyayana | Varttika
  [21:5:4.3] Patanjali | Mahabhashya; Yoga Sutras
[21:5:5] - Darshana founders: Nyaya – Gautama; **Vaisheshika – Kanada**; Sankhya – Kapila; Yoga – Patanjali; Purva Mimamsa – Jaimini; Uttara Mimamsa – Badarayana.
[21:5:6] - **Gayatri chandas** = **24 syllables** (3 × 8).
[21:5:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.25; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.1-5; old app notes 1:21
## SUB 6 | Epics, Puranas and Smritis
[21:6:0] # Mahabharata
[21:6:1] - By **Vyasa**; original **Jaya / Jayasamhita** (8,800 shlokas) → Bharata → **Shatasahasri Samhita** (~1 lakh verses), **18 books (parvas)**, **Harivamsa** appended; older than the Ramayana; Bhagavad Gita (part of it) in **Sanskrit**.
[21:6:2] - **Vaisampayana** told it to **Janamejaya**; **Ugrashrava Sauti** narrated it to Shaunaka's sages at **Naimisharanya**.
[21:6:3] - War at Kurukshetra for **18 days**; Arjuna's grandfather = **Vichitravirya** (Pandu's nominal father); Karna spent Indra's **Vasavi Shakti** on **Ghatotkacha**.
[21:6:4] # Ramayana
[21:6:5] - By **Valmiki**: **24,000** verses, 7 kandas, five stages from the 5th century BCE; Rama first met Hanuman in the **Kishkindha Kanda**.
[21:6:6] - **Janaka**'s brother = **Kushadhvaja** (king of Sankashya); Janaka's family priest-guru = **Shatananda**, son of sage **Gautama** (the Upanishadic Janaka learnt from Yajnavalkya).
[21:6:7] - **Samudra manthan:** serpent **Vasuki** was the churning rope.
[21:6:8] # Puranas and Smritis
[21:6:9] - **18 Mahapuranas**; five marks (**pancha-lakshana**): **Sarga, Pratisarga**, Vamsa, Manvantara, Vamshanucharita. Complete **Dasavatara** narration: **Bhagavata (Maha-bhagavatam)**.
[21:6:10] - Yugas: **Krita (Satya) → Treta → Dvapara → Kali**.
[21:6:11] - **Manu** = first law-giver (Manusmriti; disapproves **widow remarriage**); **Mitakshara** on the Yajnavalkya Smriti = **Vijnaneshwara**.
[21:6:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.34; old app notes 1:21; Valmiki Ramayana Bala Kanda (Shatananda, Kushadhvaja)

=== NOTES 1:22 | Vedic Religion, Ritual and Philosophy; the Six Orthodox Schools
## SUB 0 | Six Orthodox Schools – Founders, Texts and Pairs
[22:0:0] TABLE head: School (darshana) | Founder | Key text | Core idea
  [22:0:0.0] Samkhya (oldest) | Kapila | Samkhya Sutra; Samkhya Karika (Ishvarakrishna) | Dualism of Purusha and Prakriti; Satkaryavada
  [22:0:0.1] Yoga | Patanjali | Yoga Sutra | Ashtanga (eight-limbed) discipline; Samkhya metaphysics
  [22:0:0.2] Nyaya | Gautama (Akshapada) | Nyaya Sutra | Logic; four pramanas; 16 padarthas
  [22:0:0.3] Vaisheshika | Kanada | Vaisheshika Sutra | Atomism (paramanu); 9 dravyas
  [22:0:0.4] Purva Mimamsa | Jaimini | Mimamsa Sutra | Vedic ritual and duty (karma)
  [22:0:0.5] Uttara Mimamsa (Vedanta) | Badarayana (Vyasa) | Brahma Sutra | Brahman the only reality; knowledge of Brahman
[22:0:1] - **Three pairs:** **Samkhya–Yoga, Nyaya–Vaisheshika, Mimamsa–Vedanta**.
[22:0:2] - **Oldest darshana = Samkhya** (APPSC 2018 flashcard). Kapila is its **earliest exponent**.
[22:0:3] - **Uttara Mimamsa = Badarayana = Vyasa** (APPSC G1 2002) – not Kapila, Patanjali or Gautama; an old APPSC key giving Kapila is wrong.
[22:0:4] - **Not among the six:** **Smriti** (a class of texts), **Lokayata** (Charvaka materialism), **Kapalika** (a Shaiva sect) (UPSC 2014), Charvaka, Ajivika.
[22:0:5] - **Fully articulated / perfected in the Gupta age** (SSC CPO 2003); their sutras are older.
[22:0:6] - **Navya-Nyaya** ("new logic") was founded by **Gangesha Upadhyaya** of Mithila (Tattvachintamani, 14th c.); Raghunatha Shiromani came later.
[22:0:7] - **Kapila and the sons of Sagara:** in the Ramayana and Puranas the sage **Kapila** burnt the 60,000 sons of King Sagara to ashes; Bhagiratha brought the Ganga down to redeem them.
[22:0:8] > Founder matches: Kapila–Samkhya, Patanjali–Yoga, Gautama–Nyaya, Kanada–Vaisheshika, Jaimini–Purva Mimamsa, Badarayana–Uttara Mimamsa.
[22:0:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.25, p.36-37; PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.97-102; NextGen Indian History Part 3 (Guptas); Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.121; Britannica 'Nyaya'
## SUB 1 | Mimamsa – Jaimini, Kumarila Bhatta, Karma and Apurva
[22:1:0] - **Founder:** **Jaimini** (Mimamsa Sutra). Other exponents: **Kumarila Bhatta** and **Prabhakara**.
[22:1:1] - **Kumarila Bhatta** = **Purva Mimamsa** (APPSC G2 2012, 2019; AP History PYQs) – not Uttara Mimamsa, Advaita, Dvaita, Yogachara or Jnana marga. Works: **Slokavartika**, Tantravartika. He **defended Vedic ritual (karma-kanda)** and attacked Buddhist doctrines.
[22:1:2] - Also called **Karma-Mimamsa**: it centres on ritual action → the **theory of karma** belongs to Mimamsa (UPPSC 1997).
[22:1:3] - **Liberation through karma** – correct performance of Vedic rites and duties (UPSC 2005).
[22:1:4] - The **Vedas are eternal** and contain eternal truth (CGPSC 2013).
[22:1:5] - **Apurva** = the **unseen force** that links a ritual act (karma) with its later result.
[22:1:6] - **Purva Mimamsa = Karmakanda** (ritual part of the Vedas); **Uttara Mimamsa = Jnanakanda** (knowledge part).
[22:1:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.100-101; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.121; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.37; old app notes row 22
## SUB 2 | Rigvedic Gods – Indra, Agni, Varuna, Soma
[22:2:0] TABLE head: God | Domain | Exam fact
  [22:2:0.0] Indra | Lightning, storm, war | ~250 hymns (most); ranked first; Purandara (fort-breaker); most popular god; wife Shachi (Indrani)
  [22:2:0.1] Agni | Fire | ~200 hymns (second); messenger between gods and men; first hymn of the Rigveda (1.1)
  [22:2:0.2] Varuna | Water, cosmic order | Ranked third; upholder of Rita; ethically the highest
  [22:2:0.3] Soma | Plant and ritual drink | Whole 9th Mandala; god of plants; Haoma of the Avesta
  [22:2:0.4] Surya | Sun | Aspects: Savitri (Gayatri), Mitra, Pushan, Vishnu
  [22:2:0.5] Pushan | Paths, herdsmen, cattle | Solar aspect; god of the Shudras in later Vedic times
  [22:2:0.6] Brihaspati | Prayer | Priest (purohita) and preceptor of the gods
  [22:2:0.7] Dyaus | Sky | Celestial father, like Zeus
  [22:2:0.8] Ushas | Dawn | Female
  [22:2:0.9] Aditi | Mother of the gods | Female; not Prithvi (Prithvi = fertility goddess)
  [22:2:0.10] Aranyani | Forest | Female
  [22:2:0.11] Rudra | Disease | Archer god of the mountains; later merged with Shiva
  [22:2:0.12] Yama | Death | –
  [22:2:0.13] Vishnu | Aspect of Surya | Only 3 hymns; rose later
[22:2:1] - **War-god** = Indra (UPPSC 2011, Uttarakhand 2016). When Indra is not offered, the most hymns = **Agni** (UPPSC 2010).
[22:2:2] - **Priest of the gods** = **Brihaspati** in most keys; Agni is also hailed as purohita in Rigveda 1.1.
[22:2:3] - **Later Vedic:** **Prajapati** became supreme creator; **Vishnu** rose as preserver; **Rudra** grew; **Indra and Agni lost importance**.
[22:2:4] > Indra 250 > Agni 200 > Varuna third; 9th Mandala = Soma; Aditi (not Prithvi) = mother of gods.
[22:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.28, p.34-36; Britannica 'Brihaspati', 'Indra'; old app notes row 22
## SUB 3 | Vedanta Schools – Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva
[22:3:0] TABLE head: School | Teacher | Meaning | Path to mukti
  [22:3:0.0] Advaita | Adi Shankaracharya (8th c., Kaladi, Kerala) | Non-dualism: Brahman alone is real, Atman = Brahman, world = Maya | Jnana (knowledge)
  [22:3:0.1] Vishishtadvaita | Ramanujacharya (11th c., Sriperumbudur; Srirangam) | Qualified non-dualism: souls and world real, inseparable from Vishnu | Bhakti and divine grace
  [22:3:0.2] Dvaita | Madhvacharya | Dualism | Bhakti
  [22:3:0.3] Dvaitadvaita | Nimbarka | Dualistic non-dualism | –
  [22:3:0.4] Shuddhadvaita | Vallabhacharya | Pure non-dualism | –
[22:3:1] - **Shankara:** founded **four mathas** – **Sringeri** (south), **Puri** (east), **Dwarka** (west), **Badrinath / Jyotirmath (Joshimath)** (north); not Prayag, Kanchi or Varanasi. Called a "**crypto-Buddhist**" (Buddhist in disguise). Also Dashanami order and Panchayatana worship.
[22:3:2] - **Ramanuja:** first great promoter of the **Bhakti** movement; Sri Vaishnava.
[22:3:3] - **Bhagavad Gita:** gives **equal importance to Jnana, Karma and Bhakti** as means of liberation (UPPSC 2005).
[22:3:4] - **Swami Vivekananda's Neo-Vedanta** reworked Advaita.
[22:3:5] - Other teachers: **Lakulisha** – Pashupata Shaivism; **Nagarjuna** – Madhyamika (Shunyavada).
[22:3:6] > Advaita = Shankara = non-dualism = jnana; Vishishtadvaita = Ramanuja = bhakti; Dvaita = Madhva.
[22:3:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.98, p.105-110; Britannica 'Bhagavadgita'; old app notes row 22
## SUB 4 | Doctrines of the Schools – Samkhya, Nyaya, Vaisheshika
[22:4:0] TABLE head: Doctrine | School
  [22:4:0.0] Satkaryavada (effect pre-exists in the cause) | Samkhya (MPPSC 2025)
  [22:4:0.1] World formed by the blending of nature (Prakriti) | Samkhya
  [22:4:0.2] Atom as the basis of the world | Vaisheshika (Kanada)
  [22:4:0.3] Pramanas – perception, inference, comparison, testimony | Nyaya
  [22:4:0.4] Apurva; theory of karma | Mimamsa
  [22:4:0.5] Niyati (predetermined fate) | Ajivika (Makkhali Gosala)
  [22:4:0.6] Materialism | Lokayata / Charvaka
  [22:4:0.7] Syadvada | Jaina
  [22:4:0.8] Shunyavada / Madhyamika | Nagarjuna
[22:4:1] - **Samkhya:** **accepts rebirth**; liberation by **self-knowledge** (discriminating Purusha from Prakriti), not by an outside agent → UPSC 2013 "only 2". Kapila taught that man's life is shaped by the **forces of nature, not a divine agency** (CGPSC 2020: both true).
[22:4:2] - **Nyaya:** "nyaya" = logic or decision; **16 padarthas**. **Vaisheshika:** 9 dravyas; beginning of physics in India.
[22:4:3] - **APPSC G1 2023 match:** Samkhya – blending of nature; Vaisheshika – atom; Lokayata – materialism; Ajivika – predetermined fate.
[22:4:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.99-104; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.37-38; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.121; old app notes row 22
## SUB 5 | Astika vs Nastika; Charvaka (Lokayata)
[22:5:0] - **Test:** **belief in the authority of the Vedas** – astika accept it, nastika reject it (UPPSC 2005); not belief in God, rebirth or heaven.
[22:5:1] - **Astika:** the six darshanas. **Nastika:** **Charvaka, Buddhism (Bauddha), Jainism, Ajivika**.
[22:5:2] - **Charvaka = Lokayata** ("of the common people"); credited to **Brihaspati**; **materialism**; **perception** the only valid knowledge; no soul, rebirth or afterlife.
[22:5:3] - **Ajita Kesakambali** – early materialist of the Buddha's time.
[22:5:4] > Odd-one-out lists slip a nastika school (Charvaka, Bauddha, Ajivika) among the six.
[22:5:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.97, p.105; old app notes rows 22-23
## SUB 6 | Upanishadic Philosophy
[22:6:0] TABLE head: Concept | Meaning
  [22:6:0.0] Brahman | Ultimate reality (cosmic principle)
  [22:6:0.1] Atman | The self – not body or mind
  [22:6:0.2] Karma | Links action with consequence
  [22:6:0.3] Samsara | Rebirth – transmigration first in the Brihadaranyaka
  [22:6:0.4] Moksha | Liberation – not a Vedic Samhita term; first discussed in the Upanishads
[22:6:1] - **Main theme = philosophy** (UPPSC 2004, UP Lower 1998); anti-ritualistic; **Atman is Brahman**.
[22:6:2] - Criticised **mechanical sacrifice**; stressed meditation and the guru-disciple relationship; **ignorance** = cause of sorrow.
[22:6:3] - **Katha (Katha) Upanishad:** **Nachiketa** questions **Yama** on death and the Atman (UPSC 1997).
[22:6:4] - Basic approach is universal – it does not reject other schools or scriptures.
[22:6:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.25, p.29; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.2; old app notes row 22
## SUB 7 | Ashtanga Yoga
[22:7:0] TABLE head: No. | Limb | Group
  [22:7:0.0] 1 | Yama | Bahiranga (outer)
  [22:7:0.1] 2 | Niyama | Bahiranga
  [22:7:0.2] 3 | Asana | Bahiranga
  [22:7:0.3] 4 | Pranayama | Bahiranga
  [22:7:0.4] 5 | Pratyahara | Bahiranga (the bridge to the inner limbs)
  [22:7:0.5] 6 | Dharana | Antaranga (inner)
  [22:7:0.6] 7 | Dhyana | Antaranga
  [22:7:0.7] 8 | Samadhi | Antaranga
[22:7:1] - **Antaranga sadhana = Dharana, Dhyana, Samadhi** (MPPSC 2024 → Dharana). **Anusmriti** is NOT a limb (CGPSC 2015).
[22:7:2] - **Bahiranga = 5** (Yama to Pratyahara); **antaranga = 3**; **Pranayama** is the 4th limb.
[22:7:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.99-100; old app notes row 22
## SUB 8 | Nature of Vedic Religion – Rita, Dharma, Sacrifice
[22:8:0] - **Nature worship**; male gods dominate; worship for material gains; **sacrifice (yajna) central**, in the open air – **no temples, no idols** (UPPSC 1993: "sacrifice and rituals").
[22:8:1] - **Henotheism** (term of **Max Müller**): each god praised in turn as supreme.
[22:8:2] - **Rita** = cosmic and moral order, upheld by **Varuna**; **Dharma** = obligation and duty to oneself and others, grown from Rita → UPSC 2011 "both".
[22:8:3] - Iranian parallels: **Mitra–Mithra, Rita–Asha, Soma–Haoma**.
[22:8:4] TABLE head: Ritual / term | Associated with
  [22:8:4.0] Hotri (Rig), Adhvaryu (Yajur), Udgatri (Sama) | Priests
  [22:8:4.1] Ceremonial chanting | Samaveda
  [22:8:4.2] Agnistoma | Regular Soma sacrifice
  [22:8:4.3] Rajasuya, Vajapeya, Ashvamedha | Royal sacrifices
  [22:8:4.4] Grihya Sutras | Domestic rites
[22:8:5] - **Sanskaras: 16** = 3 before birth, 12 during life, **1 after death**.
[22:8:6] - **Later Vedic:** elaborate, costly sacrifices; Prajapati supreme; Indra and Agni decline; priests grow powerful.

=== NOTES 1:24 | Second Urbanisation – Nbpw, Punch-marked Coins, Guilds and Towns
## SUB 0 | Guilds (Shreni), Merchants and Trade Terms
[24:0:0] - **Shrenis:** associations of artisans, merchants, moneylenders under elected or hereditary heads (**jetthaka / pamukha**). Craft shrenis trained workers, procured raw materials, sold products; merchant shrenis organised trade.
[24:0:1] - **Powers (UPSC 2012 → II and III):** fixed **wages, rules of work, standards and prices**; had **their own laws (shreni-dharma)** and **judicial powers** over members. They were **autonomous – the king did not interfere**, so "every guild registered with the central authority, king the chief administrator" is **wrong**.
[24:0:2] - **Guilds as banks:** deposits invested at interest – **Nashik inscription** records guild deposits at fixed interest.
[24:0:3] - **Satapatha Brahmana:** first reference to **money-lending**; usurer = **kusidin**.
[24:0:4] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [24:0:4.0] Sarthavaha (satthavaha) | Caravan / convoy of merchants, or its leader
  [24:0:4.1] Setthi / Shreshthi | Rich merchant-banker
  [24:0:4.2] Gahapati | Wealthy householder / landowner
  [24:0:4.3] Vanija | Trader
  [24:0:4.4] Kusidin | Usurer
[24:0:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.15-17; NextGen Indian History Part 3 (guilds' own laws); old app notes row 24
## SUB 1 | Punch-marked Coins and Early Money
[24:1:0] - **Punch-marked (Aahat) coins:** **earliest extant coins** of India (7th–6th c. BC to the Mauryan period); **mostly silver**, some copper; symbols only (**sun, animals, trees, hills**), no writing.
[24:1:1] - Called **panas / karshapanas**; issued under Haryankas, Nandas and Mauryas; first definite literary references in **Pali texts**.
[24:1:2] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [24:1:2.0] Nishka | Gold / a gold ornament in Vedic texts (nishka-griva = gold necklace); a prestige object, later a unit – not cows or copper/silver coins
  [24:1:2.1] Karshapana / kahapana | Standard silver or copper punch-marked coin
  [24:1:2.2] Satamana | Value or weight unit of 100 mana
  [24:1:2.3] Suvarna | Gold coin (Satavahana usage)
[24:1:3] - **Satavahanas** first used inherited punch-marked coins, then die-struck coins of **lead**, potin, copper, silver; **ship-mast** coins of **Yajnasri Satakarni**.
[24:1:4] - **Gold coins in large numbers:** **Kushanas** (not Mauryas).
[24:1:5] - **Vaishya Tekri** (near Ujjain): Mauryan-era (BCE) stupa bigger than Sanchi; punch-marked and cast Avanti coins; MP to re-excavate it (2026).
[24:1:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 1 p.33; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.17; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.55; Rocket Indian History Part 2 (Sheet #90); old app notes row 24
## SUB 2 | Northern Black Polished Ware and the Second Urbanisation
[24:2:0] - **NBPW:** fine, glossy black, mirror-like **deluxe tableware of the rich**; **c. 700–200 BCE**; **after Painted Grey Ware**; the hallmark of the second urbanisation.
[24:2:1] - **NBPW sites:** mainly the Ganga valley – Hastinapur, Kaushambi, Shravasti, Ayodhya, Varanasi, Rajgir, Pataliputra, Vaishali, Champa; also Ujjain, Vidisha, Taxila (not Lothal).
[24:2:2] TABLE head: Cause | Effect
  [24:2:2.0] Iron tools | Forest clearance in the Ganga plain; surplus
  [24:2:2.1] Trade, crafts, coinage | Taxes and wages in money
  [24:2:2.2] State formation | Mahajanapada capitals became administrative centres
  [24:2:2.3] New merchant classes | Vaishyas backed Buddhism and Jainism
[24:2:3] - **Over 60 towns** in 600–300 BCE; the Mahajanapadas and Magadha = the **second urbanisation**.
[24:2:4] - **Rajghat (Varanasi):** pre-NBPW levels, punch-marked coins, **Greek-inscribed seals**; BHU re-study (Sep 2026) puts urban Varanasi at **c. 800 BCE**.
[24:2:5] TABLE head: Development | Period
  [24:2:5.0] Iron at Mayiladumparai (AMS dating) | c. 2172 BCE; southern Iron Age c. 2100 BCE – older than the Gangetic Iron Age
  [24:2:5.1] Iron ploughshares, axes in the Ganga valley | Later Vedic, c. 1000–600 BCE
  [24:2:5.2] Urban Varanasi | c. 800 BCE
  [24:2:5.3] NBPW | c. 700–200 BCE
  [24:2:5.4] Punch-marked coins begin | 7th–6th c. BCE
  [24:2:5.5] Gold coins in large numbers | Kushanas, 1st–2nd c. CE
[24:2:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.16; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 (NBP Ware); old app notes row 24
## SUB 3 | Towns and Trade Routes
[24:3:0] TABLE head: Town | Region | Feature
  [24:3:0.0] Rajagriha | Magadha | Ringed by five hills
  [24:3:0.1] Shravasti | Kosala | Crescent-shaped plan
  [24:3:0.2] Kaushambi | Vatsa | On the Yamuna; fortified
  [24:3:0.3] Ujjayini | Avanti | On the Sipra; Ptolemy's "Ozene"
  [24:3:0.4] Taxila | Gandhara | Learning centre; Uttarapatha junction
  [24:3:0.5] Vaishali | Vajji | Republican capital
  [24:3:0.6] Champa | Anga | Near Bhagalpur, on the Ganga
[24:3:1] - **Uttarapatha:** linked **Taxila** (north-west) with the Ganga valley up to Tamralipti.
[24:3:2] - **Dakshinapatha:** southern route to the Deccan (Kaushambi–Ujjayini–Pratishthana), through **Assaka**.
[24:3:3] - AP angle: Satavahana trade centres **Kotilingala, Dhulikatta, Kondapur**.
[24:3:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.17; old app notes row 24

=== NOTES 1:25 | Rise of Magadha – Haryankas, Shishunagas, Nandas and Causes of Supremacy
## SUB 0 | Capitals of Magadha – Rajgriha, Pataliputra, Vaishali
[25:0:0] # Capitals in order
[25:0:1] TABLE head: Capital | Ruler | Fact
  [25:0:1.0] Girivraja / Rajgriha (modern Rajgir) | Brihadratha line (Jarasandha); Bimbisara, Ajatashatru | First capital; ringed by five hills, walled – impregnable
  [25:0:1.1] Pataliputra (fort) | Ajatashatru | Fortified the village Pataligrama and built the city as a base against the Vajjis
  [25:0:1.2] Pataliputra (capital) | Udayin | Shifted the capital from Rajgriha to Pataliputra
  [25:0:1.3] Vaishali | Shishunaga | Capital moved there temporarily
  [25:0:1.4] Pataliputra again | Kalashoka | Capital moved back; it stayed the capital of the Mauryas and Guptas
[25:0:2] - **First / earliest / initial capital:** **Girivraja (Rajgriha, Rajgir)** – asked 6 times (State PSC ×3, BPSC 2004, NDA 2001). Not Pataliputra, Vaishali, Champa (capital of **Anga**) or Varanasi.
[25:0:3] - **⚠ Option missing:** a State PSC paper asked the first capital with only Pataliputra, Vaishali, Champa and Anga – none is right; the answer is **Rajgriha**.
[25:0:4] - **Vaishali:** capital of the **Lichchhavi (Vajji) republic**, named after King **Vishal**; near **Mahavira's birthplace**; venue of the **Second** (not First) Buddhist Council.
[25:0:5] - **Not a Magadhan capital:** **Kaushambi** – capital of **Vatsa** (CGPSC 2011).
[25:0:6] # Who founded Pataliputra
[25:0:7] - **Ajatashatru** fortified Pataligrama and **built the city of Pataliputra** – the answer when Udayin is not offered (APPSC G1 2002 and G1 PYQ: Ajatashatru; Dhanyakataka, Nalanda, Lumbini are distractors).
[25:0:8] - **Udayin** made it the **capital**; Jain texts call him the **founder of Pataliputra** – the answer when Ajatashatru is not offered ("who founded Pataliputra": Udayin, not Ashoka, Bimbisara, Mahapadma).
[25:0:9] - **⚠ Disputed:** with both offered, most books and keys give **Ajatashatru** for the city and **Udayin** for the capital.
[25:0:10] - **"First chose Pataliputra as capital":** **Udayin** (not Ajatashatru, Kalashoka or Kanishka).
[25:0:11] # Pataliputra – site and remains
[25:0:12] - **Site:** modern **Patna**, at the **confluence of the Ganga and the Son**; surrounded by rivers – a **water-fort (jaladurga)**.
[25:0:13] - **Excavated remains:** **Kumrahar** (Mauryan pillared hall) and **Bulandibagh** (wooden palisade) – both = Pataliputra, not Vaishali, Kapilavastu, Shravasti or Varanasi.
[25:0:14] - **Decline:** Hiuen-Tsang (7th c. CE) found it in ruins.
[25:0:15] # Rajgir today
[25:0:16] - **Vishwa Shanti Stupa:** the World Peace Pagoda on **Ratnagiri hill, Rajgir** – billed as the highest in the world (BPSC 2008).
[25:0:17] - **Rajgriha** was also the place of **Mahavira's first sermon** and of the **First Buddhist Council** (Saptaparni cave).
[25:0:18] > Exam angle: "first capital" → **Rajgriha**; "built Pataliputra / Pataligrama fort" → **Ajatashatru**; "made it the capital" → **Udayin**; Kumrahar, Bulandibagh → **Pataliputra**.
[25:0:19] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.100-101, p.103; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 2 p.40-41; app notes 1:25 (sub 0, 6); nalanda.nic.in (Vishwa Shanti Stupa)
## SUB 1 | Haryankas – Bimbisara, Ajatashatru, Udayin
[25:1:0] # Bimbisara (c. 545–493 BCE)
[25:1:1] - **Founder of the Haryanka dynasty** (NextGen Rocket; APPSC; SSC CGL 2019) – PMF adds that many scholars give the founding to his grandfather, but exams key **Bimbisara**. Brihadratha belongs to the earlier legendary line.
[25:1:2] - **Real founder of the Magadhan empire**; also called **Seniya / Shrenika** (WBCS 2017).
[25:1:3] - **Contemporary of the Buddha** and of Mahavira (APPSC GS 2018; FRO 2020; Sachivalayam).
[25:1:4]   - **⚠ Disputed:** Ajatashatru was also a contemporary – the Buddha died in his reign – but keys give **Bimbisara** when both are offered.
[25:1:5] - **Conquest:** defeated Brahmadatta of **Anga** and put **Kunika (Ajatashatru)** as viceroy at **Champa**.
[25:1:6] - **Diplomacy:** friendship with **Pradyota of Avanti**; when Pradyota had jaundice, Bimbisara sent his royal physician **Jivaka** to Ujjain.
[25:1:7] - **Jivaka:** physician of Bimbisara's court (UP UDA 2006; State PSC); son of the Rajgriha courtesan **Salavati** (MPPSC 2009) – not Amrapali (Vaishali).
[25:1:8] TABLE head: Queen | Clan / kingdom | Note
  [25:1:8.0] Kosaladevi (Mahakosala) | Kosala, sister of Prasenajit | Brought Kashi as dowry
  [25:1:8.1] Chellana | Lichchhavi of Vaishali | Mother of Ajatashatru (not Udayin)
  [25:1:8.2] Khema | Madra (Punjab) | –
[25:1:9] - **Death:** imprisoned and starved to death by his son **Ajatashatru**.
[25:1:10] # Ajatashatru (c. 493–462 BCE)
[25:1:11] - **Parricide:** killed his father Bimbisara (UPPCS 2011) – Jain name **Kunika**, "Pitruhanta"; he was in turn **killed by his son Udayin** (UPPCS 2007; UPPSC 2007).
[25:1:12] - **Patricide chain (Buddhist texts):** **Bimbisara → Ajatashatru → Udayin**.
[25:1:13] - **Kosala:** war with **Prasenajit** over Kashi; Prasenajit gave his daughter **Vajira** with Kashi as dowry; later annexed Kosala.
[25:1:14] - **Vajji:** annexed after a **16-year** war; minister **Vassakara** split the Lichchhavi chiefs.
[25:1:15] - **War engines:** **mahashilakantaka** (stone-throwing catapult) and **rathamusala** (chariot fitted with a mace).
[25:1:16] - **Buddhism:** met the Buddha (Bharhut relief); hosted the **First Buddhist Council** at Rajgriha.
[25:1:17] # Udayin (c. 462–444 BCE)
[25:1:18] - **Shifted the capital to Pataliputra**; a devout Jain in Jain tradition. Not to be confused with **Udayana of Vatsa**.
[25:1:19] - Probably killed at the urging of **Palaka of Avanti**; his weak successors ended with **Nagadasaka**.
[25:1:20] # Contemporaries
[25:1:21] - **Milinda (Menander)**, the 2nd-century-BCE Indo-Greek, was **not** a contemporary of Bimbisara, the Buddha and **Prasenajit (Kosala)** (IAS 2005).
[25:1:22] > Exam angle: "founder of Haryanka" → **Bimbisara**; "killed his father and was killed by his son" → **Ajatashatru**; "Jivaka" → **Bimbisara's court**.
[25:1:23] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.99-101; NextGen Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.29-30; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 2 p.40; britannica.com/biography/Bimbisara; app notes 1:25 (sub 3, 8)
## SUB 2 | Shishunagas and Nandas
[25:2:0] # Shishunaga dynasty (c. 413–345 BCE)
[25:2:1] - **Shishunaga:** a viceroy at Banaras / amatya **chosen by the people** after Udayin's weak successors; moved the capital to **Vaishali**.
[25:2:2] - **Malwa:** Shishunaga **destroyed Avanti** (capital **Ujjayini**) and annexed Avanti and Vatsa – the expansion over Malwa (UP Lower 2008 ×2).
[25:2:3] - **Kalashoka:** moved the capital **back to Pataliputra**; **Second Buddhist Council** at Vaishali (383 BCE).
[25:2:4] - **End:** the last Shishunaga, **Mahanandin**, was killed by **Mahapadma Nanda**.
[25:2:5] # Conquests in order
[25:2:6] TABLE head: Ruler | Annexed
  [25:2:6.0] Bimbisara | Anga
  [25:2:6.1] Ajatashatru | Kosala, Vajji
  [25:2:6.2] Shishunaga | Avanti, Vatsa
  [25:2:6.3] Mahapadma Nanda | Kalinga, Kshatriya kingdoms of the north
[25:2:7] # Nanda dynasty (c. 345–321 BCE)
[25:2:8] - **Sequence:** Haryanka → **Shishunaga → Nanda → Maurya** (State PSC; BPSC 2005).
[25:2:9] - **Mahapadma Nanda:** founder; **first non-Kshatriya dynasty**; **first empire-builder** of India; titles **Ekarat** (sole sovereign) and **Sarvakshatrantaka** (destroyer of Kshatriyas) → hence **Aparoparashurama**, "a second Parashurama" (UPUDA 2010).
[25:2:10] - **Hathigumpha inscription** of Kharavela: a **Nanda king dug a canal in Kalinga** and carried off a Jina image (UPPCS 1999).
[25:2:11] - **Dhana Nanda:** **last Nanda** (RRB 2001); Greek **Agrammes / Xandrames**; ruled at **Alexander's invasion** (326 BCE) – the dynasty ruling North India then was the **Nanda** (UPSC 2000).
[25:2:12] - **Fall:** Chandragupta Maurya, with Chanakya, overthrew Dhana Nanda in **c. 321 BCE**.
[25:2:13] - **Army (Greek accounts):** about 200,000 infantry, 60,000 cavalry, 3,000–6,000 elephants.
[25:2:14] > Exam angle: "after the Shishunagas" → **Nandas**; "after the Nandas" → **Mauryas**; "Malwa added" → **Shishunaga**; "Aparoparashurama" → **Mahapadma Nanda**.
[25:2:15] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.101-102, p.105-106; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 2 p.40-41; app notes 1:25 (sub 4, 5)
## SUB 3 | Causes of Magadhan Supremacy
[25:3:0] - **Most powerful and richest Mahajanapada** (6th–4th c. BCE); it became the base of the **Mauryan Empire**. Puranas: the first dynasty was the **Brihadratha** (Jarasandha ruled from **Girivraj**).
[25:3:1] TABLE head: Factor | Effect
  [25:3:1.0] Iron mines nearby (Jharkhand) | Weapons and tools; forest clearing
  [25:3:1.1] Alluvial soil, ample rainfall | Agricultural surplus, taxes
  [25:3:1.2] Ganga and Son (navigable) | Cheap transport and trade
  [25:3:1.3] Elephants from the eastern forests | First large-scale use of war elephants
  [25:3:1.4] Naturally fortified capitals | Rajgriha (five hills), Pataliputra (water-fort)
  [25:3:1.5] Unorthodox society | Little Vedic hold; ambitious rulers and ministers
[25:3:2] - **⚠ Not a cause:** control of western sea ports, gold mines, superior cavalry or a republican system.
[25:3:3] - **Buddhist councils linked to Magadhan kings:** First – **Ajatashatru** (Rajgriha); Second – **Kalashoka** (Vaishali); Third – **Ashoka** (Pataliputra).
[25:3:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.103-104; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 1 p.67; app notes 1:25 (sub 0, 2, 7)

=== NOTES 1:27 | Jain Councils, Digambara–svetambara Split, Jain Literature, Spread and Royal Patrons
## SUB 0 | Jain Councils and the Canon
[27:0:0] # The two councils
[27:0:1] TABLE head: Council | Place, date | President | Outcome
  [27:0:1.0] First | Pataliputra, c. 300 BCE (Chandragupta Maurya's reign) | Sthulabhadra | Teachings arranged into 12 Angas; boycotted by Bhadrabahu's returning monks → first split
  [27:0:1.1] Second | Vallabhi (Valabhi), Gujarat, 512 CE (Maitraka patronage) | Devardhi Kshamashramana | Canon finally compiled and written down in Ardhamagadhi; Upangas added; 12th Anga lost
[27:0:2] - **First council:** **Pataliputra** (UKPSC 2021; UPPCS 2004) – not Vaishali, Mathura, Ujjain, Vallabhi, Abu or Pava.
[27:0:3] - **Svetambara Agama finally edited:** **Valabhi (Balabhi)** (UPPCS 2008).
[27:0:4] - **CGPSC 2020:** "Svetambara canon includes 12 Angas" ✓; "Angas compiled at Vallabhi" ✗ (compiled at Pataliputra; Vallabhi only recompiled them) → **I true, II false**.
[27:0:5] - **Andhra:** a **Jain conference at Venkatathatipuri** (Satavahana era), presided over by **Arhabali** – not one of the two councils.
[27:0:6] # The canon
[27:0:7] TABLE head: Term | Fact
  [27:0:7.0] Agamas / Siddhanta | Sacred books of the Jains (APPSC G2 2011), compiled by the Ganadharas
  [27:0:7.1] 14 Purvas | Earliest scriptures, preached by all Tirthankaras; held in the 12th Anga (Drishtivada); now lost
  [27:0:7.2] 12 Angas | Main body of the canon – Acharanga, Sutrakritanga, Bhagavati …
  [27:0:7.3] Ang-bahya | 12 Upangas, 10 Prakirnas, 6 Chhedasutras, 4 Mulasutras
  [27:0:7.4] Language | Ardhamagadhi Prakrit (UPPSC 2006) – not Pali (Buddhist) or Sanskrit
[27:0:8] - **Earliest holy book:** the **Fourteen Purvas** (State PSC) – not the 12 Angas or Upangas.
[27:0:9] - **Acharanga Sutra:** code of conduct for monks; **Bhagavati Sutra:** doctrines.
[27:0:10] - **Digambaras** hold that the Purvas and original Angas were **all lost** and reject the Svetambara canon; their chief texts are the Satkhandagama and Kasaya-pahuda.
[27:0:11] - **Not Jain:** **Therigatha** – verses of Buddhist nuns in the Pali Khuddaka Nikaya (UPSC 1996); Acharanga, Sutrakritanga and Brihatkalpa are early Jain texts.
[27:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 1 p.46, p.48; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.53, p.77-78, p.83; app notes 1:27 (sub 0, 2)
## SUB 1 | Jain Monuments and Pilgrim Sites
[27:1:0] TABLE head: Site | State | Fact
  [27:1:0.0] Shravanabelagola – Gommateshwara (Bahubali) | Karnataka | 57-ft monolith raised c. 981 CE by Chamundaraya, minister of Western Ganga Rachamalla IV (UP Lower 2009 ×2; IAS 1994)
  [27:1:0.1] Dilwara temples, Mount Abu | Rajasthan | Built of marble (UPPCS 2010); Vimala Shah (Solanki minister), 1031
  [27:1:0.2] Udayagiri–Khandagiri | Odisha | Rock-cut caves of Kharavela
  [27:1:0.3] Prabhasgiri (Pabhosa) | Uttar Pradesh, near Kaushambi | Jain site, linked with the 6th Tirthankara Padmaprabha (UPPCS 2008)
  [27:1:0.4] Kaushambi | Uttar Pradesh | Sacred to both Buddhists and Jains – the Buddha's Ghoshitarama; birthplace of Padmaprabha (UPUDA 2010; RAS 2007)
  [27:1:0.5] Sammed Shikhar | Jharkhand (Parasnath hill) | Nirvana of Parshvanatha and 19 other Tirthankaras
[27:1:1] - **Mahamastakabhisheka:** the anointing of **Bahubali (Gommateshwara)** every **12 years** at Shravanabelagola (UPSC 2009 ×2) – not the Buddha, Mahavira or Nataraja. The 88th was held in **February 2018**.
[27:1:2] - **Odd one out (APPSC JL 2003):** Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Ajanta = Buddhist; **Gomateshwara** = Jain.
[27:1:3] - **⚠ Trap:** Bahubali, son of Rishabhadeva, is **not** a Tirthankara; Sarnath and Kushinagar are Buddhist only.
[27:1:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.83; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 3 (Gommateswara table); jainheritagecentres.com (Kaushambi); app notes 1:27 (sub 6)
## SUB 2 | Spread of Jainism and Royal Patrons
[27:2:0] # Spread
[27:2:1] - **South:** during a **12-year famine** in Magadha (Chandragupta Maurya's reign) **Bhadrabahu** led monks with Chandragupta to **Shravanabelagola** – he is credited with taking Jainism south (CDS 2008), not Sthulabhadra, Sudharma or Indrabhuti.
[27:2:2] - **Kalinga:** under **Kharavela** (c. 1st century BCE); his **Hathigumpha** inscription records Jain patronage.
[27:2:3] - **Early Christian era centres:** **Mathura and Ujjain**.
[27:2:4]   - **APPSC G1 2004:** the centre that grew under **Vajramuni** (1st–2nd c. CE) is keyed **Kausali** (official key; not confirmed in the notes).
[27:2:5] - **Later:** Karnataka (Gangas, Kadambas, Rashtrakutas), Tamil country, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Malwa; it survives in **Gujarat, Rajasthan, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu**, mainly among **traders**.
[27:2:6] - **UPSC 2004:** Kharavela's patronage (1st c. BCE) ✓; "spread south under Sthulabhadra" ✗; "Bhadrabahu's followers = Svetambaras" ✗; "early Jains worshipped images, unlike Buddhists" ✗ (initially neither worshipped images).
[27:2:7] # Royal patrons
[27:2:8] TABLE head: Patron | Dynasty | Jain link
  [27:2:8.0] Udayin | Haryanka | Devout Jain (Jain tradition)
  [27:2:8.1] Chandragupta Maurya | Maurya | Disciple of Bhadrabahu; sallekhana at Shravanabelagola
  [27:2:8.2] Samprati | Maurya, Ashoka's grandson | "Ashoka of Jainism"
  [27:2:8.3] Kharavela | Chedi (Mahameghavahana), Kalinga | Ardent Jain (APPSC G2 Mains 2025; CDS 2006)
  [27:2:8.4] Simuka (Srimukha) | Satavahana | First Satavahana Jain patron; 52 army chiefs built 52 temples (Kalpa Pradeepa)
  [27:2:8.5] Amoghavarsha I | Rashtrakuta | Patron of Jinasena
  [27:2:8.6] Indra III | Rashtrakuta | Danavulapadu
  [27:2:8.7] Chamundaraya | Minister of Western Ganga Rachamalla IV | Gommateshwara statue
  [27:2:8.8] Kumarapala | Chalukya (Solanki) of Gujarat | Patron of Hemachandra
[27:2:9] - **Kharavela's dynasty:** **Chedi** (UPPCS 2015) – Kalinga was his kingdom, not his dynasty.
[27:2:10] - **Not Jain patrons:** Pulakeshin II (Brahmanical); Bimbisara is claimed by both Jains and Buddhists.
[27:2:11] - **Samrat Samprati Museum:** inaugurated by the PM at **Koba Tirth, Gandhinagar (Gujarat)** on **31 March 2026** (Mahavir Jayanti).
[27:2:12] - **Migration route:** Magadha → **Rayalaseema (Kurnool, Anantapur)** → Shravanabelagola.
[27:2:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 1 p.47-48; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.73; NextGen Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.31; pmindia.gov.in (Samrat Samprati Museum, 31 Mar 2026); app notes 1:27 (sub 4, 5)
## SUB 3 | Jainism in Andhra and Telangana
[27:3:0] # Royal patronage and centres
[27:3:1] - **Early Kakatiyas** patronised **Jainism** (APPSC; Junior Asst) before turning to Shaivism; Andhra Jainism was mainly **Digambara** → "Jainism of the Digambara sect". Source: **Siddeshwara Charitra**.
[27:3:2] - **Potla Cheruvu (Patancheru)** was a popular **Jain** centre in the **Eastern Chalukya** period (APPSC G2 2017 ×2).
[27:3:3] - **Jain kshetras of Telangana:** Bodhan, Vemulawada, Potlacheruvu, Anmakonda (Hanamkonda), Kolanupaka.
[27:3:4] TABLE head: Centre | Note
  [27:3:4.0] Nedumba Vasati, Bejawada | Built by Ayyana Mahadevi, wife of Eastern Chalukya Vishnuvardhana
  [27:3:4.1] Kathikabharana Jinalaya, Dharmavaram | Durgaraja
  [27:3:4.2] Ramatirtham (Vizianagaram) | Hill centre; Ugradityacharya wrote Kalyanakaraka
  [27:3:4.3] Kadalalaya Basadi | Mailama, wife of Kakatiya minister Betana (1117 CE)
  [27:3:4.4] Aryavatam, Kolanupaka, Munugodu | Other Jain centres
[27:3:5] - Under the Eastern Chalukyas, **Shudras** took up Jainism for social advancement; a Jain monk fled **Rajaraja Narendra's** persecution to Hanamkonda (**Orugallu Kaifiyat**).
[27:3:6] - **Vijayanagara:** **Devaraya II** built a Jinalaya in the Pan Supari Bazar.
[27:3:7] - Jainism held rocky **Rayalaseema**; **Buddhism** held the Krishna–Godavari delta.
[27:3:8] # Decline
[27:3:9] - **Serious blow:** the **Virashaiva (Lingayat)** movement (APPSC G1) – Kalamukhas and Vira Shaivas persecuted Jains (Brahmaya at Govur and Potlacheru; **Ganapatideva** at Anmakonda).
[27:3:10] - **Karnataka:** **Basavanna's** 12th-century Lingayat movement; **Tamil country:** the **Alvars and Nayanars**.
[27:3:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History previous papers p.8, p.46; NextGen AP History Part 11 p.11-12; NextGen Satavahanas p.27; app notes 1:27 (sub 7)
## SUB 4 | Jain Literature, Authors and Language
[27:4:0] TABLE head: Work | Author / note
  [27:4:0.0] Jinendra Kalyanabhyudayamu | Appayacharya, in Kakatiya Prataparudra's time (APPSC ×2) – not Pampa
  [27:4:0.1] Parishishtaparvan (Sthaviravali Charitra) | Hemachandra, 12th c. – famine story and early Jain teachers
  [27:4:0.2] Trishashtilakshana Mahapurana | Jain (Jinasena–Gunabhadra; Kannada Chavundaraya Purana by Chamundaraya)
  [27:4:0.3] Kalpasutra | Bhadrabahu
  [27:4:0.4] Samayasara, Pravachanasara | Kundakundacharya (Saraswati gachcha at Konakondla)
  [27:4:0.5] Tattvartha Sutra | Umasvati – accepted by both sects
  [27:4:0.6] Adipurana (Mahapurana) | Jinasena
  [27:4:0.7] Kalyanakaraka (medicine) | Ugradityacharya
  [27:4:0.8] Yasastilaka Champu | Somadeva Suri
[27:4:1] - **UPSC 2022 ×2:** Jain texts = **Parishishtaparvan and Trishashtilakshana Mahapurana** (2 and 4 only); **Nettipakarana and Avadanashataka are Buddhist**.
[27:4:2] # Language
[27:4:3] - **Early Jains discarded Sanskrit** and preached in **Prakrit**; the Agamas are in **Ardhamagadhi**.
[27:4:4] - **Apabhramsha:** the Jains composed its **earliest important works** and its **first grammar** – so "they never used Apabhramsa for the earliest important works" is the **incorrect** statement (APPSC G1).
[27:4:5] - Jain writers enriched **Prakrit, Apabhramsa, Kannada and Telugu**.
[27:4:6] # Social base and decline
[27:4:7] - **Traders and merchants** formed the social base (war and agriculture were barred); stressed **action / conduct** over birth.
[27:4:8] - **Decline:** lack of **missionary zeal**, loss of royal patronage, sectarian split, severe austerity, Bhakti revival.
[27:4:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.78-79, p.83-84; app notes 1:27 (sub 3, 8)
## SUB 5 | Digambara–Svetambara Split and Sub-sects
[27:5:0] # The split
[27:5:1] - **Story:** after the 12-year famine, **Bhadrabahu's** monks returned from the south, still naked and strict; those who stayed under **Sthulabhadra** wore **white** → **Digambaras** (sky-clad) and **Svetambaras** (white-clad), c. 300 BCE.
[27:5:2] - **First founder of the Svetambara creed:** **Sthulabhadra** (RAS 1999) – Bhadrabahu led the Digambaras.
[27:5:3] TABLE head: Aspect | Digambara | Svetambara
  [27:5:3.0] Leader | Bhadrabahu | Sthulabhadra
  [27:5:3.1] Dress | Sky-clad monks | White robes
  [27:5:3.2] Women | Must be reborn as men for moksha | Can attain liberation
  [27:5:3.3] Mahavira | Never married | Married Yashoda
  [27:5:3.4] Monk's items | Broom and water pot | 14 items incl. clothes
  [27:5:3.5] Canon | Original Angas lost | Keep the 12 Angas
[27:5:4] # Sub-sects
[27:5:5] TABLE head: Sub-sect | Branch | Feature
  [27:5:5.0] Sthanakvasi | Svetambara | Non-idolatrous, prayer halls (sthanakas); Lonka Shah – a Jain sect (UPSC 2018)
  [27:5:5.1] Terapanthi | Svetambara (from the Sthanakvasis) | Acharya Bhikshu, 18th c.
  [27:5:5.2] Murtipujaka | Svetambara | Idol-worshipping original Svetambaras
  [27:5:5.3] Yapaniya | Grew from the Digambaras | Bridge sect; some Svetambara views; nude images; active in Karnataka and Andhra – a Jain sect (UPPCS 2010)
  [27:5:5.4] Bisapantha, Terapantha, Taranapantha | Digambara | Taranapanthis worship books, not idols
[27:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 1 p.48-49; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.73-76; app notes 1:27 (sub 1)
