## SUB 0 | Places of the Buddha's Life – Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar
[28:0:0] TABLE head: Event | Place | Today / marker
  [28:0:0.0] Birth | Lumbini grove (near Kapilavastu) | Rumindei / Rummindei, Nepal; Ashoka's inscribed pillar records "here the Buddha Shakyamuni was born"
  [28:0:0.1] Great Renunciation | Kapilavastu | –
  [28:0:0.2] Enlightenment | Uruvela = Bodh Gaya, under the Bodhi (pipal) tree, on the Niranjana (Lilajan) | Bihar; Mahabodhi Temple
  [28:0:0.3] First sermon | Deer Park (Mrigadava), Sarnath = Rishipatana, near Varanasi | UP; Ashoka's Lion Capital (State Emblem)
  [28:0:0.4] Mahaparinirvana (death) | Kusinara / Kushinagar (Kasia), capital of the Mallas | Deoria–Kushinagar district, UP; Mahaparinirvana Temple
[28:0:1] - **Match (APPSC ASO, CDS 2011):** birth – **Lumbini**, enlightenment – **Bodh Gaya**, first sermon – **Sarnath**, death – **Kushinagar**; Rajgriha is the spare distractor.
[28:0:2] - **Kushinagar:** the **Malla republic**, not the Lichchhavis or Sakyas; the Buddha died there at **80** under sal trees.
[28:0:3] - **Mahaparinirvana Temple, Kushinagar:** reclining dying Buddha of **Chunar sandstone**, unearthed **1876–77**.
[28:0:4] - **Niranjana river:** only **Bodh Gaya** of the sacred places stands on it (not Kushinagar, Lumbini, Rishipatana).
[28:0:5] - **Rummindei pillar** marks the **birth** (Ashoka visited in his 20th regnal year); the king whose inscription names Lumbini = **Ashoka**.
[28:0:6] - **"Birthplace of Buddhism":** APPSC G2 2011 calls **Sarnath** the "birthplace of Buddhism" – the **Dharma** and **Sangha** began there with the first sermon; Lumbini is only the Buddha's birthplace.
[28:0:7] - **Ashtamahasthanas** (eight great sites): **7 in India**, Lumbini (Nepal) the eighth.
[28:0:8] # Bodh Gaya facts
[28:0:9] - **Mahabodhi Temple:** UNESCO World Heritage Site since **2002**.
[28:0:10] - Original Bodhi tree destroyed by **Shashanka** (7th c., per **Hiuen Tsang**; earlier Pushyamitra Sunga by legend); the present tree was planted under **Alexander Cunningham** (1881) and is called the **fifth generation** (Bihar Tourism) – some count it the sixth, so BPSC dropped the question.
[28:0:11] - **Maha Bodhi Society (1891):** **Anagarika Dharmapala**, to restore Bodh Gaya to Buddhists.
[28:0:12] > Lumbini = birth; Bodh Gaya = enlightenment (Niranjana); Sarnath = first sermon; Kushinagar = death (Mallas).
[28:0:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.63; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.42-43; PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.73-74; old app notes row 28 (sub 2)
## SUB 1 | Core Teachings – Nirvana, Karma, Anatta, Middle Path
[28:1:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [28:1:0.0] Nirvana (nibbana) | Main goal; "extinction of the flame of desire"; end of suffering and of rebirth
  [28:1:0.1] Middle Path (Madhyama Marga) | Avoids both self-indulgence and self-mortification – the path to nirvana, not the goal
  [28:1:0.2] Anicca | Impermanence – "the world is unstable and transient"
  [28:1:0.3] Anatta / Anatmavada | No permanent self (soul) – a Buddhist doctrine, not Sankhya, Vedanta or Jain
  [28:1:0.4] Dukkha | Suffering
  [28:1:0.5] Karma | Intention-based morality; present state from past actions; rebirth till nirvana
  [28:1:0.6] Raft simile | Teaching as a raft – upaya (skilful means), not dogma
[28:1:1] - **Three marks:** Anicca, Anatta, Dukkha.
[28:1:2] - **Beliefs (UPPSC 1992):** karma ✓, rebirth ✓, nirvana ✓; **God neither affirmed nor denied** – belief in God ✗; belief in God not needed for the Sangha.
[28:1:3] - **Rejected Vedic authority**, animal sacrifice and ritual; stressed **purity of conduct / a moral life** over philosophical problems (the seed of later Buddhist philosophy lies in his own teachings – CGPSC 2023: both true).
[28:1:4] - **Caste (UPPSC 1998):** Buddhism **did not abolish caste and class** as social facts, **challenged the Brahmins' top rank** (Kshatriyas listed first), and texts call some **jatis and crafts (hina-sippa) low** – exam key: all three true (PMF instead says the Buddha condemned varna).
[28:1:5] - **Statements on the Buddha:** born in (the Sakya state of) **Kapilavastu** – strictly at Lumbini near it; enlightened at **Bodh Gaya**; **discarded the Vedic religion**; preached the **noble truths** – key: all four.
[28:1:6] > Nirvana = goal; Middle Path = means; Anatta = no soul; God neither affirmed nor denied.
[28:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.65-66; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.45-46; old app notes row 28 (sub 6)
## SUB 2 | Life Story – Dates, Renunciation, Epithets and Texts
[28:2:0] - **Born 563 BC** (traditional; PMF "566–563 BCE"), Vaishakha Purnima; **died 483 BCE** at 80 (NextGen: c. 486 BC).
[28:2:1] - **Four sights:** old man, sick man, corpse, ascetic → **Mahabhinishkramana** (Great Renunciation = **departure from home**) at **29**, with charioteer **Channa** and horse **Kanthaka**.
[28:2:2] - **Six years** of austerities with **five ascetics**; tempted by **Mara**; **enlightenment at 35** on the 49th day of meditation.
[28:2:3] - **Last words:** **"appamadena sampadetha"** – "all composite things decay; **strive diligently**".
[28:2:4] # Epithets
[28:2:5] TABLE head: Epithet | Belongs to
  [28:2:5.0] Buddha (Awakened), Tathagata ("thus-gone"), Shakyamuni (sage of the Shakyas), Mahamuni | Gautama Buddha
  [28:2:5.1] "Light of Asia" | Buddha – Edwin Arnold's poem (1879, subtitle "The Great Renunciation"), based on the Lalitavistara
  [28:2:5.2] Jina, Kevalin, Nigantha Nataputta, Nayaputta | Mahavira
  [28:2:5.3] Prachhanna Buddha ("crypto-Buddhist") | Shankaracharya, not the Buddha
[28:2:6] - **UPSC 2024:** Shakyamuni ✓, Tathagata ✓, Nayaputta ✗ → "2 and 3 only".
[28:2:7] # Texts on his life
[28:2:8] - **Buddhacharita** (Ashvaghosha, Sanskrit) = the **life history of the Buddha**; **Jatakas** = stories of his **previous births** (in the Sutta Pitaka); **Tripitakas** = the canon.
[28:2:9] > 29 – 35 – 80 = Renunciation – Enlightenment – Parinirvana.
[28:2:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.63, p.66; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 2 p.21 (Ashvaghosha); Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.40 (Buddhacharita – life of Buddha); PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.42-44; old app notes row 28 (sub 1, 5)
## SUB 3 | Family, Teachers and Disciples
[28:3:0] TABLE head: Relation | Person
  [28:3:0.0] Name / clan | Siddhartha Gautama, Sakya Kshatriya clan of Kapilavastu
  [28:3:0.1] Father | Suddhodana, chief of the Sakyas
  [28:3:0.2] Mother | Maya (Mahamaya), a Koliya princess – died days after his birth
  [28:3:0.3] Foster-mother | Mahapajapati (Prajapati) Gotami
  [28:3:0.4] Wife / son | Yashodhara / Rahula
  [28:3:0.5] Charioteer, horse | Channa (Chhandaka), Kanthaka
  [28:3:0.6] Cousin | Devadatta – wanted to lead the Sangha in the Buddha's lifetime
  [28:3:0.7] Teachers | Alara Kalama (meditation), Uddaka Ramaputta
[28:3:1] - **Not in the Buddha's life (CDS 2013):** **Goshala Maskariputra (Makkhali Gosala)** – the **Ajivika** leader; Kanthaka, Channa, Alara Kalama are.
[28:3:2] # Disciples
[28:3:3] TABLE head: Person | Role
  [28:3:3.0] Mahakassapa | Presided over the First Council (Saptaparni Cave, Rajagriha, under Ajatashatru)
  [28:3:3.1] Ananda | Personal attendant; recited the Sutta; got women admitted
  [28:3:3.2] Upali | Recited the Vinaya
  [28:3:3.3] Sariputta, Mahamoggallana | Chief disciples; relics at Sanchi
  [28:3:3.4] Subhadda | Last convert – ordained at Kushinagar on the Buddha's last night
  [28:3:3.5] Tapassu, Bhallika | First lay disciples (merchants)
[28:3:4] - **No successor:** the Buddha **nominated nobody** (not Ananda, Mahakassapa or Upali) – the **Dhamma and Vinaya** were to be the teacher.
[28:3:5] - **Current (May–June 2026):** relics of **Sariputta and Mahamoggallana** taken from **Sanchi to Mongolia** (Gandan monastery, Ulaanbaatar) for Buddha Purnima by the Ministry of Culture, then returned.
[28:3:6] > Maya = mother (Koliya); Mahapajapati = foster-mother; Devadatta = rival cousin; Subhadda = last convert.
[28:3:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.63; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.42; PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.73; newsonair.gov.in (1 June 2026, relics in Mongolia); old app notes row 28 (sub 0, 10)
## SUB 4 | Sangha, Triratna and Monastic Terms
[28:4:0] - **Triratna** (three jewels / refuges) = **Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha** – not the Tripitaka, not Sheel-Samadhi-Sangha; not Trivarga or Trimurti.
[28:4:1] - **Match (APPSC G2 Mains 2025):** Jainism – **Triratna**; Buddhism – **Ashtanga Margam**; Saivism – **Linga**; Animism – **Nature worship**.
[28:4:2] - **Ajivika – Niyati; Charvaka – materialism; Jainism – Anekantavada; Buddhism – Ashtangika Marga.**
[28:4:3] # Admission
[28:4:4] - Open to all **above 15**, **caste no bar**; barred: **criminals, lepers, those with infectious diseases**; slaves, debtors, children needed permission.
[28:4:5] - **Women** admitted at **Vaishali** at the request of **Ananda** and **Mahapajapati Gotami** – the **first nun** (not Shravasti).
[28:4:6] - **Sanghamitta** took the Bhikkhuni Sangha to **Sri Lanka**; it lasted till the **Chola invasion of 1017 AD**.
[28:4:7] # Terms
[28:4:8] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [28:4:8.0] Bhikkhu / Bhikkhuni | Monk / nun living on alms
  [28:4:8.1] Pravrajya | Going forth (head shaved, robes)
  [28:4:8.2] Upasampada | Full ordination
  [28:4:8.3] Uposatha | Fortnightly confession and recitation of rules
  [28:4:8.4] Vassa | 3-month rainy-season retreat
  [28:4:8.5] Pavarana | Confession of offences by monks at the end of the Vassa (UPSC 2002)
  [28:4:8.6] Vihara / Chaitya / Stupa | Monks' residence / prayer hall / relic mound
  [28:4:8.7] Upasaka / Upasika | Lay follower
  [28:4:8.8] Donors | Anathapindika – Jetavana; Vishakha – Pubbarama; Bimbisara – Venuvana
[28:4:9] - **AP angle:** sage **Bavari's** disciples from the **Godavari** region brought Buddhism to **Andhra**.
[28:4:10] > Triratna = Buddha-Dhamma-Sangha; Pavarana = end-of-Vassa confession; nuns admitted at Vaishali.
[28:4:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.67; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.47-49; PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.77; old app notes row 28 (sub 10)
## SUB 5 | First Sermon – Dhammachakkappavattana
[28:5:0] - **Name:** **Dhammachakra Pravartana / Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta** = "setting in motion the **Wheel of Dharma**" – the **first sermon at Sarnath** (not his "sight", norms or rituals).
[28:5:1] - **Theme:** the **Four Noble Truths** and the **Eightfold Path** – so the Eightfold Path "forms the theme of" the **Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta** (UPSC 1998), not the Dipavamsa, Divyavadana or Mahaparinibbana Sutta.
[28:5:2]   - **Mahaparinibbana Sutta** = his last journey and death; **Brahmajala Sutta** = first sutta of the Digha Nikaya.
[28:5:3] - **Audience:** the **five former companions** – **Kondanna (Kaundinya), Bhaddiya, Vappa, Mahanama, Assaji (Ashvajit)** – who became **arhats**.
[28:5:4] - **Vesak / Buddha Purnima** (Vaisakha full moon) marks **birth, enlightenment and Mahaparinirvana** – **not the first sermon**.
[28:5:5] > Dhammachakra = first sermon = Sarnath = Four Truths + Eightfold Path.
[28:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.63; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.43; PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.74; old app notes row 28 (sub 3)
## SUB 6 | Other Sites – Shravasti, Vaishali, Rajgir and the Kingdoms
[28:6:0] TABLE head: Place | Association
  [28:6:0.0] Shravasti (Kosala capital) | Most sermons; Jetavana Vihara (Anathapindika); Twin Miracle
  [28:6:0.1] Vaishali (Lichchhavis) | Last rainy season (at Beluva, a suburb); women admitted to the Sangha; monkey's honey offering; Second Council
  [28:6:0.2] Rajagriha (Rajgir) | Taming of the elephant Nalagiri; Venuvana; First Council
  [28:6:0.3] Sankasya | Descent from the Trayastrimsa heaven
  [28:6:0.4] Pava | Fell ill after Sukaramaddava offered by Chunda
[28:6:1] - **Council venues:** **Rajgir, Vaishali, Pataliputra, Kashmir** – not Sarnath, Bodh Gaya or Kushinagar.
[28:6:2] - **Pairs (UPPSC 2004):** Lothal – dockyard ✓, Sarnath – first sermon ✓, Nalanda – seat of Buddhist learning ✓; **Rajgir – Lion Capital ✗** (the Lion Capital is at **Sarnath**).
[28:6:3] # Kingdoms and royal followers
[28:6:4] - **Magadha:** **Bimbisara, Ajatashatru**; **Kosala:** **Prasenjit** (a disciple with his family); **Vatsa / Kausambi:** **Udayana**.
[28:6:5] - **UPSC 2015 – kingdoms associated with the Buddha's life:** **Kosala and Magadha** (official key); PMF also counts **Chanda Pradyota of Avanti** a disciple, but Avanti and **Gandhara** are not in the key.
[28:6:6] > Shravasti = most sermons; Vaishali = last rainy season + nuns; Rajgir = Nalagiri + First Council.

## SUB 7 | Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path
[28:7:0] TABLE head: Truth | Content
  [28:7:0.0] 1. Dukkha | The world is full of suffering ("sabbam dukkham")
  [28:7:0.1] 2. Samudaya | Suffering has a cause – craving (tanha), ignorance, attachment
  [28:7:0.2] 3. Nirodha | Cessation of suffering = Nirvana
  [28:7:0.3] 4. Magga | The path to cessation = the Eightfold Path
[28:7:1] - **Order:** suffering → cause → cessation → path = **A-D-B-C / I-IV-II-III** (UPPSC 2006).
[28:7:2] - **Buddha and Mirabai** both held the **world full of sorrow** (first Noble Truth).
[28:7:3] # Eightfold Path (Ashtangika Marga)
[28:7:4] TABLE head: Group | Components
  [28:7:4.0] Prajna (wisdom) | Right View (samma-ditthi), Right Intention (sankappa)
  [28:7:4.1] Sila (ethics) | Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood
  [28:7:4.2] Samadhi (mental discipline) | Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration
[28:7:5] - Called the **Middle Path** because it **avoids self-indulgence as well as self-mortification** (APSC 2017).
[28:7:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.63-64; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.44-45; old app notes row 28 (sub 7, 8)
## SUB 8 | Symbols in Early Buddhist Art
[28:8:0] TABLE head: Event | Symbol
  [28:8:0.0] Birth | Lotus and bull
  [28:8:0.1] Great Renunciation | Horse
  [28:8:0.2] Meditation | Empty seat
  [28:8:0.3] Enlightenment | Bodhi (peepal) tree
  [28:8:0.4] First sermon | Wheel (Dharmachakra), often with deer (Deer Park)
  [28:8:0.5] Mahaparinirvana | Stupa
[28:8:1] - Early (aniconic) art showed the Buddha only through such symbols; **UPSC 2026:** the **empty seat = meditation** of the Buddha (not enlightenment, which is the tree).
[28:8:2] - **Wheel with deer** = the **first preaching** at Sarnath.

## SUB 9 | Pratityasamutpada – Dependent Origination
[28:9:0] - **Pratityasamutpada (Paticca-samuppada):** every phenomenon arises from a cause; a **12-link** chain (**12 nidanas**, bhavachakra); removing ignorance ends the chain.
[28:9:1] TABLE head: Order | Links
  [28:9:1.0] 1–4 | Avidya (ignorance) → Samskara (impressions) → Vijnana (consciousness) → Namarupa
  [28:9:1.1] 5–8 | Shadayatana (six senses) → Sparsha (contact) → Vedana (feeling) → Trishna (craving)
  [28:9:1.2] 9–12 | Upadana (clinging) → Bhava (becoming) → Jati (birth) → Jara-marana (old age–death)
[28:9:2] - **Cause of Samskara = Avidya** (CGPSC 2024) – the first link and root of suffering; Vijnana comes after Samskara.
[28:9:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.45; old app notes row 28 (sub 9)

=== NOTES 1:29 | Buddhist Councils, Hinayana–mahayana–vajrayana, Tripitakas and Pali Literature
## SUB 0 | The Four Buddhist Councils – Place, Patron, President
[29:0:0] TABLE head: Council | Place / year | Patron | President | Outcome
  [29:0:0.0] First | Rajagriha (Rajgir), Saptaparni Cave; c. 483 BCE, soon after the Buddha's death | Ajatashatru (Haryanka) | Mahakassapa | Vinaya (recited by Upali) and Sutta (by Ananda) compiled
  [29:0:0.1] Second | Vaishali; 383 BCE, 100 years after the Buddha's death | Kalashoka (Shishunaga) | Sabakami (Sabbakami) | Dispute on monastic rules; split into Sthaviravadins and Mahasanghikas
  [29:0:0.2] Third | Pataliputra (Ashokarama monastery); c. 250 BCE | Ashoka (Maurya) | Moggaliputta Tissa | Abhidhamma Pitaka, Kathavatthu; heretics expelled; missions abroad
  [29:0:0.3] Fourth | Kundalavana, Kashmir; 1st c. CE | Kanishka (Kushana) | Vasumitra (Ashvaghosha deputy) | In Sanskrit; Mahavibhasa commentaries; division into Mahayana and Hinayana
[29:0:1] - **Order of venues:** **Rajagriha → Vaishali → Pataliputra → Kundalavana** = codes "2, 1, 4, 3" (UPPCS 2025; UP Lower 2002).
[29:0:2] - **Presidents (match):** 1st **Mahakassapa** – 2nd **Sabakami** – 3rd **Moggaliputta Tissa** – 4th **Vasumitra** → "1-(b), 2-(a), 3-(d), 4-(c)" (APPSC DAO 2020, FRO 2020).
[29:0:3] - **Patrons in order:** **Ajatashatru → Kalashoka → Ashoka → Kanishka**.
[29:0:4] - **First council:** presided by **Mahakassapa** (not Ananda, Upali, Ajatashatru or Nagasena); Ajatashatru was the patron.
[29:0:5] - **Third council:** at **Pataliputra**, in the **Ashokarama** monastery; recorded only in the Sri Lankan **Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa** – not in Ashoka's inscriptions or the Divyavadana (UPPCS 1999).
[29:0:6] - **Fourth council:** held on the advice of the monk **Parsva**; settled **Sarvastivada** disputes of Kashmir–Gandhara; after it Buddhism split into **Mahayana and Hinayana** (SSC 2018; IAS 1993).
[29:0:7] > Chronology of rulers: Ashoka (3rd c. BCE) → Milinda/Menander (2nd c. BCE) → Kanishka (1st–2nd c. CE).
[29:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.67-68, p.72; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.50, p.61; Rocket Indian History Part 2 p.25, p.115; Mahavamsa ch. 5
## SUB 1 | Hinayana, Mahayana, Vajrayana and the Bodhisattvas
[29:1:0] TABLE head: Sect | Ideal / features | Buddha | Texts / spread
  [29:1:0.0] Hinayana / Theravada | Arhat – individual liberation; original teachings | Symbols, no idols; a great man, not a god | Pali canon; Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand; Ashoka patronised it
  [29:1:0.1] Mahayana (after the 4th council, Kanishka) | Bodhisattva – delays own nirvana to help all beings; Sunyata | Image worship – Buddha as god | Sanskrit – Prajnaparamita, Lotus Sutra; China, Japan, Korea, Tibet; Kanishka, Harsha patrons
  [29:1:0.2] Vajrayana ("vehicle of the thunderbolt") | Salvation through magical power (vajra); mantras, mudras, mandalas | Taras, wrathful deities | Guhyasamaja, Arya Manjushrimulakalpa; Bengal–Bihar, Tibet, Nepal
[29:1:1] - **Fundamental difference:** Mahayana made **images of the Buddha and worshipped him as God**; Hinayana did not (UPPCS 1996). The Buddha was **elevated to God in Kanishka's period**.
[29:1:2] - **Vajrayana:** emerged in the **7th century CE** (APPSC AP History), flourished from the 8th c.; **most prominent in the Sultanate period** (JPSC 2013); centre **Vikramashila**; linked with **Padmasambhava**. In Andhra: **Salihundam**.
[29:1:3] - **Arya Manjushrimulakalpa** = **Vajrayana** (Mahayana tantra; MPPSC 2023 key also accepted Mahayana).
[29:1:4] - **Bodhisattva** – central to **Mahayana, not Hinayana**; a compassionate one on the way to enlightenment who **delays his own salvation** to help all beings (UPSC 2016: B and C only).
[29:1:5] - **Six paramitas** (perfections) of the Bodhisattva: **dana, sila, kshanti, virya, dhyana, prajna**.
[29:1:6] - **Avalokiteshvara** = **Padmapani** ("lotus-bearer") = Lokeshvara, Bodhisattva of **compassion** (IAS 1997). **Maitreya** = the **future Buddha** yet to come (UPSC 2018). Manjushri = wisdom; Vajrapani = power.
[29:1:7] - **Sthaviravadins** = Hinayana (not Mahayana); **Lokottaravadins** = offshoot of the **Mahasanghikas**; Mahasanghika **deification of the Buddha** fostered Mahayana (UPSC 2020: II and III).
[29:1:8] - **Satavahana-period Andhra:** **Madhyamika, Mahayana and Hinayana** (Chaityaka sects) – not Zen or Theravada (APPSC ATWO).
[29:1:9] - **Tibetan** Buddhism merges Mahayana and Vajrayana with Bon; Mahayana reached Tibet in the 7th c.; **Gelug** school dominant by the 15th c.; canon = **Kangyur and Tengyur**. **Karmapa Lama** = **Kagyu (Kangyupa)** sect, seat Rumtek (Sikkim) (UPPCS 2000).
[29:1:10] > Arhat = Hinayana; Bodhisattva = Mahayana; vajra, Taras, Guhyasamaja = Vajrayana.
[29:1:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.68-70; NextGen Part 2 p.21; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.54-59; PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.79; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.122; old app notes 1:29
## SUB 2 | Buddhist Scholars – Nagarjuna, Ashvaghosha, Buddhaghosa, Bhavaviveka
[29:2:0] TABLE head: Scholar | School / fact | Work
  [29:2:0.0] Nagarjuna | Founder of Madhyamika (Shunyavada) of Mahayana; doctrine of Shunyata (void); friend of a Satavahana king | Mulamadhyamakakarika, Suhrllekha, Ratnavali (Rajaparikatha)
  [29:2:0.1] Ashvaghosha | Kanishka's court poet; deputy at the 4th council | Buddhacharita (Sanskrit), Saundarananda
  [29:2:0.2] Buddhaghosa | Theravada, 5th c.; born near Guntur (Kota Nemapuri); worked at Anuradhapura | Visuddhimagga (Pali); Samantapasadika
  [29:2:0.3] Bhavaviveka | Madhyamika; acharya at the Dhanyakataka (Amaravati) vihara | Tarkajvala
  [29:2:0.4] Aryadeva | Nagarjuna's disciple; Madhyamika – a Buddhist, not Jaina scholar | Chatuhshataka
  [29:2:0.5] Dignaga (Dinnaga) | Buddhist logician; "Father of Indian logic"; Yogachara | Pramana Samuccaya
  [29:2:0.6] Dharmakirti (7th c.) | "Kant of India"; developed Dignaga's logic; taught at Nalanda | Pramana Vartika
  [29:2:0.7] Asanga, Vasubandhu | Brothers (4th c.); Yogachara | Vasubandhu – Abhidharmakosa
  [29:2:0.8] Nagasena | Dialogue with Menander | Milindapanho
  [29:2:0.9] Sanghabhuti | Monk in China, 381–384 CE | Commentary on the Sarvastivada Vinaya
[29:2:1] - **Nagarjuna – welfare state:** set out the theory of the welfare state (**Shreyorajya**) in the **Ratnavali** (Rajaparikatha-ratnavali), addressed to a Satavahana king (APPSC AP History).
[29:2:2] - **Nagarjuna** formulated the **basic ideas of Mahayana** (NDA 2014) and taught **Shunyata** (UPPCS 1998; CDS 2006) – not Nagasena, Ashvaghosha or Shankaracharya.
[29:2:3] - **Suhrllekha** – letter to a friend; **I-tsing** saw students memorising it. Title "**Einstein of India**" – idea of relativity.
[29:2:4] - **Sriparvata:** royal friend **Yajna Sri Satakarni** built the **1,500-room Maha Vihara (Parvata Vihara)** for Nagarjuna.
[29:2:5] - **Siddha Nagarjuna** (Vajrayana alchemist at Sriparvata, later period) is a **different person** from the philosopher.
[29:2:6] - **Bhavaviveka = Dhanyakataka** (NextGen; Hiuen Tsang) – a printed key of "Sriparvatam" (APPSC G2 2019) is wrong.
[29:2:7] - **Wrong pair:** "**Nagarjuna – Buddhacharita**" (Ashvaghosha wrote it); Hala – Gathasaptasati, Vatsyayana – Kamasutra, Gunadhya – Brihatkatha are right.
[29:2:8] - **UPSC 2022:** Aryadeva – Jaina ✗, Dignaga – Buddhist ✓, **Nathamuni – Vaishnava** ✓ → **only two pairs** correct.
[29:2:9] > Visuddhimagga = Buddhaghosa (not Nagarjuna, Vasubandhu, Padmasambhava, Dignaga).

## SUB 3 | Tripitaka – Vinaya, Sutta, Abhidhamma and the Nikayas
[29:3:0] TABLE head: Pitaka | Content | Books / compiler
  [29:3:0.0] Vinaya | Rules and discipline of the Sangha (monastic life) | Patimokkha (227 rules for monks), Vibhanga, Khandhaka; Upali
  [29:3:0.1] Sutta | Buddha's sermons on ethics and doctrine (Buddhavacana) | 5 Nikayas; Ananda
  [29:3:0.2] Abhidhamma | Philosophical analysis of the Dhamma | 7 books; added at the 3rd council (Moggaliputta Tissa)
[29:3:1] - **Tripitaka** = the collection of the Buddha's teachings, the **Buddhist** canon (not Jain, Sikh or Hindu); written in **Pali**.
[29:3:2] - **Patimokkha** = the **rules of the Sangha** (CDS 2009), recited every fortnight.
[29:3:3] - **Seven Abhidhamma books:** **Dhammasangani** (first), Vibhanga, Dhatukatha, Puggalapannatti, **Kathavatthu**, **Yamaka**, **Patthana** (seventh). Yamaka belongs to the **Abhidhamma** (JPSC 2016).
[29:3:4] TABLE head: Nikaya (Sutta Pitaka) | Content
  [29:3:4.0] Digha | Long discourses in Pali; Mahaparinibbana Sutta; Samannaphala Sutta
  [29:3:4.1] Majjhima | Middle-length discourses
  [29:3:4.2] Samyutta | Grouped discourses
  [29:3:4.3] Anguttara | Arranged by number; lists the 16 Mahajanapadas
  [29:3:4.4] Khuddaka | 15 books: 550 Jatakas, Dhammapada, Suttanipata, Buddhavamsa, Theragatha, Therigatha
[29:3:5] - **Branches of Buddhist literature:** **Pitakas and Jatakas**; the **Angas** are the **Jain** canon (CDS 2006).
[29:3:6] - **Early literature** is generally **canonical**, but schools do not class their canon as "only the Pitakas" (NDA 2014: only I).
[29:3:7] > 16 Mahajanapadas = Anguttara; Jatakas, Dhammapada = Khuddaka; Kathavatthu, Yamaka = Abhidhamma.
[29:3:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 2 p.6-8; NextGen Part 3 p.31; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.47-54; PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.5; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.131
## SUB 4 | Non-canonical Texts – Language and Sect
[29:4:0] TABLE head: Text | Language | Note
  [29:4:0.0] Milindapanho (Milinda-Panha) | Pali | Dialogue of monk Nagasena and Indo-Greek king Milinda (Menander)
  [29:4:0.1] Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa | Pali | Sri Lankan chronicles; Ashoka, councils; Mahavamsa by Mahanama
  [29:4:0.2] Nettipakarana, Visuddhimagga | Pali | Visuddhimagga by Buddhaghosa
  [29:4:0.3] Divyavadana | Sanskrit | Buddhist legends (Ashoka)
  [29:4:0.4] Avadanashataka | Sanskrit | Avadana tales
  [29:4:0.5] Arya Manjushrimulakalpa | Sanskrit | Mahayana–Vajrayana, historical data
  [29:4:0.6] Buddhacharita | Sanskrit | Ashvaghosha – the Buddha's biography
  [29:4:0.7] Lalitavistara | Buddhist hybrid Sanskrit | Buddha biography; source of Edwin Arnold's The Light of Asia
  [29:4:0.8] Mahavastu | Mixed Sanskrit–Prakrit | Biography of the Buddha (Lokottaravada)
  [29:4:0.9] Dohakosa | Apabhramsa | Songs of the Vajrayana siddhas – the last Buddhist text produced in India (SSC 2011)
  [29:4:0.10] Vinayavatthu | Pali | Mentions the "Andhrapatha"
[29:4:1] - **Language of propagation:** **Pali**, the people's language (SSC 2017); Sanskrit came with Mahayana.
[29:4:2] - **Sanskrit group:** Divyavadana and Manjushrimulakalpa (RAS 2024: 1 and 4); **Pali group:** Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa, Milindapanho.
[29:4:3] - **Account of Ashoka:** the **Mahavamsa** (CDS 2018), not the Pitakas.
[29:4:4] > Divyavadana is Sanskrit, Milindapanho is Pali; Mahavamsa is by Mahanama, not Ashvaghosha.
[29:4:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 2 p.5-8; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.60-63; Britannica 'Saraha', 'The Light of Asia'; old app notes 1:29
## SUB 5 | Philosophical Schools – Sarvastivada to Yogachara
[29:5:0] TABLE head: School | Founder / teacher | Doctrine
  [29:5:0.0] Sthaviravada | Elders at the 2nd council | Orthodox, strict Vinaya → Theravada
  [29:5:0.1] Mahasanghika | Mahadeva's group | Relaxed rules; parent of Chaitika, Lokottaravada and Mahayana
  [29:5:0.2] Vaibhashika (Sarvastivada) | Based on the Mahavibhasa | Dharmas exist in past, present and future ("all exists")
  [29:5:0.3] Sautrantika | Kumaralata | Relies on the Suttas; Hinayana
  [29:5:0.4] Madhyamika / Shunyavada | Nagarjuna; Aryadeva, Buddhapalita, Bhavaviveka | Sunyata (emptiness); midway between realism and idealism
  [29:5:0.5] Yogachara / Vijnanavada | Maitreyanatha, Asanga, Vasubandhu | Only consciousness is real
[29:5:1] - **Nagarjuna's school = Madhyamika** (UK UDA 2007) – not Sautrantika, Vaibhashika or Yogachara.
[29:5:2] - **Aryadeva** = Madhyamika (not Yogachara); Yogachara and Vijnanavada are one school.
[29:5:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.69-70; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.54, p.57-59; old app notes 1:29

## SUB 1 | Major Stupas – Largest, Oldest, Location
[30:1:0] TABLE head: Stupa | Location | Builder / period / fact
  [30:1:0.0] Piprahwa | UP (ancient Kapilavastu) | Among the earliest, c. 5th c. BCE; inscribed relic vessel
  [30:1:0.1] Sanchi | Raisen, MP | Ashoka's brick stupa (3rd c. BCE); stone casing under the Shungas; four toranas by the Satavahanas; UNESCO 1989; rediscovered 1818 (General Taylor); not linked to any event of the Buddha's life
  [30:1:0.2] Bharhut | Satna, MP | Shunga, 2nd c. BCE; stone railing; found by Cunningham, 1873
  [30:1:0.3] Amaravati | AP | Satavahana Mahachaitya (Pulumavi II's time); largest stupa in AP and South India
  [30:1:0.4] Devnimori | near Shamlaji, Aravalli district, Gujarat | Western Kshatrapas, c. 4th c. CE; relic casket; relics taken to Sri Lanka in Feb 2026
  [30:1:0.5] Dhamek | Sarnath, UP | Gupta, c. 500 CE; marks the first sermon
  [30:1:0.6] Kesariya | East Champaran, Bihar | ASI: largest and tallest excavated stupa (c. 104 ft) – key "largest stupa in the world" (UP RO 2023)
  [30:1:0.7] Borobudur | Java, Indonesia | Largest Buddhist monument in the world; UNESCO
[30:1:1] - **Largest stupa:** **Borobudur** (world, NextGen); **Kesariya** when Borobudur is not offered; NextGen gives **Sanchi** as largest in India; **Amaravati** largest in South India (APPSC).
[30:1:2] - **Event sites:** Bodh Gaya – enlightenment; Sarnath – first sermon; Kusinara – death; **Sanchi – none** (UPPCS 2011).
[30:1:3] - **"Most ancient stupa" (own-MCQ angle):** **Sanchi** (Ashokan, 3rd c. BCE, one of the oldest stone structures in India) is older than Bharhut (2nd c. BCE).
[30:1:4] - **Relics** of the Buddha were divided among **nine stupas** after his death.
[30:1:5] - **Sarnath:** B. R. Mani's excavations (2013–14) showed activity **before Ashoka**; on the UNESCO **Tentative List since 1998**, nominated in 2025–26.
[30:1:6] - **Recent digs:** **Vaishya Tekri** (near Ujjain) – believed a Mauryan stupa linked to **Ashoka's wife Devi**, possibly larger than Sanchi; **Ratnagiri (Jajpur, Odisha)** – ASI resumed in Dec 2024, colossal Buddha head found; Odisha's **Diamond Triangle = Ratnagiri, Udayagiri, Lalitagiri**.
[30:1:7] > Chronology: Piprahwa → Sanchi → Devnimori → Dhamek.
[30:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Part 2 p.11; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.68, p.137; PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.81; ASI Kesariya stupa; UNESCO 'Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi'; old app notes 1:29-30
## SUB 2 | Stupa, Chaitya and Vihara – Concept and Parts
[30:2:0] - **Stupa** = solid relic mound worshipped by circumambulation; the **concept is pre-Buddhist** (burial mounds; the word occurs in Vedic texts).
[30:2:1] - **Buddhist stupas** enshrine **relics**, are built as **objects of devotion** by monasteries and **commemorate events** of the Buddha's life – all four statements true (APPSC AEE flashcard). UPSC 2023: "Buddhist in origin" ✗, relic repository ✓, votive and commemorative ✓ → **only two**.
[30:2:2] - **Chaitya** (chaitya-shala / chaitya-griha) = **place of worship**, prayer hall with a stupa at the apsidal end – the Buddhist "temple" (**chaitya stupas**).
[30:2:3] - **Vihara** = **residence of monks**; **Arama** = complex of **stupa + vihara + chaitya + school**, e.g. Nandaluru.
[30:2:4] TABLE head: Part | Meaning
  [30:2:4.0] Anda | Hemispherical dome (the cosmos)
  [30:2:4.1] Medhi | Raised drum / terrace round the base of the dome, for circumambulation
  [30:2:4.2] Harmika | Square railing on top of the anda
  [30:2:4.3] Yashti | Central mast rising from the harmika
  [30:2:4.4] Chhatra / Chhatri | Umbrella(s) on the yashti
  [30:2:4.5] Vedika | Stone railing round the stupa
  [30:2:4.6] Torana | Ornamental gateways at the four directions
  [30:2:4.7] Pradakshinapatha | Path for clockwise circumambulation
  [30:2:4.8] Ayaka pillars / Ayakapata | Special feature of Andhra stupas
[30:2:5] - **Anda, harmika and chhatri** = parts of a **stupa** (APPSC G2 2024).
[30:2:6] TABLE head: Stupa type | Content
  [30:2:6.0] Dhatugarbha | Bodily relics (Amaravati, Bhattiprolu)
  [30:2:6.1] Paribhogika | Objects used by the Buddha
  [30:2:6.2] Uddeshika | Commemorative, no relics
  [30:2:6.3] Aniconic symbol | Event
  [30:2:6.4] Lotus and bull | Birth
  [30:2:6.5] Horse (Kanthaka) | Renunciation
  [30:2:6.6] Empty seat under the Bodhi tree | Enlightenment
  [30:2:6.7] Dharmachakra (wheel) | First sermon
  [30:2:6.8] Stupa / footprints | Parinirvana
[30:2:7] - **Hinayana** showed the Buddha by **symbols**; **Mahayana** adopted images; first human images – **1st c. CE, Gandhara and Mathura**.
[30:2:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.135-137; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 2 p.27, p.33; PMF Art & Culture Part 3 p.40, p.63-65; old app notes 1:30
## SUB 3 | Buddhist Sites and Sect Centres of Andhra Pradesh
[30:3:0] TABLE head: Site | District | Key features
  [30:3:0.0] Amaravati (Dhanyakataka) | Guntur / Palnadu, on the Krishna | Largest stupa in AP; site most linked to Satavahana patronage; identified by Colin Mackenzie (1797); Amaravati School – white limestone; Fergusson: "Epitome of Indian Architecture"
  [30:3:0.1] Bhattiprolu | Guntur (now Bapatla) | Oldest stupa in AP; Yaksha kings Savaru and Kuberaka; inscribed (crystal) relic caskets
  [30:3:0.2] Guntupalli | West Godavari (Eluru) | Only rock-cut cave temple and oldest chaitya in AP; Rajagirika centre
  [30:3:0.3] Jaggayyapeta | NTR (old Krishna), on the Krishna | Early relic stupa; Uttarasaila centre
  [30:3:0.4] Nagarjunakonda (Sriparvata / Vijayapuri) | Palnadu | Ikshvaku capital; "Dakshina Gaya"; island in Nagarjuna Sagar; Aparasaila centre
  [30:3:0.5] Salihundam | Srikakulam, on the Vamsadhara | Mahayana–Vajrayana; Tara bronzes; "Tibet of AP"; found by Gidugu Ramamurthy (1919)
  [30:3:0.6] Thotlakonda, Bavikonda | Visakhapatnam | Hilltop monasteries; the word "Tambaya Danam" is noticed at a Visakhapatnam Buddhist site
  [30:3:0.7] Sankaram (Bojjannakonda) | Anakapalli | Rock-cut caves; found by Alexander Rea, 1906
  [30:3:0.8] Ghantasala (Kantakasala) | Krishna | Ancient port
  [30:3:0.9] Bhairavakonda | Nellore | Eight caves
  [30:3:0.10] Adurru / Chandavaram | Konaseema / Prakasam | Adurru – only Divya stupa; Chandavaram – Mahastupa + 115 small stupas
[30:3:1] - **Vijayapuri** – Buddhist centre of the **3rd–4th c. CE**, now **submerged under Nagarjuna Sagar** (APPSC ZSWO).
[30:3:2] - **Sect centres:** **Purvasaila – Dhanyakataka (Amaravati)**; **Aparasaila – Sriparvata (Nagarjunakonda)**; **Rajagirika – Guntupalli**; **Siddharthaka Chaitya – Gudivada** (APPSC G2 2008).
[30:3:3] - **Wrong pair (APPSC G2 2011): "Guntupalli – Siddharthaka Chaitya"** (Guntupalli = Rajagirika). ⚠ Some scholars place the Siddharthikas at Guntupalli.
[30:3:4] - **Mahasanghika** sect was born at **Dhanyakataka**; **9 of the 18** early sects existed in Andhra; **Andhakas** attended the 3rd council (Kathavatthu); Hinayana – Amaravati, Mahayana – Sriparvata, Vajrayana – Salihundam.
[30:3:5] - **N. Venkataramanayya** identified "**Sriparvata Swamy**" with the Buddha (APPSC G2).
[30:3:6] - **Why monasteries near cities** (e.g. Amaravati near Guntur): monks lived on **daily alms**, so viharas stood close enough to towns for the alms round (merchant donations also flowed).
[30:3:7] - **Latest:** AP plans **2 Buddhist circuits** round its **40** monuments (2024–25); Feb 2026 "**Discover Andhra**" campaign – Amaravati, Bavikonda, Thotlakonda.
[30:3:8] - **Distractors:** Kondaveedu – **Reddy** kingdom; Srinatha's **Haravilasam** – Reddi sea trade.

## SUB 5 | Spread, Patrons and Decline of Buddhism
[30:5:0] - **Causes of spread:** simple doctrine, appeal to the lower orders, **missionary** zeal and the people's **language** (Pali/Prakrit) – I, II, III, IV (UPPSC 2009); not "soundness of the Vedic spirit".
[30:5:1] - **Mauryan followers:** **Ashoka** and **Dasharatha** (CGPSC 2013); Chandragupta became a Jain, Bindusara an Ajivika.
[30:5:2] - **Sites (IAS 1998):** **Lothal – dockyard**, **Sarnath – first sermon**, **Nalanda – learning** ✓; Rajgir – Lion Capital ✗ (the capital is from Sarnath).
[30:5:3] TABLE head: Ashoka's missionary | Region
  [30:5:3.0] Mahinda + Sanghamitta | Sri Lanka
  [30:5:3.1] Sona + Uttara | Suvarnabhumi
  [30:5:3.2] Majjhantika | Kashmir and Gandhara
  [30:5:3.3] Mahadeva | Mahishamandala (Mysore)
  [30:5:3.4] Rakkhita | Vanavasi
  [30:5:3.5] Maharakkhita | Yona country
[30:5:4] - Buddhism reached Central Asia and China by the Kushan-era **Silk Route**.
[30:5:5] - **Mahavamsa:** **Mahadeva Bhikshu** took Buddhism **from Andhra to Sri Lanka** (not the reverse).
[30:5:6] TABLE head: Andhra patron | Contribution
  [30:5:6.0] Satavahanas | Vedic kings but lavish donors; Sanchi toranas
  [30:5:6.1] Veerapurushadatta (Ikshvaku) | Nagarjunakonda Maha Chaitya; royal women donors
  [30:5:6.2] Upasika Bodhisri | Service in Ehuvala Chantamula's reign
  [30:5:6.3] Vishnukundins | Last dynasty to support Buddhism in Andhra; Indrapalanagara vihara
[30:5:7] - Greatest royal patronage in Andhra: **Ikshvakus** of Vijayapuri. **Lay patronage** – queens, merchants, guilds; 2,000 karshapanas with a **weavers'** guild for robes.
[30:5:8] - **Decline:** loss of royal patronage; **Brahmanical (Bhakti) revival**; Vajrayana ritualism; **Sanskrit replaced Pali**; hostile rulers **Pushyamitra Shunga, Shashanka, Mihirakula**; Turkish raids (Nalanda sacked by **Bakhtiyar Khalji**). **Hiuen Tsang** found Sriparvata **without patronage**.
[30:5:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.66; NextGen Part 2 p.43; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.123; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.68; old app notes 1:29-30

=== NOTES 1:31 | Other Heterodox Sects – Ajivikas (makkhali Gosala), Charvaka / Lokayata Materialism
## SUB 0 | Ajivikas – Makkhali Gosala and Niyati
[31:0:0] - **Founder (exam answer):** **Makkhali Gosala** (Gosala Maskariputra) – its most important leader and populariser (UPPCS 1996; UKPSC 2024; NDA 2015); earlier teachers like Nanda Vaccha are also named. Not Ananda, Upali, Vasubandhu or Dignaga.
[31:0:1] - **Niyati (fate):** "**Fate assigns everything, man is powerless**" = **Ajivikas** (UPPCS 2006; RAS 2013) – not Jains, Buddhists or Mimamsakas.
[31:0:2] - All thoughts and actions are **fixed before birth**; **no free will**; karma cannot change destiny; the **order of rebirth cannot be changed**.
[31:0:3] - **Practice:** belief in **determinism** and **severe austerities** (RAS 2024: 1 and 3); ascetics called **Sudra sannyasins**; **no caste discrimination**; held meetings in regular **sabhas** (State PSC: A, B and D).
[31:0:4] - **Atomic theory** of matter – influenced the later **Vaisheshika**.
[31:0:5] - Gosala was **Mahavira's companion for about six years**; Jain texts call him Mahavira's **disciple**; the **Bhagavati Sutra** records their quarrel; the **Majjhima Nikaya** records the Buddha's debates with Jains and Ajivikas.
[31:0:6] TABLE head: Ruler / record | Ajivika link
  [31:0:6.0] Bindusara | Popular under him; joined the sect
  [31:0:6.1] Ashoka, Dasharatha | Gifted the Barabar (and Nagarjuni) caves – among the earliest rock-cut caves in India
  [31:0:6.2] 7th Pillar Edict (Delhi-Topra) | Names Ajivikas with Brahmanas, the Sangha and Nirgranthas
[31:0:7] - Barabar caves were given by **Ashoka, not Chandragupta**; Ashoka himself was Buddhist.
[31:0:8] - **Decline:** survived about **2,000 years**, to the **14th c. CE** in **Karnataka and Tamil Nadu**; faded with the Puranic-Bhakti revival and loss of patronage.
[31:0:9] > Niyativada = Gosala (Ajivika); materialism = Charvaka.
[31:0:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.38, p.50; NextGen Part 2 p.43, p.45; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.84-85; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.123; old app notes 1:31
## SUB 1 | Charvaka / Lokayata Materialism
[31:1:0] - **Other names:** **Lokayata** / **Lokayata Darshan** ("of the common people") (State PSC; CGPSC 2018); **Barhaspatya** after the legendary founder **Brihaspati**.
[31:1:1] - **Complete materialism**; highest value = **Kama** (pleasure) – not Dharma, Artha or Moksha (CGPSC 2017).
[31:1:2] - **Dehatmavada:** "**The conscious body is the soul**" (CGPSC 2024).
[31:1:3] - **Only pramana = perception** (pratyaksha) (CGPSC 2018); rejects inference, Vedic testimony, ritualism and the afterlife. Nyaya accepts **four** pramanas.
[31:1:4] - **Aphorism (IAS 1994):** "**Yavaj jivet sukham jivet, rinam kritva ghritam pibet**" – live well while you live, even on borrowing; once cremated there is no return → **Charvakas**.
[31:1:5] - Original **Brihaspati Sutra** is lost; Lokayata is known through **rivals' criticism**, e.g. **Madhava's Sarvadarshanasangraha**.
[31:1:6] TABLE head: School | Karma | Soul
  [31:1:6.0] Jainism | Removable by penance | Eternal jiva in all things
  [31:1:6.1] Buddhism | Intention-based | Anatta
  [31:1:6.2] Ajivika | Cannot alter destiny | Accepted
  [31:1:6.3] Charvaka | Does not decide rebirth | Conscious body
[31:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.50; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.123; Rocket Part 2 p.5; PMF Art & Culture Part 5 p.105; old app notes 1:31
## SUB 2 | Six Teachers and the Age of Religious Ferment
[31:2:0] - **6th century BCE:** an age of religious upheaval across the world, while the **Vedic religion had become complex** – both true (UKPSC 2012). Shramana movements arose amid **urbanisation and Magadhan patronage**.
[31:2:1] TABLE head: Teacher | Doctrine
  [31:2:1.0] Makkhali Gosala | Niyativada – fatalism (Ajivika)
  [31:2:1.1] Purana Kassapa | Akriyavada – actions bring neither merit nor demerit
  [31:2:1.2] Ajita Kesakambalin | Materialist – nothing survives death
  [31:2:1.3] Pakudha Kaccayana | Seven eternal, uncreated elements
  [31:2:1.4] Sanjaya Belatthiputta | Sceptic – "eel-wriggling"
  [31:2:1.5] Nigantha Nataputta | = Mahavira
[31:2:2] - Source: the **Samannaphala Sutta** of the **Digha Nikaya** – Ajatashatru reports the six teachers' views to the Buddha.
[31:2:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.86-87; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 1 p.50; old app notes 1:31

=== NOTES 1:32 | Persian and Macedonian Invasions – Alexander's Campaign, Battle of Hydaspes, Effects on India
## SUB 0 | Alexander's Campaign – Route, Years, Hydaspes, Retreat
[32:0:0] TABLE head: Event | Year
  [32:0:0.0] Crossed the Hindu Kush (start of the invasion) | 327 BC (APPSC G2 2008 key)
  [32:0:0.1] Entered through the Khyber Pass, crossed the Indus | 326 BC
  [32:0:0.2] Battle of the Hydaspes vs Porus | 326 BC
  [32:0:0.3] Halt at the Beas (Hyphasis) | 326 BC
  [32:0:0.4] Left India from Patala | 325 BC (about 19 months in India)
  [32:0:0.5] Died at Babylon | 323 BC, aged 32
[32:0:1] - **"When did Alexander invade?"** – **327 BC** when offered (APPSC); **326 BC** in UPPSC 2006 (Indus crossing, Hydaspes).
[32:0:2] - **Hydaspes** = Greek name of the **Jhelum** (Sanskrit **Vitasta**); Alexander defeated **Porus** there (UPRO 2013; APPSC G1 2002). Hyphasis = Beas, Acesines = Chenab, Hydraotes = Ravi.
[32:0:3] - **Porus** was **not executed** – asked how to be treated, he said "**Like a king**"; Alexander **restored and enlarged** his kingdom and made him ally/satrap.
[32:0:4] - **Bucephala** (after his horse) and **Nicaea** were founded on the Jhelum.
[32:0:5] - **Pushkalavati:** its Ashtaka raja **Astes (Hasti)** resisted and was killed – no alliance.
[32:0:6] - **Satrapies:** PMF – the land from the Indus to the Beas went into **three parts under Greek governors**; Telugu Akademi texts count **six satrapies** (hence the "a, b & d" key).
[32:0:7] - **Retreat:** army refused to cross the **Beas** (not the Ravi) – **war-weariness, homesickness, disease, fear of the Nanda army**; **12 stone altars** on its northern bank; **Nearchus** led the fleet down the Indus.
[32:0:8] - **A–R (UPPCS 1998):** Alexander left in 325 BC ✓; "defeated by Chandragupta Maurya" ✗.
[32:0:9] > Hydaspes = Jhelum = Vitasta; Hyphasis = Beas (halt point).
[32:0:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.94-96; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.78; Rocket Part 2 p.12, p.26, p.113; old app notes 1:32
## SUB 1 | India on the Eve of Alexander – Nandas and North-west Rulers
[32:1:0] - **Magadha:** **Nanda** dynasty ruled North India (IAS 2000); king **Dhana Nanda** (Greek **Agrammes**), the **last Nanda** and Alexander's contemporary – not Mahapadma Nanda or Chandragupta; commander **Bhaddasala**; huge army.
[32:1:1] - **North-west:** small independent states (Taxila, Porus's kingdom, Gandhara) – no united front.
[32:1:2] TABLE head: Ruler / people | Response
  [32:1:2.0] Ambhi (Omphis), Taxila | First to surrender; helped Alexander
  [32:1:2.1] Porus (Puru) – between Jhelum and Chenab | Resisted at the Hydaspes
  [32:1:2.2] Assakenoi (Ashvakas), capital Massaga | Women took up arms; queen Cleophis
  [32:1:2.3] Malloi (Malavas), Kshudrakas | Fought him during the retreat
[32:1:3] - **Takshashila (Taxila):** between the **Indus and the Jhelum**, near **Rawalpindi**, Pakistan (UPPCS 1996).
[32:1:4] TABLE head: Battle | Year | Between
  [32:1:4.0] Ten Kings (Dasharajnya) | – | Sudas vs ten kings, near the Parushni (Ravi); Rigveda
  [32:1:4.1] Kalinga War | 261 BC | Ashoka vs Kalinga
[32:1:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.37, p.95; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 2 p.40; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.78; old app notes 1:32
## SUB 2 | Achaemenid (Persian) Invasion and Its Influence
[32:2:0] - **Cyrus II** (c. 558–530 BC): first Achaemenid to campaign into the north-west – captured **Gandhara and Kamboja**.
[32:2:1] - **Darius I** (**522–486 BC**): usual answer for the **first Persian ruler to capture/annex Indian land** (RAS 1994) – Sindh and Punjab west of the Indus = **20th satrapy** (Hindush).
[32:2:2] - **Herodotus:** the most fertile satrapy; tribute of **360 talents of gold dust** (about one-third of the revenue).
[32:2:3] - **Influence:** **Kharosthi** from Aramaic, written **right to left**; Ashoka's **Kandahar** edict partly in **Aramaic**; words **lipi / dipi**; third-person preamble (Darius model); polished pillars; **satrapy** system.
[32:2:4] > First to campaign = Cyrus; first to annex (20th satrapy) = Darius I.
[32:2:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.94; NextGen Indian History - APPSC Exams Part 2 p.53; Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.76; Rocket Part 2 p.113; old app notes 1:32
## SUB 3 | Greek Writers and Effects of the Invasion
[32:3:0] TABLE head: Writer | Status
  [32:3:0.0] Nearchus (admiral), Onesicritus, Aristobulus | Came with Alexander; first-hand accounts
  [32:3:0.1] Arrian, Curtius, Plutarch | Later writers
  [32:3:0.2] Deimachus | Later envoy of Antiochus I to Bindusara – did not come with Alexander (UPPSC 2015)
[32:3:1] - **Effects:** direct contact and **new land and sea routes** between Greece and India; small NW states weakened, clearing the way for **Chandragupta Maurya**, who expelled the Greek satraps with **Porus (Parvataka)** as ally.
[32:3:2] - **Sandrokottas** = Chandragupta; the invasion is the **first dated event** of Indian history.
[32:3:3] - **Little lasting political mark:** the earlier Persian rule left the deeper influence.
[32:3:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.96-98, p.116; old app notes 1:32

=== NOTES 1:33 | Sources for the Mauryas – Arthashastra, Indica of Megasthenes, Mudrarakshasa, Edicts
## SUB 0 | Indica of Megasthenes
[33:0:0] # Author and text
[33:0:1] - **Author:** **Megasthenes**, Greek envoy of **Seleucus I Nicator** to **Chandragupta Maurya** at Pataliputra (c. 302 BCE) (Uttarakhand UDA 2007; MPPSC 2015; State PSC) – not Nearchus, Plutarch, Diodorus, Justin, Herodotus, Deimachus, Pliny or Vishnugupta.
[33:0:2] - **Lost original:** survives only in fragments quoted by **Diodorus, Strabo, Pliny and Arrian**; compiled by Schwanbeck (1846).
[33:0:3] # What the Indica says
[33:0:4] TABLE head: Topic | Indica's account
  [33:0:4.0] Pataliputra | Palibothra / Polibrotha = Patna; wooden palisade, 64 gates, 570 towers, palace
  [33:0:4.1] City administration | Six committees of five members each (30 in all); town officials Astynomoi
  [33:0:4.2] Society | Seven classes – philosophers, farmers, herdsmen, artisans, soldiers, overseers, councillors (no merchants) – not the fourfold varna
  [33:0:4.3] Slavery | "No slaves in India" – wrong; the Arthashastra and Ashokan edicts mention dasas
  [33:0:4.4] Andhras | 30 fortified towns, 1,00,000 infantry, 2,000 cavalry, 1,000 elephants
  [33:0:4.5] Army | Committee of 30 in six boards for six wings – infantry, cavalry, elephants, chariots, navy, transport
[33:0:5] - **Administration of Pataliputra / city administration of the Mauryas:** **Indica** (State PSC; BPSC 2004; UPPCS Mains 2009) – not the Arthashastra, Divyavadana, Mudrarakshasa or Ashoka's inscriptions.
[33:0:6] - **Seven classes:** particularly mentioned in **Megasthenes' Indica** (UP Lower 2008; State PSC) – not the Arthashastra, edicts or Puranas.
[33:0:7] - **"No slavery in ancient India":** **Megasthenes' Indica** (UPRO/ARO Mains 2013) – Arthashastra, Mudrarakshasa and Vayu Purana are distractors.
[33:0:8] - **First to mention the forts of Andhra:** **Megasthenes** (APPSC G2 2002; AP History PYQ) – not Kautilya, Ashoka's inscriptions or Gautama. **30** forts, not 80 (80 = the pillared hall at Kumrahar).
[33:0:9] - **"Polibrotha" in Greek texts:** **Pataliputra** (Uttarakhand PCS 2025) – not Purushapura, Patan or Ahichhatra.
[33:0:10] > Exam angle: city boards, seven classes, "no slaves", Andhra forts → all **Indica**.
[33:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 2 p.46-47, p.51; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.110, p.115; app notes 1:33 (sub 2)
## SUB 1 | Arthashastra and Mudrarakshasa
[33:1:0] # Arthashastra of Kautilya
[33:1:1] - **Author:** **Kautilya = Chanakya = Vishnugupta** – not Pushyagupta (the Sudarshana lake governor).
[33:1:2] - **Subject:** **principles and practice of statecraft** (UPPCS Mains 2012) – **political policies** (State PSC); also administration, economy, espionage, taxation. Not a book only on economic relations or wealth.
[33:1:3] - **Compared with "The Prince" of Machiavelli** (UPPCS 1994) – not Malavikagnimitram, Kamasutra or Thirukkural.
[33:1:4] - **Rediscovery:** manuscript identified by **R. Shamasastry** (Mysore) in **1905**, published **1909**; **15 books (adhikaranas)**.
[33:1:5] # Mudrarakshasa of Vishakhadatta
[33:1:6] - **Sanskrit drama** of the Gupta age (5th–6th c. CE) by **Vishakhadatta**.
[33:1:7] - **Plot:** **Chandragupta Maurya's revolt against the Nandas**, with Chanakya's help (APPSC G1 2002; APPSC G1 PYQ) – not the Arthashastra, Patanjali's Mahabhashya (a grammar) or Indica.
[33:1:8] - **Subject:** the **court intrigues at the time of Chandragupta Maurya** – Chanakya winning over **Rakshasa**, minister of the Nandas (UPSC 2002 ×2).
[33:1:9] - **Chandragupta Maurya figures prominently in the work of:** **Vishakhadatta** (State PSC) – not Bhasa, Sudraka or Ashvaghosha.
[33:1:10] - **Commentator Dhundiraja** made Chandragupta a scion of the Nanda house.
[33:1:11] > Exam angle: "play on Chandragupta / Nandas" → **Mudrarakshasa**; "statecraft, The Prince" → **Arthashastra**.
[33:1:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 2 p.42, p.47; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.109-110; app notes 1:33 (sub 1, 3)
## SUB 2 | Other Literary, Epigraphic and Archaeological Sources
[33:2:0] TABLE head: Source | Tradition | Covers
  [33:2:0.0] Parishishtaparvan (Hemachandra) | Jain | Chandragupta's Jain end
  [33:2:0.1] Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa (Mahavamsa – Mahanama) | Sri Lankan Pali chronicles | Ashoka, mission to Sri Lanka
  [33:2:0.2] Ashokavadana, Divyavadana | Buddhist Sanskrit | Ashoka legends
  [33:2:0.3] Puranas (18) – Vishnu Purana | Brahmanical | Mauryan king lists and genealogies
  [33:2:0.4] Mamulanar | Sangam Tamil poet | The Nandas and the Mauryas' southward push
  [33:2:0.5] Vamsatthapakasini (10th c.) | Buddhist commentary | Chanakya–Chandragupta legend
[33:2:1] - **Early Tamil poet who refers to the Nandas and Mauryas:** **Mamulanar** (IAS 1996) – not Sattanar, Ilango Adigal or Kapilar.
[33:2:2] - **Milindapanho** is about **Menander** – not a Mauryan source.
[33:2:3] TABLE head: Inscription / find | Mauryan fact
  [33:2:3.0] Ashokan edicts ("Dhammalipi") | First deciphered by James Prinsep, 1837
  [33:2:3.1] Greek–Aramaic edict | Shar-i-Kuna (Kandahar)
  [33:2:3.2] Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman I (c. 150 CE) | Sudarshana lake built in Chandragupta's reign by governor Pushyagupta
  [33:2:3.3] Hathigumpha inscription (Kharavela) | Also cited for Mauryan references
  [33:2:3.4] Kumrahar (Patna) | 80-pillared hall of Pataliputra
  [33:2:3.5] Bulandibagh (Patna) | Wooden palisade, thought to be the one Megasthenes saw
  [33:2:3.6] Punch-marked coins | Silver, peacock–hill–crescent symbols
  [33:2:3.7] NBPW | Fine pottery of the middle Ganga plains; late phase = Mauryan age
[33:2:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 2 p.42, p.47-48, p.53; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.111, p.115; app notes 1:33 (sub 0, 4, 5, 6, 7)

=== NOTES 1:34 | Chandragupta Maurya and Bindusara – Conquests, Treaty with Seleucus, Chanakya
## SUB 0 | Seleucus Nicator and the Greek Envoys
[34:0:0] - **Seleucus I Nicator**, Alexander's general and ruler of Sindh–Afghanistan, was **defeated by Chandragupta in 305 BCE** (MPPSC 2008).
[34:0:1] TABLE head: Treaty term | Detail
  [34:0:1.0] Ceded to Chandragupta | Aria (Herat), Arachosia (Kandahar), Paropanisadai (Kabul), Gedrosia (Balochistan) – not Bactria
  [34:0:1.1] Marriage | Seleucus's daughter (Helena) married Chandragupta – not the reverse
  [34:0:1.2] Chandragupta gave | 500 war elephants
  [34:0:1.3] Envoy | Megasthenes sent to Pataliputra
[34:0:2] # Greek envoys
[34:0:3] TABLE head: Envoy | Sent by | Court
  [34:0:3.0] Megasthenes | Seleucus I Nicator | Chandragupta Maurya – wrote Indica
  [34:0:3.1] Deimachus | Antiochus I (Syria) | Bindusara – replaced Megasthenes (Strabo)
  [34:0:3.2] Dionysius | Ptolemy II Philadelphus (Egypt) | Bindusara
[34:0:4] - **Megasthenes:** ambassador of **Seleucus** (State PSC); came in the reign of **Chandragupta Maurya** (UPPCS Mains 2017; RAS 1997) – not Ashoka, Harsha or Kumaragupta; the **first Greek envoy** to an Indian court.
[34:0:5] - **Deimachus:** came under **Bindusara** (UP Lower 2015); he **did not come with Alexander** – Nearchus, Onesicritus, Aristobulus did (UPPCS 2015).
[34:0:6] - **Diplomatic ties with Syria and Egypt:** the **Mauryas** (UPPSC 2010) – not Cholas, Guptas or Pallavas.
[34:0:7] - **Megasthenes on Palibothra:** a **30-member body in six boards**, **64 gates**; his seven classes had **no merchants**.
[34:0:8] > Exam angle: Megasthenes → Chandragupta; Deimachus, Dionysius → Bindusara.
[34:0:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 2 p.43; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.111, p.116; app notes 1:34 (sub 4, 7)
## SUB 1 | Chandragupta Maurya – Names, Rise and the First Empire
[34:1:0] # Greek names
[34:1:1] - **Sandrocottus / Sandrokottos:** Greek name of Chandragupta used by **Justin** (Uttarakhand PCS 2016) and Strabo; Arrian and Plutarch – **Androkottus**. Not Chandragupta I or II, or Samudragupta.
[34:1:2] - **Sir William Jones (1793)** first identified Sandrocottus with Chandragupta – the sheet-anchor of Indian chronology.
[34:1:3] - **Meeting with Alexander:** described by **Justin** (UP Lower 2008 ×2) – not Pliny, Strabo or Megasthenes. Justin also called his army a "**gang of dacoits**".
[34:1:4] # Origin and rise
[34:1:5] TABLE head: Tradition | Origin
  [34:1:5.0] Brahmanical | "Maurya" from a Shudra woman Mura
  [34:1:5.1] Buddhist and Jain | Kshatriya of the Moriya clan
  [34:1:5.2] Mudrarakshasa commentary (Dhundiraja) | A scion of the Nanda house
[34:1:6] - **Rise:** studied at **Taxila** (in **Gandhara**), met Chanakya; with the Himalayan chief Parvataka overthrew **Dhana Nanda** and took the throne in **321 BCE**; reign **324/321–297 BCE**.
[34:1:7] - **Army (Greek accounts):** **6,00,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry**, thousands of elephants.
[34:1:8] - **First Indian empire:** founded by **Chandragupta Maurya** (UP Lower 2012) – the **Mauryan** empire was the first to unite most of the subcontinent; not Kanishka, Harsha or Samudragupta.
[34:1:9] - **Oldest dynasty** among Gupta, Maurya, Vardhana and Kushana: **Maurya** (321–185 BCE) (Uttarakhand Lower 2010).
[34:1:10] - **Ashoka's dynasty:** **Maurya** (CDS 2006) – grandson of Chandragupta, son of Bindusara.
[34:1:11] > Exam angle: "Sandrocottus" → **Chandragupta Maurya**; "met Alexander" → **Justin**; first empire → **Mauryan**.
[34:1:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 2 p.42-43; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.111; app notes 1:34 (sub 0, 1)
## SUB 2 | Conquests, Western India and the Sudarshana Lake
[34:2:0] TABLE head: Region | Conquest / evidence
  [34:2:0.0] North-west | Expelled the Greek satraps; won Seleucus's provinces up to Afghanistan
  [34:2:0.1] Central and western India | Region north of the Narmada; Malwa, Gujarat (Saurashtra) and Maharashtra – Junagadh inscription
  [34:2:0.2] South | Empire reached Karnataka (Brahmagiri, Siddapura, Jatinga-Rameshwara); Tamil kingdoms (Chola, Pandya, Satyaputra, Keralaputra) stayed outside
[34:2:1] - **First king to conquer Malwa, Gujarat and Maharashtra:** **Chandragupta Maurya** (UPPCS 1991) – not Harsha, Skandagupta or Vikramaditya.
[34:2:2] - **Conqueror of the Deccan:** **Bindusara** – PMF: he "conquered the Deccan up to Mysore" (State PSC key).
[34:2:3]   - **⚠ Disputed:** some books credit Chandragupta (Jain tradition of his end at Shravanabelagola); NextGen says Bindusara made no conquests.
[34:2:4] - **Mamulanar**, a Tamil (not Greek) poet, refers to the Mauryas' southward push.
[34:2:5] - **Provincial capitals:** Pataliputra (centre), Taxila (north), **Ujjain** (west), **Tosali** (Kalinga, east), **Suvarnagiri** (south).
[34:2:6] - **Andhra:** Ashokan edicts at **Yerragudi** (major + minor) and **Rajula Mandagiri** (only minor), Kurnool; RE XIII names the Andhras among peoples following Dhamma within the domain; the **Satavahanas** began as Mauryan feudatories.
[34:2:7] # Sudarshana lake (Girnar, Saurashtra)
[34:2:8] TABLE head: Person | Role
  [34:2:8.0] Pushyagupta | Chandragupta's governor; built it – the first lake in Girnar
  [34:2:8.1] Tushaspha | Ashoka's Yavana governor; added canals
  [34:2:8.2] Rudradaman I | Repaired it (c. 150 CE) without forced labour – Junagadh inscription
  [34:2:8.3] Skandagupta | Repaired it again
[34:2:9] - **First ruler to get a lake built at Girnar:** **Chandragupta Maurya** (UPPCS Mains 2002) – who **constructed the Sudarshana lake** (UKPSC 2024).
[34:2:10] - **Resource management at Girnar some centuries BCE:** **Chandragupta Maurya and Ashoka** → codes **2, 3** (UPUDA 2006); Rudradaman was after the Christian era, Mahapadma Nanda not linked.
[34:2:11] > Exam angle: built = **Pushyagupta / Chandragupta**; canals = **Tushaspha / Ashoka**; repaired = **Rudradaman, Skandagupta**.
[34:2:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Indian History Part 1 p.6-7; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.111, p.116; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 2 p.43, p.47; app notes 1:34 (sub 3, 11)
## SUB 3 | Chanakya (Kautilya, Vishnugupta)
[34:3:0] - **Other name / childhood name:** **Vishnugupta** (UPPCS 2006; IAS 1993 ×2) – not Bhattaswami, Rajasekhara or Vishakhadatta; one Arthashastra verse names its author Vishnugupta.
[34:3:1] - **Office:** **prime minister** of **Chandragupta Maurya** (UPPCS 2002) – not Chandragupta Vikramaditya, Ashoka or Janaka.
[34:3:2] - **Taranath and Jain tradition:** he stayed on as **Bindusara's** minister; Puranas call him "dvijarshabha".
[34:3:3] - **Mudrarakshasa:** Chanakya against **Rakshasa**, minister of the **Nandas**.
[34:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 2 p.43, p.47; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.109; app notes 1:34 (sub 2)
## SUB 4 | Chandragupta's Jain End and the Religion of the Mauryas
[34:4:0] - **Went south with Chandragupta in the great famine:** **Bhadrabahu** (APPSC G2 2003) – not Sthulabhadra, Merutunga or Lakulisha.
[34:4:1] - **12-year famine** → split into **Digambaras** (Bhadrabahu) and **Svetambaras** (followers of **Sthulabhadra**).
[34:4:2] - **First Indian king to abdicate:** **Chandragupta Maurya** (APPSC G1) – gave up the throne for **Bindusara**, became a Jain ascetic and died by **Sallekhana** at **Shravanabelagola** (Karnataka); source **Parishishtaparvan**.
[34:4:3] TABLE head: Ruler | Religion
  [34:4:3.0] Chandragupta | Jainism (Bhadrabahu)
  [34:4:3.1] Bindusara | Ajivika
  [34:4:3.2] Ashoka | Buddhism; gave Barabar caves to the Ajivikas
  [34:4:3.3] Dasharatha | Buddhist (key), though he gave the Nagarjuni caves to the Ajivikas
  [34:4:3.4] Samprati | Jainism – "Ashoka of Jainism"; spread Jainism in Andhra
[34:4:4] - **Barabar caves** (Bihar): the **oldest surviving rock-cut caves**, carved in **granite** – not at Girnar; **Lomas Rishi** cave is in the Barabar hills.
[34:4:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 2 p.43, p.52; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.111; app notes 1:34 (sub 5, 10)
## SUB 5 | Bindusara
[34:5:0] - **Title:** **Amitraghata** ("**slayer of foes**", Mahabhashya) = Greek Amitrochates (UP Lower 2015) – not Chandragupta, Samudragupta or Ashoka.
[34:5:1] - **Birth name:** **Simhasena**; mother **Durdhara**; reign **297–273 BCE**.
[34:5:2] - **Antiochus I** was asked for sweet wine, dried figs and a **philosopher** – the philosopher could not be sent.
[34:5:3] - **Religion:** **Ajivika**; council of 500 ministers under Khallataka.
[34:5:4] - **Taxila revolt:** **Susima** failed, then **Ashoka** was sent (Divyavadana); a later Taxila revolt under Ashoka was handled by **Kunala**. Ashoka was viceroy at Taxila and **Ujjain**.
[34:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 2 p.43; PMF Ancient & Medieval Part 2 p.116; app notes 1:34 (sub 6)
[34:5:6] - **Ashoka's mother:** **Subhadrangi** (Dharma), Bindusara's queen – Bindusara's own mother was **Durdhara**.

=== NOTES 1:37 | Mauryan Administration – Central, Provincial, Local; Espionage, Judiciary, Revenue
## SUB 0 | Central Officers – Tirthas and Adhyakshas
[37:0:0] # The eighteen tirthas (heads of departments)
[37:0:1] TABLE head: Tirtha | Department
  [37:0:1.0] Samaharta | Collector-general of revenue – highest officer for assessment and collection of all revenue (APPSC GS 2010; UP Lower 2008); helped by the Bhagadhuk
  [37:0:1.1] Sannidhata | Treasurer – chief custodian of the state treasury and storehouses
  [37:0:1.2] Dandapala | Head of the army department (APPSC G1)
  [37:0:1.3] Pradeshtri (Pradeshtha) | Commissioner; criminal justice, heads the kantakashodhana courts
  [37:0:1.4] Antapala | Frontier officer – border forts
  [37:0:1.5] Vyavaharika | Civil judge
  [37:0:1.6] Prashasta | Prisons (also given as encampment)
  [37:0:1.7] Dauvarika / Nayaka / Paura | Palace gate / city guard / governor of the capital
  [37:0:1.8] Karmantika | Factories and mines
  [37:0:1.9] Mantri, Purohita, Senapati, Yuvaraja | Minister, chief priest, commander-in-chief, crown prince – the highest tirthas
[37:0:2] - **⚠ Do not swap:** Samaharta = revenue **collector**; Sannidhata = **treasurer** (store-keeper). Most tirthas were paid in cash.
[37:0:3] - **Andhra link:** the Saptanga + 18 Tirthas model was later used by the **Eastern Chalukyas** (Ashtadasha Tirthas) and **Kakatiyas**.
[37:0:4] # Adhyakshas (superintendents)
[37:0:5] TABLE head: Adhyaksha | Charge
  [37:0:5.0] Pautavadhyaksha | Weights and measures (APPSC G2 2024; UPPCS Mains 2012)
  [37:0:5.1] Sitadhyaksha | Crown-land agriculture; collected sita (RAS 2010: the land-revenue collector among Agronomoi, Shulka- and Akara-dhyaksha)
  [37:0:5.2] Panyadhyaksha | Commerce, state trade
  [37:0:5.3] Sulkadhyaksha | Tolls; trade and service taxes
  [37:0:5.4] Samsthadhyaksha | Markets
  [37:0:5.5] Akaradhyaksha / Lohadhyaksha | Mines / iron
  [37:0:5.6] Lakshanadhyaksha | Mint and seals
  [37:0:5.7] Koshadhyaksha | Treasury
  [37:0:5.8] Lavanadhyaksha | Salt (state monopoly)
  [37:0:5.9] Sunadhyaksha | Slaughterhouse
  [37:0:5.10] Koshthagaradhyaksha / Kupyadhyaksha | Storehouses / forest produce
[37:0:6] - **Akshapataladhyaksha:** accountant-general – currency and accounts offices.
[37:0:7] - **Rajuka** is also listed by NextGen among officers "to look after justice".
[37:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 02 p.46; NextGen Indian History APPSC 03 p.29 (18 tirthas); PMF Ancient & Medieval 02 p.113, p.115; app notes 1:37 (sub 2, 3)
## SUB 1 | Revenue System – Taxes and Penalties
[37:1:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [37:1:0.0] Sita | Revenue from crown land (UPPCS 2013) – land farmed for the state under the Sitadhyaksha
  [37:1:0.1] Bhaga | King's share of produce – normally 1/6 (PMF); NextGen and Megasthenes give 1/4 (range 1/4 to 1/6)
  [37:1:0.2] Bali | Additional levy / tribute
  [37:1:0.3] Pindakara | Tax assessed on groups of villages, paid by the village as a unit – the "pin tax" (IAS 2009)
  [37:1:0.4] Pranaya | Emergency tax ("gift of affection") (UKPCS 2021)
  [37:1:0.5] Kara | Tax on fruit and flower gardens
  [37:1:0.6] Hiranya | Tax paid only in cash
  [37:1:0.7] Vivita | Pasture-land dues
  [37:1:0.8] Setu / Vana | Gardens, orchards, root crops / forests
[37:1:1] - **Land revenue** was the main income; the land belonged to the king; an **irrigation tax** was levied on those who used state irrigation.
[37:1:2] - **Tax evasion → death:** Megasthenes says evasion of the sales tax was punished with **death** (JKPSC 2013).
[37:1:3] - **Pankodakasannirodhe:** the Arthashastra fine for **slushing the road** with dirt and water (RAS 2013) – not for filthy water, garbage or temples.
[37:1:4] - **Other income:** tolls, ferries, mines, pastures, licences, fines; state monopoly of mining, liquor, salt and arms. Lumbini: freed of bali, bhaga cut to **1/8**.
[37:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 02 p.46, p.50; PMF Ancient & Medieval 02 p.115; Rocket Indian History 01 p.4; app notes 1:37 (sub 8, 9)
## SUB 2 | District and Local Officials – Pradeshika, Rajuka, Yukta
[37:2:0] - **Ashokan district officers:** **Pradeshika, Rajuka and Yukta** were officers at the **district level** (UPSC 2025) – survey and assessment of land, tours, revenue, law and order; they toured every five years (Rock Edict III).
[37:2:1] TABLE head: Officer | Level / role
  [37:2:1.0] Pradeshika | Chief district administrator, like a modern collector – revenue, police
  [37:2:1.1] Rajuka | District – land survey and assessment, with judicial powers (Pillar Edict IV); the Mauryan officer for the head of an ahara (CDS 2009: not Krori, Faujdar or Chirastadar, which are medieval)
  [37:2:1.2] Yukta | Subordinate revenue/office officer assisting the Rajukas
  [37:2:1.3] Sthanika | Tax collector over a larger division
  [37:2:1.4] Gopa | Accountant over 5–10 (PMF: 10–15) villages
  [37:2:1.5] Gramika / Gramani | Village head, with elders
  [37:2:1.6] Anta-mahamattas | Frontier forts
  [37:2:1.7] Rakshinas | City police
[37:2:2] - **Rajjukas** were therefore **officers in the Mauryan administration** (UPPCS 1996) – not Chola traders, Gupta feudal lords or Saka soldiers.
[37:2:3] - **Not Mauryan:** **Agraharika** (RAS 2013); **Mahabaladhikrita, Mahadandanayaka, Mahasandhivigrahika** are **Gupta** titles; Bhagadugha, Sangrahitri are Vedic.
[37:2:4] - **City:** municipality under a **Nagaraka / Purmukhya**.
[37:2:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 02 p.114-115, p.124; NextGen Indian History APPSC 02 p.45-46, p.49; app notes 1:37 (sub 5)
## SUB 3 | Megasthenes – City Committees and Army Boards
[37:3:0] - **Pataliputra:** a municipal board of **30 members in 6 committees of 5** (Megasthenes).
[37:3:1] TABLE head: Committee | Function
  [37:3:1.0] 1 | Industrial arts and crafts
  [37:3:1.1] 2 | Foreigners
  [37:3:1.2] 3 | Registration of births and deaths
  [37:3:1.3] 4 | Trade and commerce, prices, weights and measures
  [37:3:1.4] 5 | Supervision of manufactured goods
  [37:3:1.5] 6 | Tax on sales (one-tenth, excise and customs) – NOT land revenue
[37:3:2] - **Continuity:** **registration of births and deaths** is the municipal function that has continued from Mauryan times to today (RAS 1992; State PSC).
[37:3:3] - **Agronomoi** = district officers in charge of **roads**, irrigation and land measurement (UPPSC 2020: "construction of roads"); **Astynomoi** = city officers.
[37:3:4] - **Army:** also **6 boards of 5** – infantry, cavalry, chariots, elephants, navy, transport/commissariat. Chandragupta's army: **6,00,000 foot, 30,000 cavalry, 9,000 elephants**.
[37:3:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 02 p.114-115; NextGen Indian History APPSC 02 p.46, p.49-50; app notes 1:37 (sub 6)
## SUB 4 | Saptanga Theory and the Nature of the State
[37:4:0] TABLE head: No. | Element | Meaning
  [37:4:0.0] 1 | Swami | King (comes first)
  [37:4:0.1] 2 | Amatya | Ministers and officials
  [37:4:0.2] 3 | Janapada | Territory and people
  [37:4:0.3] 4 | Durga | Fort
  [37:4:0.4] 5 | Kosha | Treasury
  [37:4:0.5] 6 | Danda / Bala | Army, force
  [37:4:0.6] 7 | Mitra | Ally – "the ear of the state"; the seventh limb (UPPCS 2015)
[37:4:1] - **Order varies by book** (PMF: Swami, Amatya, Durga, Danda, Janapada, Kosha, Mitra) but **Swami is first and Mitra last** in every list.
[37:4:2] - **Saptanga includes king, territory, administration (ministers) and treasury** (NDA 2010) – not ragas, monks or traders.
[37:4:3] - **Shatru (enemy)** is NOT one of the standard seven; NextGen adds it only as an eighth. Allies help in peace and war; natural allies are better than artificial ones.
[37:4:4] - **Nature of the state:** **highly centralised and bureaucratic** (AP High Court 2026) – "**paternal despotism**", the king heading executive, legislature and judiciary.
[37:4:5] - **Checks:** the **Mantriparishad**; Kautilya – "**a chariot cannot move on one wheel**" (the king needs ministers).
[37:4:6] - **Mauryan achievements** (UPPSC 1990): culture, art and literature; **provincial division**; kingship up to the **Hindukush** – but **not gold coins** (the Mauryan currency was punch-marked silver).
[37:4:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 02 p.107-108, p.112; NextGen Indian History APPSC 02 p.42, p.46, p.48; app notes 1:37 (sub 0, 1)
## SUB 5 | Provinces and Settlement Units
[37:5:0] TABLE head: Province | Capital
  [37:5:0.0] Uttarapatha (north) | Taxila
  [37:5:0.1] Avantipatha (west) | Ujjain
  [37:5:0.2] Dakshinapatha (south) | Suvarnagiri – southern capital, ruled the Deccan and Andhra
  [37:5:0.3] Kalinga (east, added by Ashoka) | Tosali
  [37:5:0.4] Magadha (centre) | Pataliputra
[37:5:1] - **Four provinces** under Chandragupta, ruled by **Kumaras** (princes) or viceroys with **Mahamatras**; districts = **Vish / Ahara**.
[37:5:2] TABLE head: Unit | Villages
  [37:5:2.0] Sthaniya | 800
  [37:5:2.1] Dronamukha | 400
  [37:5:2.2] Kharvatika (Karvatika) | 200
  [37:5:2.3] Sangrahana | 10
[37:5:3] - **Order:** **Sthaniya → Dronamukha → Kharvatika → Sangrahana** (largest to smallest; JPSC 2023 asks it as the "ascending" order of the hierarchy).
[37:5:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 02 p.113; NextGen Indian History APPSC 02 p.46; app notes 1:37 (sub 4)
## SUB 6 | Judiciary and Espionage
[37:6:0] TABLE head: Court | Cases | Presided by
  [37:6:0.0] Dharmasthiya | Civil – marriage, contract, inheritance | 3 dharmasthas
  [37:6:0.1] Kantakashodhana ("removal of thorns") | Criminal | 3 pradeshtris
[37:6:1] - **Pradvivaka:** chief judge / legal adviser to the king (judicial system).
[37:6:2] - **Ladder:** village court → **Sangrahana** → Dronamukha → Janapada → **king** (supreme judge).
[37:6:3] - **Punishments:** fines, maiming, death; severity varied by **varna**. Megasthenes: **no written code**.
[37:6:4] - **Spies:** **Gudhapurushas** watched officials and provinces; **Samstha** (stationary – kapatika, grihapatika, vaidehaka, tapasa) and **Sanchara** (wandering – satri, tikshna, rasada, **parivrajika**); Prativedakas were special reporters.
[37:6:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 02 p.46, p.50-51; PMF Ancient & Medieval 02 p.116; app notes 1:37 (sub 7, 8)

=== NOTES 1:40 | Early Historic Andhra – Andhras in Literature, Mauryan Contact, Early Buddhist Centres
## SUB 0 | Buddhist Texts and Jatakas on Andhra
[40:0:0] TABLE head: Name / reference | Text
  [40:0:0.0] Andhra Padha / Andhrapatha – demarcation of the Andhra region | Bhimasena Jataka (APPSC G2 2019 and G2 Mains 2019 key; NextGen) – not Vinayavatthu, Serivanija Jataka or Suttanipata
  [40:0:0.1] Andhapatha (also cited) | Vinayavatthu, in some lists
  [40:0:0.2] Andhakarattha / Andhakaratta | Buddhist literature (Pali) – the Andhra country on the Godavari, near Bavari's hermitage (APPSC G2)
  [40:0:0.3] Andhakas | Kathavatthu – a Buddhist school (Third Council)
  [40:0:0.4] Andhapura / Andhakapura = Andhranagari (Dhanyakataka) | Serivanija Jataka – reached by merchants across the river Telavaha
  [40:0:0.5] Asmaka (Assaka) king defeats Kalinga | Chulla-Kalinga Jataka – the APPSC G2 2008 key reads it as Satakarni of Asmaka defeating Kharavela of Kalinga
  [40:0:0.6] Bavari's 16 disciples | Suttanipata (Parayana-vagga)
  [40:0:0.7] Mahavamsa / Dipavamsa | Sri Lankan Buddhist chronicles
[40:0:1] - **Jain texts** have no distinctive name for the Andhra country; "Andhakaratta" is Buddhist.
[40:0:2] - **First inscriptional "Andhrapatha":** Mayidavolu copper plates of **Sivaskandavarma** (c. 300 CE).
[40:0:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History 01 p.6; NextGen previous papers p.8, p.13; https://education.sakshi.com/sites/default/files/pdf/2019/11/30/previouspapers-appsc-paper_ii_ap_social_history_and_constitution.pdf; app notes 1:40 (sub 2, 3)
## SUB 1 | Andhras in Vedic, Epic and Greek Sources
[40:1:0] TABLE head: Source | Reference
  [40:1:0.0] Aitareya Brahmana | First mention of the word "Andhra" – as a race, in the Sunahshepa story: Vishwamitra cursed his 50 sons to become Andhras, Pundras, Pulindas (APPSC SI 2011)
  [40:1:0.1] Rigveda | No mention of the Andhras – the text that does not mention the Telugu people (APPSC G2 2002); the Arthashastra and Rajatarangini do
  [40:1:0.2] Mahabharata | Andhras fought on the Kaurava side (APPSC 2011; Tribal Welfare 2012)
  [40:1:0.3] Vayu Purana | Places the Andhra people in the Deccan
  [40:1:0.4] Megasthenes' Indica | The Greek ambassador who mentions the Andhras – first foreign source; 30 walled towns (first to mention Andhra forts), 1,00,000 infantry, 2,000 cavalry, 1,000 elephants (report preserved by Pliny)
  [40:1:0.5] Ashoka's 13th Rock Edict | Andhras among peoples within the empire following his Dhamma
[40:1:1] - **Megasthenes** was the envoy of **Seleucus** – not Pliny, Ptolemy or Marco Polo, who wrote later.
[40:1:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History 01 p.6-8; app notes 1:40 (sub 0, 1, 6)
## SUB 2 | Early Buddhist Centres and Excavated Sites
[40:2:0] TABLE head: Site | Fact
  [40:2:0.0] Bhattiprolu (Guntur/Bapatla) | Oldest stupa of Andhra; very large bricks; dome 132 ft across on a base of 148 ft (the figure APPSC asked as its "height"); relic caskets name Raja Kubhiraka (Kuberaka), ruler of Bhattiprolu in the 3rd c. BCE
  [40:2:0.1] Dhanyakataka (Amaravati–Dharanikota) | On the Krishna in Andhra; Buddhist centre of the Mahasanghikas; capital of the later Satavahanas; Buddhism here predates the Mauryas (UPSC 2023)
  [40:2:0.2] Gottiprolu (Nellore region) | ASI dig 2019: early-historic trade centre in a massive brick wall (2nd–1st c. BCE), near an ancient port; imitation amphorae; declared a Monument of National Importance (July 2026)
  [40:2:0.3] Gudiwada Dibba (Krishna) | Early historic mound; occupation from Mauryan to Satavahana times; Siddharthaka chaitya identified with Gudivada
  [40:2:0.4] Adurru (East Godavari) | Mahasanghika Buddhist centre
  [40:2:0.5] Vaddamanu (near Amaravati) | Jain stupa, excavated 1981–85
  [40:2:0.6] Sriparvata / Vijayapuri | Nagarjunakonda
[40:2:1] - **Guntupalli** = Rajagirika centre; **P.C. Ray** identified the river at Amaravati-Dharanikota as the Krishna.
[40:2:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen previous papers p.13; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhattiprolu (dome 132 ft, base 148 ft, citing A. Rea); app notes 1:40 (sub 8, 9)
## SUB 3 | Assaka, Mulaka and the Bavari Legend
[40:3:0] TABLE head: Janapada | Capital | Note
  [40:3:0.0] Assaka (Asmaka) | Bodhan (Potali / Podana) (APPSC G2 2012) – not Paithan, Kotilingala or Dhanyakataka | The only Mahajanapada in the Deccan, on the Godavari
  [40:3:0.1] Mulaka | Pratishthana | Neighbour of Assaka
[40:3:1] - **Bavari:** a Brahmin teacher from **Kosala** who settled on the **Godavari** in Assaka territory; sent **16 disciples** to the Buddha (Suttanipata) – Buddhism reached the Godavari region **before the Mauryan expansion**.
[40:3:2] - **Trade:** Andhra lay on the **Dakshinapatha**; merchant guilds used Kalingapatnam and later Masulipatnam.
[40:3:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History 01 p.6; app notes 1:40 (sub 4, 5)
## SUB 4 | Ashokan Edicts and Mauryan Contact
[40:4:0] - **Before the Satavahanas** Andhra was already a distinct people and region; by the 3rd c. BCE it was ruled by **Mauryan feudatories**, and the Mauryan phase made Buddhism **institutional** here.
[40:4:1] TABLE head: Site | District | Content
  [40:4:1.0] Erragudi | Kurnool (now Nandyal) | Major and minor rock edicts; teachers must inculcate Dhamma in pupils
  [40:4:1.1] Rajula Mandagiri | Kurnool | Minor rock edict (not a pillar edict)
  [40:4:1.2] Amaravati | Guntur | Fragment of an Ashokan pillar edict
[40:4:2] - **Mahadeva Bhikshu:** by Andhra tradition sent by Ashoka to **Amaravati** – first Buddhist teacher in Andhra; enshrined the Buddha's bone relics.
[40:4:3] - **End of Mauryan rule:** Andhra rulers declared independence; the **Satavahanas** rose.
[40:4:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History 01 p.6; PMF Ancient & Medieval 02 p.141; app notes 1:40 (sub 7)
