=== NOTES 1:41 | Sungas and Kanvas – Pushyamitra Sunga, Bharhut and Sanchi, Patanjali, the Besnagar Pillar
## SUB 0 | Dynastic Succession – Mauryas to Satavahanas
[41:0:0] TABLE head: Dynasty | Period | Founder | End
  [41:0:0.0] Maurya | c. 321–185 BCE | Chandragupta | Brihadratha, the last Maurya, killed by Pushyamitra
  [41:0:0.1] Sunga | c. 185–73 BCE (NextGen: from 187 BC) | Pushyamitra | Devabhuti killed by his Brahmana minister (Amatya) Vasudeva Kanva
  [41:0:0.2] Kanva | c. 73–28 BCE, 4 kings | Vasudeva Kanva | Susharman overthrown by the Andhras (Satavahanas) – Simuka
[41:0:1] - **After the Sungas came the Kanvas** (State PSC); both were **Brahmins**.
[41:0:2] - **UPSC 2003:** all three statements correct – Brihadratha killed by Pushyamitra; Devabhuti killed by Vasudeva Kanva; the last Kanva deposed by the Andhras.
[41:0:3] - **Most powerful dynasty in the south after the Mauryas:** the **Satavahanas** (UPPCS 1993); the Puranas say they defeated the Sungas and Kanvas; **Satakarni I** is said to have defeated Pushyamitra.
[41:0:4] - **Magadhan order:** **Haryanka (544–412 BC) → Shishunaga → Nanda (344–321 BC) → Maurya → Sunga → Kanva** (CGPSC 2008: Haryanka, Nanda, Maurya, Sunga); sequence Maurya – Sunga – Kanva – **Kushana**.
[41:0:5] TABLE head: Founder | Replaced | Dynasty ended
  [41:0:5.0] Pushyamitra | Brihadratha | Maurya
  [41:0:5.1] Vasudeva Kanva | Devabhuti | Sunga
  [41:0:5.2] Simuka (Sindhuk, Shiprak) | Susharma(n) | Kanva
  [41:0:5.3] Mahapadma Nanda | last Shishunaga | Shishunaga
[41:0:6] - **Mahapadma Nanda** (Ugrasena): **Sarvakshatrantaka** and Ekarat in the Puranas.
[41:0:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 02 p.106, p.139; PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.4-5, p.25; Rocket Indian History 01 p.29-30, p.93, p.95; Rocket Indian History 02 p.117; app notes 1:41 (sub 0)
## SUB 1 | Pushyamitra Sunga – Coup, Ashvamedhas and Buddhism
[41:1:0] - **Mauryan commander-in-chief (senani)**, a **Brahmin**; killed Brihadratha while showing him the army (Harshacharita) – the last Mauryan king was killed by **Pushyamitra Shunga** (APPSC 2023), not Dattamitra, Vibhuti or Indrabhattarika.
[41:1:1] - **Ancestors of the Sungas came from Ujjain** (MPPSC 2018); heartland **Magadha, Malwa–Vidisha, Narmada valley**.
[41:1:2] - **Two Ashvamedhas** – recorded in the **Ayodhya inscription of Dhanadeva** (UPPCS 2018) – not Sarnath, Besnagar or Hathigumpha; not three.
[41:1:3] - **Wars:** beat the Indo-Greeks (Demetrius), fought the Deccan powers and **Kharavela** of Kalinga.
[41:1:4] - **Buddhism:** Pushyamitra **did not contribute to the expansion of Buddhism** (CGPSC 2018) – unlike Ashoka, Kanishka and Harsha; the **Divyavadana** and **Taranatha** call him a persecutor, yet Bharhut and Sanchi were renovated under him (Romila Thapar, Lamotte: exaggerated). Hostility was probably aimed at monasteries allied with the **Indo-Greeks**.
[41:1:5] - **Bodhi Tree:** tradition links its destruction to Pushyamitra and later **Shashanka of Gauda**.
[41:1:6] - **Society:** feudatories rose – **Bhojas, Maharathis, Rastrikas**; classical **Sanskrit** revived; **Manusmriti** took shape, classing foreigners as **Vratya Kshatriyas**; Brahmanical revival with the rise of Bhagavatism and stone Buddhist art.
[41:1:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.4-5; Rocket Indian History 01 p.7; app notes 1:41 (sub 1, 5)
## SUB 2 | Literary Sources – Malavikagnimitram, Mahabhashya, Gargi Samhita
[41:2:0] TABLE head: Source | Author | What it gives
  [41:2:0.0] Gargi Samhita (Yuga Purana) | Garga | Yavana march on Saketa, Panchala, Mathura, Pataliputra
  [41:2:0.1] Mahabhashya | Patanjali | Yavana siege of Saketa and Madhyamika; sacrifices for Pushyamitra
  [41:2:0.2] Malavikagnimitram | Kalidasa | Love story of Agnimitra (son of Pushyamitra) and Malavika; Vasumitra beats the Yavanas on the Sindhu; war with Vidarbha
  [41:2:0.3] Divyavadana | Buddhist text | Pushyamitra as persecutor
  [41:2:0.4] Harshacharita | Banabhatta | Brihadratha killed at the army review
[41:2:1] - **Yavana invasion under Pushyamitra** is in Gargi Samhita, Mahabhashya and Malavikagnimitram – **NOT Visakhadatta's Mudrarakshasa**, which tells **Chandragupta Maurya's** rise (APPSC G1 2023).
[41:2:2] - **Malavikagnimitram:** the book with the love story of the **son of the Sunga founder** (UPSC 2016) – protagonist **Agnimitra** (UPPCS 1998), not Pushyamitra; Kalidasa's **first play**, **5 acts**; not Swapnavasavadatta, Meghaduta or Ratnavali. Mrichchhakatikam is by **Sudraka**.
[41:2:3] - **Patanjali** (Mahabhashya) was the **contemporary** and, it is believed, **royal priest** of **Pushyamitra Sunga** (UPPCS 2011) – not of Chandragupta Maurya, Ashoka or Chandragupta I; he explained **Panini's Ashtadhyayi** through **Katyayana's Varttikas**. Panini is earlier (not Pushyamitra's).
[41:2:4] TABLE head: Sunga ruler | Fact
  [41:2:4.0] Pushyamitra | Founder
  [41:2:4.1] Agnimitra | Son; viceroy at Vidisha; fought Yajnasena of Vidarbha
  [41:2:4.2] Vasumitra | Grandson; defeated the Yavanas
  [41:2:4.3] Bhagabhadra | Heliodorus came to his court
  [41:2:4.4] Devabhuti | Last Sunga
[41:2:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.4-5; NextGen Indian History APPSC 03 p.26-27; Rocket Indian History 01 p.35; app notes 1:41 (sub 2, 3, 4)
## SUB 3 | Besnagar (Heliodorus) Pillar
[41:3:0] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [41:3:0.0] Donor | Heliodorus, a Yavana from Taxila, calling himself a Bhagavata
  [41:3:0.1] Envoy of | Indo-Greek king Antialcidas
  [41:3:0.2] At the court of | Sunga king Bhagabhadra
  [41:3:0.3] Site | Besnagar (Vidisha), MP
  [41:3:0.4] Nature | Garuda-dhvaja of Vasudeva only (IAS 1998) – not Sankarshana or Pradyumna
  [41:3:0.5] Language/script | Prakrit / Brahmi
[41:3:1] - **Earliest inscriptional evidence of the Bhagavata religion** (UPPSC Mains 2008) – earlier than the Allahabad, Bhitari or Mehrauli inscriptions; shows a foreigner absorbed into an Indian religion.
[41:3:2] - **Not Gupta:** the Besnagar pillar (2nd c. BCE) is the item NOT related to Gupta art, unlike the Sarnath Buddha images, Deogarh temple and the Nalanda copper Buddha.
[41:3:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.5; PMF Art & Culture 04 p.29; app notes 1:41 (sub 6)
## SUB 4 | Sunga Art – Bharhut and Sanchi
[41:4:0] TABLE head: Site | Feature
  [41:4:0.0] Bharhut (Satna, MP) | Fine example of Sunga architecture (RPSC 2023); railings and gateways of early narrative art; inscriptions name guilds (ivory workers, stone carvers) as donors
  [41:4:0.1] Sanchi | Ashoka's brick stupa enlarged and cased in stone; railings (vedika) and toranas; gateway shows Ashoka's pilgrimage to the Bodhi tree with his two queens (MPPSC 2022)
  [41:4:0.2] Bodh Gaya | Early stone railing
  [41:4:0.3] Mathura | The Mathura school of sculpture began under the Sungas
[41:4:1] - **Transition** from wood/ivory to stone; Sanchi's south torana carries an inscription of **Ananda** linking it to **Satakarni II**, so the gateways are often dated Satavahana.
[41:4:2] - **Gupta temple architecture did not begin under the Sungas.**
[41:4:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 02 p.137; PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.4-5; app notes 1:41 (sub 7)

=== NOTES 1:42 | Indo-greeks – Menander, Milindapanho and Indo-greek Coinage
## SUB 0 | Milindapanho – Menander and Nagasena
[42:0:0] # The text
[42:0:1] - **Milindapanho (Milinda-Panha, "Questions of Milinda"):** a **Pali** Buddhist text – a dialogue on Buddhist doctrine between the Indo-Greek king **Milinda = Menander** and the Buddhist monk **Nagasena** (UPSC 1997 ×2; UPPCS 2023; UKPCS 2012).
[42:0:2] - **⚠ Trap:** the monk is **Nagasena**, not Nagarjuna (later Mahayana Madhyamika thinker), Nagabhatta (Pratihara king) or Kumarila Bhatta (Mimamsa philosopher); the text is in **Pali**, not Sanskrit.
[42:0:3] - **Which king it throws light on:** **Menander** – not Demetrius, Diodotus II or Strato I (UKPCS 2012).
[42:0:4] - **Agriculture:** the Milindapanho explains **eight phases of agricultural work** (UKPCS 2021); Avadanashataka, Aryamanjushrimulakalpa and Dipavamsa are distractors.
[42:0:5] # Menander (Milinda), c. 165-145 BCE
[42:0:6] - **Greatest Indo-Greek:** capital **Sakala (Sialkot)**, not Taxila; the only Indo-Greek king named in Indian sources; turned **Buddhist** under Nagasena.
[42:0:7] - **Coins:** early coins carry Greek deities; later ones Buddhist motifs – **elephant, bull, wheel of Dharma**.
[42:0:8] - **Bairat (Rajasthan):** a hoard of **16 coins of Menander** (RAS 2018); Nagari, Rairh and Nagar are distractors.
[42:0:9] - **Raids:** invaded the Ganga-Yamuna doab but could not hold it against the Shungas.
[42:0:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 02 p.146-147; NextGen Indian History APPSC 02 p.6; Rocket Indian History 01 p.40, p.55; app notes 1:42 (sub 2)
## SUB 1 | Indo-Greek Coins – Firsts, Deities and Metals
[42:1:0] # Firsts
[42:1:1] TABLE head: Feature | Fact
  [42:1:1.0] Coins definitely attributed to kings | First issued by the Indo-Greeks – first inscribed coins with names and portraits of kings
  [42:1:1.1] Gold coins | First issued in India by the Indo-Greeks (rare); increased under the Kushanas
  [42:1:1.2] Metals | Mostly silver, also copper; gold rare
  [42:1:1.3] Legends | Bilingual: Greek on the obverse, Prakrit in Kharoshthi on the reverse (rarely Brahmi)
  [42:1:1.4] Number of kings | More than 30 Indo-Greek kings are known mainly from their coins
[42:1:2] - **Kushana trap:** Kushana coins did NOT precede Indo-Greek portrait coins; Indo-Greeks = first gold, **Kushanas** = large-scale gold.
[42:1:3] # Indian deities on coins
[42:1:4] - **Sankarshana (Balarama) and Vasudeva (Krishna):** on the coins of **Agathocles** (c. 190-180 BCE) from **Ai-Khanoum** – the first known depiction of Krishna (UPPCS Mains 2017); not Huvishka, Kanishka or Samudragupta.
[42:1:5]   - Agathocles held the Paropamisadae and also issued **Greek + Brahmi** coins.
[42:1:6] - **Indian deities on Indo-Greek coins = Agathocles:** a question asking which Indo-Greek ruler "issued coins depicting Indian deities" is answered **Agathocles**; Menander's coins carry Buddhist **symbols** (wheel, elephant), not Indian deities (APPSC ASO; printed key Menander I).
[42:1:7] - **Balarama holds the plough** (hala) – hence **Halayudha**; Krishna, Kartikeya and Maitreya are not shown with it (UPPSC Mains 2007).
[42:1:8] # Other coin facts
[42:1:9] - **Lead coins:** **Strato II** (UPPSC 2014); Strato I, Demetrius and Menander are distractors.
[42:1:10] - **Largest ancient gold coin:** **Eucratides** (20 staters).
[42:1:11] - **Other early coinages:** Saka-Kshatrapas (Rudradaman) – **silver and copper**; **Chandragupta II** – silver **Rupaka** after defeating the Sakas; **Muhammad Ghori** – coins with **Lakshmi**, some with the Arabic **Kalma**; Kanishka – the Buddha; Mahmud of Ghazni – silver coins with Arabic and Sanskrit legends.
[42:1:12] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 02 p.147-148; Rocket Indian History 01 p.55; app notes 1:42 (sub 1, 3, 8); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agathocles_of_Bactria
## SUB 2 | Bactria, Rulers and the Order of Invaders
[42:2:0] - **Bactria (north Afghanistan):** the Indo-Greek kingdom set up there at the start of the 2nd century BC (UPSC 1999); Scythia = land of the Sakas, Gedrosia = **Balochistan**, Aria = Herat region.
[42:2:1] - **Independence:** **Diodotus** revolted against the **Seleucids** (mid-3rd c. BCE) and founded the Graeco-Bactrian kingdom.
[42:2:2] - **Why they came south:** Scythian (Saka) pressure behind them and the weak successors of Ashoka in India.
[42:2:3] TABLE head: Ruler | Exam fact
  [42:2:3.0] Demetrius | First Bactrian Greek to cross the Hindu Kush and invade India (c. 180 BCE); Greek defeat is credited to Pushyamitra Shunga, and Kharavela's Hathigumpha mentions a Yavana king retreating
  [42:2:3.1] Menander | Greatest; Sakala; Milindapanho
  [42:2:3.2] Antialcidas | Sent Heliodorus to Vidisha
  [42:2:3.3] Eucratides | 20-stater gold coin
  [42:2:3.4] Strato | Menander's son; Strato II issued lead coins
  [42:2:3.5] Hermaius | Last; Greek rule south of the Hindu Kush ended with him
[42:2:4] - **Raids:** Patanjali's **Mahabhashya** says the Yavanas reached **Saketa** and **Madhyamika**; the Yuga Purana takes them towards **Pataliputra**.
[42:2:5] - **Successors:** the **Sakas** replaced the Indo-Greeks first (Azes defeated the last Indo-Greek kings), then the Parthians, then the Kushanas.
[42:2:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 02 p.145-146; PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.5; app notes 1:42 (sub 0, 1)
## SUB 3 | Greek Impact – Military Governors, Heliodorus and Culture
[42:3:0] - **Military governorship:** first introduced in India by the **Greeks** (UPSC 2000) – governors called **strategos**; not the Shakas, Parthians or Mughals.
[42:3:1] - **Heliodorus:** a **Bhagavata** from **Takshashila (Taxila)** (UP UDA/LDA 2010), envoy of **Antialcidas** to the Shunga king **Bhagabhadra**; set up the **Besnagar (Vidisha) Garuda pillar** in honour of **Vasudeva**.
[42:3:2] - **Other envoys:** **Daimachos** – Antiochus I to **Bindusara**; **Megasthenes** – Seleucus I to Chandragupta Maurya.
[42:3:3] - **Why foreigners chose Buddhism:** Greeks, Kushanas and Shakas embraced Buddhism because it **provided easier access to Indian society** – no caste barrier to entry (UPSC 1998); "caste-ridden Hinduism did not attract them" is the tempting half-truth.
[42:3:4] - **Absorption:** the Smritis call the absorbed Greeks **Vratya Kshatriyas** (second-class Kshatriyas).
[42:3:5] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [42:3:5.0] Yavanika | Stage / theatre curtain
  [42:3:5.1] Hora | Horoscope
  [42:3:5.2] Romaka Siddhanta | Greek influence on Indian astronomy
[42:3:6] - **Art:** Hellenistic art fed the **Gandhara** school of the Kushana period.
[42:3:7] - **Philosophical exchange:** Milindapanho; religious interaction: Heliodorus; artistic synthesis: Gandhara.
[42:3:8] - **Match:** Milindapanho – Menander; **Taxila copper plate – Patika** (a Shaka); Junagadh – Rudradaman I; Gandhara art – Kushanas.
[42:3:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.5-6, p.20-21; PMF Ancient & Medieval 02 p.148; app notes 1:42 (sub 2, 5)

=== NOTES 1:46 | Satavahanas – Origin, Simuka, Gautamiputra Satakarni, Nasik Prasasti, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi
## SUB 0 | Founder, Firsts and Independence from the Mauryas
[46:0:0] # The firsts
[46:0:1] - **First historical ruling dynasty of the Deccan:** the **Satavahanas** (c. 200 BC – 200 AD), the oldest Deccan dynasty (Sainik Welfare 2012; UP 2001).
[46:0:2]   - Distractors: Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Cholas, Pallavas – all centuries later.
[46:0:3] - **First dynasty to rule Andhra:** the **Satavahanas** (G1 2010 re-exam; G1 PYQ); not the Cholas, Eastern Chalukyas or Rashtrakutas.
[46:0:4] - **Puranic name:** the Puranas call them **Andhras** or **Andhrabhrityas** ("servants of the Andhras", or Andhras who had been feudatories); the dynasty identified with the Puranic Andhras = Satavahanas.
[46:0:5] - **Caste:** **Brahmins**; the Nasik inscription calls Gautamiputra **"Ekabrahmana"** (APPSC PYQ).
[46:0:6] - **⚠ Trap:** they claimed **Brahmana** status, not Buddhist descent – a statement "Satavahanas claimed Buddhist descent" is false.
[46:0:7] # Founder – Simuka
[46:0:8] - **Founder:** **Simuka** = Simukha = Srimukha = Shimukha (Puranic "Sinthaka"); asked 13 times (G2 2000, 2008; Geologist 2007; SI 2011; UPPSC 2008).
[46:0:9] - **Founder of the administration too:** Simuka (G2 2008); he united several principalities into one kingdom.
[46:0:10] - **Rise:** killed the **Kanva** king **Susarma** and ended the Kanvas; ruled from **Pratishthana**; said to have ruled 23 years.
[46:0:11] - **Progenitor:** per the **Puranas = Srimukha**; per inscriptions, coins and Kathasaritsagara = **Satavahana** (Srimukha's father) – exams answer Simuka.
[46:0:12] - **Successors:** brother **Kanha (Krishna)**, 2nd king; then son **Satakarni I**, 3rd king. Purnotsanga (Vedasri) and Kanha are distractors for "founder".
[46:0:13] # Independence and span
[46:0:14] - **Freedom from the Mauryas:** the Satavahanas began as Mauryan feudatories; the Andhras won freedom from Mauryan rule under them (APPSC PYQ).
[46:0:15] - **Rule of ~450 years:** after Mauryan decline they ruled the Deccan for **456 years** (Matsya Purana) – "about 450 years" (Social & Cultural History of AP).
[46:0:16] - **Ashoka's 13th Rock Edict:** lists the Andhras among his vassal peoples.
[46:0:17] - **Sequence in Magadha:** Mauryas → Sungas → Kanvas → Satavahanas.
[46:0:18] - **Successor states:** Ikshvakus (Andhra), Abhiras (Maharashtra), Chutus (Karnataka), Pallavas (Tamil Nadu), Vakatakas (Vidarbha).
[46:0:19] > Statement angle: "Founded by Simuka" ✓; "claimed Buddhist descent" ✗; "long conflict with the Sakas over the premier (western) ports" ✓ (Periplus) → answer "1 and 3".
[46:0:20] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.5-7, p.12; Rocket AP History p.3, p.22, p.46, p.56; app notes 1:46 (sub 0, 3)
## SUB 1 | Nasik Prasasti and Gautamiputra's Conquests
[46:1:0] # Nasik Prasasti – the record
[46:1:1] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [46:1:1.0] Issuer | Gautami Balasri, mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni
  [46:1:1.1] Date | 19th regnal year of her grandson Vasishthiputra Pulumavi (G2 2008)
  [46:1:1.2] Place | Nasik, Pandavleni Cave 3 (Maharashtra)
  [46:1:1.3] Language, script | Prakrit prose, Brahmi
  [46:1:1.4] Content | Gautamiputra's military victories, empire and titles
[46:1:2] - **Most-asked fact:** the inscription describing Gautamiputra's achievements = **Nasik** (G1 1987; G2 2008; Welfare Officers; APPSC PYQ ×3).
[46:1:3] - **⚠ Trap:** issued by **Gautami Balasri in Pulumavi's reign**, not by Gautamiputra and not in his reign.
[46:1:4] - **⚠ Trap:** Naneghat = Naganika (Satakarni I); Kodavali = Chanda Satakarni; Hathigumpha = Kharavela; Junnar, Pitalkhora = distractors.
[46:1:5] - **Gift recorded:** a village and **100 nivartanas** of land to monks on **Trirashmi** hill.
[46:1:6] # Conquests
[46:1:7] - **Nahapana:** Gautamiputra defeated the **Kshaharata Saka** king **Nahapana** (G1 1990-91); not Pulumayi, Yajna or Rudra Satakarni.
[46:1:8] - **Lost lands regained:** Malwa, Saurashtra, Konkan, Nasik regained from Nahapana in Gautamiputra's reign (G2 2000).
[46:1:9] - **Enemy faced:** the **Sakas** (not Hunas, Greeks or Parthians); praised as "destroyer of **Sakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas**".
[46:1:10] - **Jogalthambi hoard (Nasik district):** **13,270** silver coins of Nahapana **restruck** by Gautamiputra – proof of the victory.
[46:1:11] # Regions named in the Prasasti
[46:1:12] TABLE head: Region | Area
  [46:1:12.0] Anupa | Narmada valley, capital Mahishmati (G2 2017 ×2; APPSC PYQ)
  [46:1:12.1] Akara / Avanti | East Malwa (Vidisha) / West Malwa (Ujjain)
  [46:1:12.2] Asika, Asaka (Asmaka), Mulaka | Godavari valley, Paithan area
  [46:1:12.3] Suratha, Kukura | Saurashtra; western Malwa–Rajasthan
  [46:1:12.4] Aparanta / Vidarbha | North Konkan / Berar
[46:1:13] - **⚠ Trap:** Vidisha and Ujjain are Akara and Avanti, not Anupa; Podana is a distractor.
[46:1:14] # Social claims
[46:1:15] - **Protector of the varna system:** **Varnasankarya-nirodhaka** – stopped the mixing of the four varnas (Chhattisgarh PSC 2013); not Pushyamitra, Kharavela or Vasudeva.
[46:1:16] - **Brahmanical image:** Ekabrahmana, "crusher of Kshatriya pride" (Kshatriya-darpa-mana-mardana), Agama-nilaya.
[46:1:17] - **⚠ Sources differ:** NextGen says he "started the Salivahana era (AD 78)".
[46:1:18]   - Settled: 78 CE begins the **Shaka era**, tied to Chashtana's accession; the "Salivahana era" is a later legend (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaka_era).
[46:1:19] - **Dates:** traditionally c. 106-130 CE (23rd king, ruled 34 years per NextGen); some scholars now prefer c. 60-85 CE.
[46:1:20] - **Ayama:** minister of the Kshaharata **Nahapana** – linked with the **Junnar** inscription (a Kshaharata record, not Satavahana); Ushavadatta was Nahapana's son-in-law.
[46:1:21] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.10, p.25; Rocket AP History p.6, p.8; app notes 1:46 (sub 4, 5); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gautamiputra_Satakarni; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaka_era
## SUB 2 | Queens and Metronymics
[46:2:0] # Queens
[46:2:1] TABLE head: Queen | Role
  [46:2:1.0] Devi Naganika | Wife of Satakarni I; daughter of Maharathi Tranakayiro (Amgiya family); regent for her minor son; issued Naneghat
  [46:2:1.1] Gautami Balasri | Mother of Gautamiputra; issued the Nasik Prasasti; gave a Nasik cave vihara to Bhadrayaniya monks
  [46:2:1.2] Lilavati | Sri Lankan princess, queen of Hala – distractor
[46:2:2] - **Regent queen:** **Devi Naganika** ruled as guardian during her son's minority (G2 2019; APPSC PYQ ×2).
[46:2:3] - **Whose queen:** Naganika = queen of **Satakarni I** (APSLPRB 2023; APPSC PYQ) – not Srimukha, Satakarni II or Gautamiputra.
[46:2:4] - **Her father:** Maharathi **Tranakayiro** – the marriage allied the Satavahanas with the Maharathis (APPSC PYQ ×2).
[46:2:5] - **⚠ Trap:** regent = Naganika, not Gautami Balasri; Devi Mathari, Rudradamanika, Chashtana's or Nahapana's daughter are distractors.
[46:2:6] # Metronymics
[46:2:7] - **What:** kings put their **mother's name** before their own – Gautamiputra (son of Gautami), Vasishthiputra.
[46:2:8] - **Began with:** **Gautamiputra Satakarni** (G2 2008 key; asked 6 times) – not Simuka, Hala or Vasishthiputra Pulumavi.
[46:2:9] - **Precisely:** the prefix is the **mother's gotra** name (Gotami < Gautama, Vasithi < Vasishtha) (JA Panchayat Raj 2012).
[46:2:10] - **Dynasty known by metronymics:** the **Satavahanas** (CDS 2020) – not the Mallas, Videhas or Yaudheyas.
[46:2:11] - **Meaning:** usually explained by **polygamy**; shows respect for mothers, but succession stayed **patriarchal**.
[46:2:12] > Statement angle: "Gautamiputra took pride in calling himself son of Gautami" ✓ (Sachivalayam).
[46:2:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.7, p.10, p.15; Rocket AP History p.53; app notes 1:46 (sub 7)
## SUB 3 | Key Kings in the Matsya List
[46:3:0] TABLE head: No. | King | Exam fact
  [46:3:0.0] 1 | Simuka | Founder; ended the Kanvas
  [46:3:0.1] 2 | Kanha (Krishna) | First Satavahana inscription (Nasik); expanded to Nasik
  [46:3:0.2] 3 | Satakarni I | Greatest early king; 2 Ashvamedhas; Dakshinapathapati; Kharavela's contemporary
  [46:3:0.3] 6 | Satakarni II | Longest reign, 56 years; southern torana of Sanchi
  [46:3:0.4] 13 | Kuntala Satakarni | Made Sanskrit the royal language
  [46:3:0.5] 17 | Hala | Gathasaptasati; Kavivatsala; ruled 5 years
  [46:3:0.6] 23 | Gautamiputra Satakarni | Greatest of all; last of the early Satavahanas
  [46:3:0.7] 24 | Vasishthiputra Pulumavi (Pulomavi II) | Nasik Prasasti issued; capital to Amaravati; Navanagaraswami
  [46:3:0.8] – | Vasishthiputra (Sivasri) Satakarni | Married Rudradaman's daughter
  [46:3:0.9] 27 | Yajnasri Satakarni | Greatest of the later kings; Nagarjuna's patron; ship coins
  [46:3:0.10] – | Chanda Sri (Chandasri) | Kodavali inscription
  [46:3:0.11] 30 | Pulomavi III | Last king; Myakadoni inscription
[46:3:1] - **Greatest Satavahana:** **Gautamiputra Satakarni** (APPSC PYQ); **⚠ Trap:** Yajnasri = greatest of the **later** kings.
[46:3:2] - **Successor of Gautamiputra:** **Vasishthiputra Pulumavi** – "succeeded by Yajnasri" is false (Sachivalayam).
[46:3:3] - **Navanagara (new city):** built by **Pulomavi II**, title Navanagaraswami (G2 2000 backlog).
[46:3:4] - **Rudradaman's son-in-law:** **(Vasishthiputra/Sivasri) Satakarni**; Rudradaman twice defeated him but spared him as a near relative (Junagadh) (APPSC PYQ).
[46:3:5] - **Nagarjuna at whose court:** **Yajnasri Satakarni** (Sachivalayam) – not Pulomavi III, Satakarni I or Srimukha.
[46:3:6] - **Last king (Puranas):** **Pulomavi III**, the 30th (G2 2011 ×2); Sivasri, Vijayasri, Chandrasri are distractors.
[46:3:7] - **⚠ Trap:** the APPSC 2011 key printed **Chandasri**, but the Matsya list ends with Pulomavi; our key is Pulomavi III. Rocket numbers the Myakadoni king "Pulumavi IV".
[46:3:8] # End of the dynasty
[46:3:9] - **Fall:** the Ikshvaku **Santamula (Srisantamula)** overthrew Pulomavi III (c. AD 225-230) and took Dharanikota and Nagarjunakonda; Pulomavi III spent his last days at **Myakadoni** (Bellary).
[46:3:10] > A-R angle: "Dynasty ended in the mid-3rd century CE" ✓; "break-up paved the way for the Ikshvakus" ✓ – but R is a result, not the cause → both true, R not the explanation.
[46:3:11] - **Bodhisri's king:** Upasika **Bodhisri** made her gifts at Nagarjunakonda in the reign of the Ikshvaku **Virapurushadatta** – the golden age of Buddhism there.
[46:3:12] - **Recovery from the Western Kshatrapas:** **Yajnasri Satakarni** won back the lost territory late in the dynasty's history.
[46:3:13] - **First silver coins:** issued by **Satakarni I**.
[46:3:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.5-11; Rocket AP History p.5; app notes 1:46 (sub 2, 3)
## SUB 4 | Royal Titles
[46:4:0] TABLE head: Title | King
  [46:4:0.0] Dakshinapathapati, Apratihatachakra (Naneghat) | Satakarni I
  [46:4:0.1] Kavivatsala (lover of poets) | Hala
  [46:4:0.2] Ekabrahmana, Varnasankarya-nirodhaka, Kshatriya-darpa-mana-mardana, Agama-nilaya, Trisamudra-toya-pita-vahana | Gautamiputra Satakarni
  [46:4:0.3] Dakshinapatheshwara, Navanagaraswami | Vasishthiputra Pulumavi
  [46:4:0.4] Trisamudradhipati (lord of the three oceans) | Yajnasri Satakarni (Harshacharita)
[46:4:1] - **Dakshinapathapati:** **Satakarni I (Sri Satakarni)**, the earliest Satavahana king to win wide recognition; named so in Naganika's **Naneghat** inscription (Sachivalayam; Welfare Officers; APPSC PYQ).
[46:4:2] - **Kavivatsala:** **Hala** (G2 2008 ×2; APPSC PYQ); distractors Madhava Varma III, Rajaraja Narendra, Gautamiputra.
[46:4:3] - **Trisamudra-toya-pita-vahana:** Gautamiputra, "whose horses drank the waters of the three oceans" (Nasik).
[46:4:4] - **⚠ Sources differ:** Rocket gives "Trisamudradhipati" to Gautamiputra, NextGen to Yajnasri.
[46:4:5]   - Settled: Bana's Harshacharita calls Nagarjuna's friend "Satavahana, the lord of the three oceans" = Yajnasri (https://franpritchett.com/00litlinks/harshacharita/chapter08.htm).
[46:4:6] - **Exam rule:** if Yajnasri is not an option, mark **Gautamiputra** (APPSC PYQ key; distractors Vikramaditya VI, Pulakeshi II, Vinayaditya).
[46:4:7] - **⚠ Trap:** Dakshinapath**apati** = Satakarni I; Dakshinapath**eshwara** = Vasishthiputra Pulumavi.
[46:4:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.3, p.8-10; Rocket AP History p.47; app notes 1:46 (sub 6); https://franpritchett.com/00litlinks/harshacharita/chapter08.htm
## SUB 5 | Origin Debate – Sukthankar and Others
[46:5:0] - **V.S. Sukthankar:** "**Andhras and Satavahanas are not the same**" (G2 2012; APPSC PYQ ×2).
[46:5:1] - **Sukthankar again:** Satavahanas were **not Andhras but Andhrabhrityas** (G2 2008 ×2; printed "V.N. Sukthankar").
[46:5:2] - **Bellary theory:** Sukthankar placed their home in **Bellary (Ballari)** on the basis of the **Myakadoni** inscription (G2 2017 – "Macedonian" is a misprint for Myakadoni; G2 PYQ).
[46:5:3] - **⚠ Trap:** **R.G. Bhandarkar** held the opposite – Andhras and Satavahanas were the same people.
[46:5:4] - **Distractors:** V.V. Mirashi, S.A. Joglekar, P.T. Srinivasa Iyengar, V.A. Smith, Rapson, Gopalachari.
[46:5:5] TABLE head: Scholar | View
  [46:5:5.0] V.V. Mirashi | Home in Vidarbha (Berar)
  [46:5:5.1] E.J. Rapson, R.G. Bhandarkar | Origin in eastern Deccan (Andhra), from Puranic "Andhra" names
  [46:5:5.2] Gopalachari | Rejected Bellary; favoured Maharashtra
  [46:5:5.3] D.C. Sircar | Andhras, not Andhrabhrityas
  [46:5:5.4] K.A. Nilakanta Sastri | Andhra = tribal, Satavahana = dynastic, Satakarni = family name
  [46:5:5.5] B.S.L. Hanumantha Rao | Belonged to the original Andhra janapada
  [46:5:5.6] R.S. Sharma | Dravidians
[46:5:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 1:46 (sub 1); Rocket AP History p.6
## SUB 6 | Capitals
[46:6:0] - **Principal capital / main town:** **Pratishthana (Paithan)** on the **Godavari**, Aurangabad district, Maharashtra (Welfare Officers; UP Lower 2008; AMVI 2009; APPSC PYQ).
[46:6:1] - **Andhra capital:** **Dhanyakataka** (Dharanikota, near Amaravati, on the Krishna) (APPSC PYQ); distractors Vengi (E. Chalukyas), Warangal (Kakatiyas), Kondapur.
[46:6:2] - **Shift east:** after Rudradaman's attacks **Vasishthiputra Pulumavi** moved the capital to **Amaravati (Dhanyakataka)**.
[46:6:3] - **Current link:** **Amaravati**, the designated capital of Andhra Pradesh today, was the historical Satavahana capital (APPSC AEE).
[46:6:4] - **Only-option rule:** if Paithan is absent, mark **Amaravati** (UPPCS Mains 2005; distractors Nanded, Naldurg, Durg).
[46:6:5] - **First capital – debated:** Srikakulam, Krishna dt (Barnett, V.A. Smith, Burgess); Pratishthana (Mirashi, Raychaudhuri); Dhanyakataka (Bhandarkar).
[46:6:6] - **⚠ Trap:** Taxila, Kanchi, Pataliputra, Arikamedu, Nagarjunakonda (Ikshvaku capital Vijayapuri) are not Satavahana capitals.
[46:6:7] - **Other centres:** Kotilingala (Karimnagar) – claimed early centre; Mahishmati – capital of Anupa.
[46:6:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.5, p.10; Rocket AP History p.42, p.54; app notes 1:46 (sub 9)
## SUB 7 | Sources – Puranas, Literature, Foreign Accounts
[46:7:0] # Puranas
[46:7:1] - **Main Purana:** the **Matsya Purana** – genealogy and reign of each king; Satavahana political history rests on it (Welfare Officers).
[46:7:2] - **Matsya figures:** **30 kings, 456 years** (271 BC – 174 AD); kings 1-23 = early, 24-30 = later Satavahanas.
[46:7:3] - **Compiled under:** **Yajnasri Satakarni** (APPSC PYQ).
[46:7:4] - **Vayu / Vishnu:** 17 kings, 272 years – not treated as standard.
[46:7:5] - **⚠ Trap:** the **Vishnudharmottara Purana** (Chitrasutra) is the "sourcebook of Indian painting", not a Satavahana source (Animal Husbandry GS).
[46:7:6] # Literature
[46:7:7] - **Early Satavahana history:** told in **Kathasaritsagara, Pratishthanapura-kalpa, Dvatrimsatputtalika**.
[46:7:8] - **⚠ Trap:** the **Gathasaptasati** does **not** narrate early Satavahana history (G2 2017; APPSC PYQ).
[46:7:9] # Kharavela
[46:7:10] - **Contemporary:** Kharavela of Kalinga was the contemporary of **Satakarni I** (G2-B 1989); the Hathigumpha inscription and the Chulakalinga Jataka record the contact.
[46:7:11] - **⚠ Sources differ:** NextGen says Kharavela "attacked and defeated" Satakarni I.
[46:7:12]   - Settled: Hathigumpha line 4 says he sent an army west "disregarding Satakarni", to the Kanhabenna; no defeat is recorded (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hathigumpha_inscription).
[46:7:13] # Foreign accounts
[46:7:14] TABLE head: Writer | Work / fact
  [46:7:14.0] Megasthenes | Indica; first foreign source on the Andhras
  [46:7:14.1] Pliny | Natural History (Latin); Roman gold drained to India
  [46:7:14.2] Periplus (anonymous Greek) | Saka–Satavahana conflict; Koddura the only east-coast port; Arikamedu
  [46:7:14.3] Ptolemy | Geography; Pulumavi vs Chashtana; Maisolia a great market
[46:7:15] - **⚠ Sources differ:** NextGen: Megasthenes gives the Andhras "30 forts and one lakh infantry"; app notes: Pliny's army figures.
[46:7:16]   - Settled: Pliny quoting Megasthenes – **30 walled towns, 1,00,000 foot, 2,000 horse, 1,000 elephants** (https://www.philipharland.com/Blog/2023/06/indians-taprobanians-and-serians-pliny-the-elder-on-peoples-and-customs-in-india-and-beyond-first-century-ce/)
[46:7:17] - **Kanhabenna:** the Hathigumpha inscription's name for the **Krishna** river.
[46:7:18] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.3-5, p.7; app notes 1:46 (sub 2); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hathigumpha_inscription
## SUB 8 | Other Inscriptions – Issuer and Findspot
[46:8:0] TABLE head: Inscription | Issuer / king | Fact | Findspot
  [46:8:0.0] Kodavali | Chanda Satakarni | Later Satavahana record | Near Pithapuram, East Godavari (now Kakinada district)
  [46:8:0.1] Naneghat | Devi Naganika | Satakarni I's sacrifices and gifts | Naneghat pass, Pune
  [46:8:0.2] Nasik (Kanha) | Krishna, 2nd king | First Satavahana inscription | Nasik
  [46:8:0.3] Karle | Vasishthiputra Pulumavi (Pulomavi II) | Village to Mahasanghika monks | Karle, Pune
  [46:8:0.4] Amaravati | Pulomavi II | First AP inscription; Telugu word "Nagabu" | Amaravati
  [46:8:0.5] Myakadoni | Pulomavi III | Fall of the dynasty; officer Gulmika | Bellary, Karnataka
  [46:8:0.6] Kanheri | Queen of Vasishthiputra Satakarni | She was Rudradaman's daughter | Mumbai
  [46:8:0.7] Junagadh | Rudradaman | First complete Sanskrit inscription | Gujarat
  [46:8:0.8] Chinaganjam | Yajnasri | Donation to the Buddha | Prakasam
[46:8:1] - **Kodavali:** = Chanda Satakarni (G2 2017 ×3); distractors Kanheri, Amaravati, Karle.
[46:8:2] - **⚠ Outdated:** Kodavali's district "East Godavari" — now **Kakinada district** (2022 AP district reorganisation).
[46:8:3] - **Karle village grant:** to Mahasanghika monks by **Pulomavi II** (APPSC PYQ); ⚠ the king's name is damaged – Senart reads Vasishthiputra Pulumavi; a separate Karajaka record names Gautamiputra.
[46:8:4] - **Earliest inscriptions:** of the early kings are in **Maharashtra** (Naneghat, Kanha's Nasik) (G2 PYQ) – not Andhra, Karnataka or Telangana.
[46:8:5] - **Language:** all in **Prakrit**, **Brahmi** script.
[46:8:6] - **Patagandigudem copper plates:** of the Ikshvaku king **Ehuvala Chamtamula** (3rd c. CE) – the earliest known copper-plate land grant of south India; they record a grant to a **Buddhist monastery**.
[46:8:7] - **Bhairavakonda:** a **Saiva** centre with **eight** rock-cut caves, in **Nellore** district.
[46:8:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.6, p.10-11; Rocket AP History p.6; app notes 1:46 (sub 8)

=== NOTES 1:47 | Satavahana Administration, Economy, Coinage and Prakrit Literature (hala's Gathasaptasati)
## SUB 0 | Gathasaptasati and Hala
[47:0:0] - **Compiler:** the Satavahana king **Hala** (17th king, ruled 5 years), himself a poet – the most repeated fact of the topic (G2-A 1984, G2-B 1989, G2-A 1991, G2 2008 ×2; Welfare Officers 2017 ×2; APPSC PYQ ×5).
[47:0:1] - **Distractors:** Gunadhya, Sarvavarma, Kuntala Satakarni, Shudraka, Pulomavi, Lilavati, Rudramadevi, Yajnasri.
[47:0:2] - **Work:** **Gathasaptasati** (Sattasai) – **700** Prakrit gathas, in **Maharashtri Prakrit**.
[47:0:3] - **Themes:** **love and romance**, rural life and nature (G2 PYQ statement ✓); first work to cover all the **Navarasas**.
[47:0:4] - **Women poets:** **Anulakshmi, Anupalabdha (Anupamalabdha), Reva (Revati), Madhavi** – the text "containing writing by women" (G2 PYQ; APPSC PYQ); not Brihatkatha, Kamasutra or Lilavati.
[47:0:5] - **Religion in it:** opens with a prayer to **Shiva**, ends with a Gauri stotra; names Gauri, Indra, Ganesha; Radha-Krishna stories.
[47:0:6] - **Social picture:** sugar and jaggery, hanging of criminals, sati, no child marriage, prostitution, group dances, plight of wives of seafaring merchants.
[47:0:7] - **Desi (Telugu) words:** atta, addam, potta, pilla, padi, pandi, tuppu – earliest traces of Telugu.
[47:0:8] - **⚠ Trap:** a source for **society**, not for early **political** history (G2 2017).
[47:0:9] # Hala
[47:0:10] - **Title:** **Kavivatsala**; honoured poets **Kumarila** and **Sripalita**; married the Sri Lankan princess **Lilavati**.
[47:0:11] - **Golden age of Prakrit:** Hala's reign. **⚠ Trap:** NextGen p.23 prints "golden age of Sanskrit" – its own p.9 says Prakrit; Sanskrit was Kuntala Satakarni's cause.
[47:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.1-2, p.9, p.23; Rocket AP History p.9, p.52; app notes 1:47 (sub 10)
## SUB 1 | Guilds (Srenis) and Guild Banking
[47:1:0] - **Shreni:** guild of traders or artisans of one craft; fixed work rules, **quality and prices**, controlled its members' conduct; head = **Shreshthi (Sethi / Setti)**.
[47:1:1] - **⚠ Trap:** guilds existed in **north and south** India – "prevalent only in northern India" is the untrue statement (State PSC).
[47:1:2] - **Number:** **18** guilds in Satavahana records; they later hardened into castes.
[47:1:3] TABLE head: Guild | Members
  [47:1:3.0] Kolika | Weavers (strongest guild; Padmashalis) (G2 2019 ×2)
  [47:1:3.1] Padhika (Vadhaka) | Carpenters (G2 2012; APPSC PYQ)
  [47:1:3.2] Kularika | Potters (JA Panchayat Raj 2012)
  [47:1:3.3] Gandhika | Perfumers – noted donors to Buddhist causes (JA NTR UHS)
  [47:1:3.4] Tilapishaka | Oil pressers
  [47:1:3.5] Udayantrika | Makers / operators of water machines
  [47:1:3.6] Halika | Farmers
  [47:1:3.7] Malakara | Florists
  [47:1:3.8] Kasakara / Kamara / Suvarnakara | Brass workers / blacksmiths / goldsmiths
  [47:1:3.9] Chammakara | Leather workers
[47:1:4] - **⚠ Trap:** butchers = Katika, oil pressers = Ganugavaru, weavers = Salevaru – distractors for Padhika.
[47:1:5] # Guilds as banks
[47:1:6] - **Interest:** guilds took deposits and lent at **12% a year** (1% a month) (G2 2008 ×2; G2 2019 ×2).
[47:1:7] - **Rishabhadatta (Ushavadatta):** Nahapana's son-in-law; his **Nasik inscription** records **2,000 karshapanas** with the **Govardhana weavers' guild** at 12% for monks' robes (G2 2017; G2 PYQ; APPSC PYQ).
[47:1:8]   - A second deposit: 1,000 karshapanas at 3/4% a month. NextGen says "borrowed" – the inscription records a permanent deposit.
[47:1:9] - **⚠ Trap:** Sopara, Kanheri and Pratishthana inscriptions are distractors.
[47:1:10] - **Not Satavahana guilds:** **Chitrameli** = guild of **agriculturists** in medieval Deccan and South India (G2 2019); **Nigamalu** = Ikshvaku trade guilds.
[47:1:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.17-18; Rocket AP History p.41, p.48; app notes 1:47 (sub 4)
## SUB 2 | Other Works and Authors
[47:2:0] TABLE head: Work | Author | Note
  [47:2:0.0] Katantra Vyakaranam | Sarvavarma (Sharvavarma) | Short Sanskrit grammar, for Kuntala Satakarni
  [47:2:0.1] Brihatkatha | Gunadhya | Paishachi Prakrit; seven stories; lost; source of Kathasaritsagara
  [47:2:0.2] Lilavati Parinayam | Kutuhala | Prakrit; Hala marries Lilavati at Draksharama
  [47:2:0.3] Prajnaparamita Shastra | Acharya Nagarjuna | Sanskrit; foundation text of Mahayana
  [47:2:0.4] Samayasara | Kundakundacharya | Jain treatise
  [47:2:0.5] Kathasaritsagara | Somadeva (Kashmir, 11th c.) | Sanskrit retelling of Brihatkatha
  [47:2:0.6] Brihatkatha Manjari | Kshemendra | Sanskrit retelling
  [47:2:0.7] Harshacharita | Banabhatta | Calls a Satavahana "lord of the three oceans"
[47:2:1] - **Katantra:** = Sarvavarma (G1 2010 re-exam; G1 PYQ; Welfare Officers; APPSC PYQ); distractors Patanjali, Agastya, Gunadhya, Hala.
[47:2:2] - **Brihatkatha:** = Gunadhya (Polytechnic Lecturers 2020; Social & Cultural History ×2).
[47:2:3] - **⚠ Trap:** Brihatkatha is in **Paishachi**, not Sanskrit (G2 PYQ statement: "Gunadhya wrote it in Sanskrit" ✗).
[47:2:4] - **Legend:** Gunadhya lost a bet with Sarvavarma on how fast the king could learn Sanskrit, gave up Sanskrit and wrote in Paishachi.
[47:2:5] - **⚠ Sources differ:** Gunadhya's patron – NextGen: **Kuntala Satakarni**; keys: **Hala** ("minister under Hala").
[47:2:6]   - Settled: tradition names only "king Satavahana" of Pratishthana, so mark Hala when Kuntala is not offered (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brihatkatha).
[47:2:7] - **⚠ Sources differ:** NextGen "7 stories, 7000 verses" and "Somadevasuri".
[47:2:8]   - Settled: tradition gives **7 lakh (700,000) verses**; Kathasaritsagara is by **Somadeva of Kashmir**, not the Jain Somadeva Suri (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathasaritsagara).
[47:2:9] > Match angle (G1 2023 ×2): Prajnaparamita–Nagarjuna, Samayasara–Kundakunda, Lilavati Parinayam–Kutuhala, Katantra–Sarvavarma → a-III, b-I, c-IV, d-II.
[47:2:10] > Wrong-pair angle (G1 2003 ×2): **Harshacharita–Harshavardhana** is wrong (Banabhatta wrote it); Brihatkatha–Gunadhya, Gathasaptasati–Hala, Mallana–Rajasekhara Charitramu are right.
[47:2:11] - **⚠ Trap:** Mallana's **Rajasekhara Charitramu** (Ashtadiggaja prabandha) ≠ Veeresalingam's novel Rajasekhara Charitram.
[47:2:12] - **⚠ Trap:** **Naganandam** is Harsha's play, not Kalidasa's; Meghasandesam, Raghuvamsam, Vikramorvasiyam are Kalidasa's (SI 2016).
[47:2:13] - **Yashastilaka:** Sanskrit champu by the Jain **Somadeva Suri** (c. 959 CE), written at Gangadhara in the **Vemulavada Chalukya** kingdom – not Somadeva of Kashmir.
[47:2:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.1-3, p.9, p.23-24, p.28, p.30; Rocket AP History p.9; app notes 1:47 (sub 10); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brihatkatha; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathasaritsagara
## SUB 3 | Administration – Units and Officers
[47:3:0] # Units
[47:3:1] - **Largest administrative division:** the **Ahara** (APPSC PYQ; APSLPRB 2023) – not Janapada, Vishaya, Nadu, Sima or Sthala.
[47:3:2] - **Hierarchy:** kingdom → **Ahara** → Nigamas (towns) / Vishaya → **Grama** (village); Janapadas = vassal territories.
[47:3:3] - **Head of an Ahara:** the **Amatya**, usually a blood relative or son of the king (Sachivalayam 2019 ×2; APPSC PYQ); distant aharas under **Mahasenadhipatis**.
[47:3:4] - **⚠ Trap:** not Yuvaraja, Rajuka, Mahamatra, Kumaramatya or Vishayapati.
[47:3:5] - **'Amatya' meant:** **minister** (APPSC PYQ); four grades – Vishva-amatya (inner adviser), Raja-amatya (executes orders), Maha-amatya (special/finance), Amatya.
[47:3:6] - **Mantri Parishad:** council that helped the king.
[47:3:7] # Town and village
[47:3:8] - **Nigama Sabha:** ran **cities/towns**, not villages (G2 2008; APPSC PYQ); members = **Gahapatis**; named in the **Bhattiprolu** inscription.
[47:3:9] - **Gramika:** **village headman** (APPSC PYQ); Gramani – over 5 or 10 villages; Gahapati – farmers' representative.
[47:3:10] - **Gaulmika (Gulmika):** head of a **gulma** (cluster of villages / military outpost) – controlled the **military bases** (APPSC PYQ); also border-defence commander (Myakadoni).
[47:3:11] - **⚠ Trap:** NextGen calls the Gulmika the village head; the exam answer for "village headman" is **Gramika**.
[47:3:12] # Officers
[47:3:13] TABLE head: Officer | Role
  [47:3:13.0] Heranika (Hiranika) | Treasurer – cash revenue (Welfare Officers 2017; Asst Social Welfare)
  [47:3:13.1] Bhandagarika | Stores; revenue in kind
  [47:3:13.2] Nibandhanakara | Keeper of state documents = director of archives (Welfare Officers 2017)
  [47:3:13.3] Lekhaka | King's secretary; drafted documents and edicts
  [47:3:13.4] Pratihara | Defender of the fortress
  [47:3:13.5] Mahatalavara | Commander of border provinces
  [47:3:13.6] Akshapatala | Secretariat; kept the king's orders
  [47:3:13.7] Mahadharmika / Mahaaryaka | Religious-educational / legal disputes
  [47:3:13.8] Visvamaatyulu / Rajaamatyas | Consulted on important decisions / advisers
  [47:3:13.9] Rajjugahaka / Pradeshika | Land surveyor / police
  [47:3:13.10] Akshapatakas | Kept records of the king's orders
[47:3:14] - **⚠ Trap:** Mahataraka, Dhutaka, Pratihari, Patlika-palaka are distractors for treasurer and archivist.
[47:3:15] - **Most prominent Ahara:** **Govardhana** (Nasik inscription); others – Satavahani, Sopara, Mamala, Kodura, Vaijayanti.
[47:3:16] - **Pattikapala:** drafted the land-grant inscriptions.
[47:3:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.12-13; Rocket AP History p.15, p.49; app notes 1:47 (sub 1)
## SUB 4 | Official Language – Prakrit
[47:4:0] - **Official, royal and inscription language:** **Prakrit** (G2 2011; Port Officer 2011; GS common paper; APPSC PYQ ×3); script **Brahmi**.
[47:4:1] - **Which Prakrit:** **Maharashtri Prakrit** (Welfare Officers).
[47:4:2] - **⚠ Trap:** not Sanskrit, Pali, Telugu, Tamil, Marathi or Aramaic.
[47:4:3] - **Early Ikshvaku inscriptions:** also **Prakrit** (Gazetted 2006); later Ikshvaku records turned to Sanskrit.
[47:4:4] - **Later shift:** Salankayanas – Sanskrit replaced Prakrit (5 of 8 inscriptions); Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi – Telugu.
[47:4:5] - **Sanskrit grew alongside:** **Kuntala Satakarni** made Sanskrit the royal language; Mahayana texts were written in Sanskrit.
[47:4:6] > A-R angle (UP RO 2017): "Sanskrit developed along with Prakrit and folk languages" ✓ because "kings promoted Sanskrit and folk languages in literature" ✓ – R explains A.
[47:4:7] > Statement angle (UPPCS 2021): "Satavahanas were nurturers of Prakrit" ✓; "public aspect of the arts got more encouragement" ✓ → both.
[47:4:8] - **Firsts:** first complete Sanskrit inscription = **Junagadh** (Rudradaman); first Telugu word **"Nagabu"** (Amaravati); "Vepuru" in Myakadoni.
[47:4:9] - **Desi bhasha:** language of the common people, of the **Dravidian** family.
[47:4:10] - **"Italian of the East":** Telugu (its words end in vowels) – phrase from Niccolo de Conti, used by the British.
[47:4:11] - **Telugu script:** developed from **Brahmi**, via the Bhattiprolu and Telugu-Kannada scripts.
[47:4:12] - **Official language of AP:** Telugu from **1966** (AP Official Languages Act), not 1956.
[47:4:13] - **Gundaram inscriptions:** 11 Satavahana-era Prakrit-Brahmi records decoded by the ASI in the **Gundaram reserve forest, Peddapalli district** (Telangana) in May 2025.
[47:4:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.9, p.23-24; Rocket AP History p.16; app notes 1:47 (sub 8)
## SUB 5 | Coinage
[47:5:0] - **Currency:** the **karshapana** (APPSC PYQ); 1 suvarna (gold unit) = **35 karshapanas**; Sathamana, Rama Raya, Venkataraya are later coins.
[47:5:1] - **Metals:** **lead** (most common), copper, bronze, potin, silver – **nickel was NOT used** (ACF 2022).
[47:5:2] - **⚠ Sources differ:** NextGen lists gold among Satavahana coin metals — settled: they minted base metals, lead dominant; gold was not a mint metal (https://iaspoint.com/satavahana-coinage/).
[47:5:3] - **⚠ Trap:** **iron coins with a thin copper coating** = **Ikshvakus** (APPSC key; G2 PYQ; APPSC PYQ) – not Satavahanas, Salankayanas or Vishnukundins.
[47:5:4] - **Ship-motif coins:** **Vasishthiputra Pulumavi** and **Yajnasri Satakarni** – proof of **sea trade** (G2-A 1989).
[47:5:5] - **Who minted ship coins:** standard answer **Yajnasri Satakarni** – anchored-ship mark (JL 2004).
[47:5:6] - **Typical symbol:** the **ship** (Asst Social Welfare) – not Lakshmi, Garuda or arrow; no later ruler issued ship-motif coins.
[47:5:7] - **Simuka's coins:** mostly at **Kotilingala** (Karimnagar), legend "Siri Chimuka Sata"; also Kondapur (Medak) (Asst Social Welfare); Dhulikatta is a distractor.
[47:5:8] > A-R angle (Welfare Officers): "Coins are a crucial source" ✓; "Satakarni's coins show only religious symbols, no portraits" ✗ – they carry elephant, horse, lion and the Ujjain symbol, and portrait coins began with Gautamiputra.
[47:5:9] - **Jogalthambi:** Nahapana's silver coins restruck by Gautamiputra.
[47:5:10] - **Portrait coins:** an indigenous innovation, beginning with Gautamiputra.
[47:5:11] - **Bilingual silver:** Vasishthiputra Satakarni – Prakrit + a Dravidian language.
[47:5:12] - **Karshapana:** the **silver** coin was called a karshapana (copper and lead karshapanas also circulated).
[47:5:13] - **Ujjain symbol:** a **cross with four circles** on the reverse; obverse motifs – elephant, horse, lion, camel, chaitya.
[47:5:14] - **Coin legends:** in **Prakrit**, **Brahmi** script – not Kharosthi.
[47:5:15] - **⚠ Trap:** lead, copper and bronze coins with **bull and lion** symbols = **Pallavas**, not Satavahanas.
[47:5:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.10, p.19-21; Rocket AP History p.14, p.19; app notes 1:47 (sub 7); https://iaspoint.com/satavahana-coinage/
## SUB 6 | Trade, Ports and Roman Contact
[47:6:0] TABLE head: Coast | Ports (Satavahana period)
  [47:6:0.0] West | Sopara (Shurparaka), Bharukachha (Bharuch / Broach; Greek Barygaza), Kalyan
  [47:6:0.1] East | Maisolia (Machilipatnam), Kantakossyla (Ghantasala), Koddura (Gudur, Krishna), Arikamedu (Puducherry)
[47:6:1] - **Western port:** **Sopara** – in the Satavahanas' Konkan heartland (G2-A 1984, owner's key).
[47:6:2] - **⚠ Trap:** Broach was often in Western Kshatrapa hands — exams mark Sopara as the Satavahana western port; Broach came under the Satavahanas only after Nahapana's defeat, and Kalyan was the main port before it.
[47:6:3] - **⚠ Sources differ:** NextGen puts Kalyan in Karnataka — settled: Kalyan is in Thane district, **Maharashtra**; the Periplus records it (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyan).
[47:6:4] - **East-coast ports:** Ghantasala and Masulipatnam (Welfare Officers: "2 and 4"); Barygaza and Kalyan are western; Koddura is eastern too.
[47:6:5] - **Ptolemy's "great market":** **Maisolia (Machilipatnam)** (APPSC PYQ); not Nizampatnam, Kalingapatnam, Kotilingala.
[47:6:6] - **⚠ Trap:** Motupalli is an east-coast port that rose under the Kakatiyas — not a western Satavahana port (Rocket Sheets misprint); "port not used in Satavahana times" = **Motupalli** (APPSC PYQ). Today in Bapatla district.
[47:6:7] - **Koddura:** the Periplus' only east-coast port of the Satavahanas.
[47:6:8] # Evidence of sea trade
[47:6:9] - **All three testify:** the **Periplus**, **Roman coins** found in Andhra-Telangana, and the **ship coins** of Pulomavi and Yajnasri (Welfare Officers Mains).
[47:6:10] - **Roman objects found most in India:** **coins** (IAS 1999) – Bhattiprolu, Nagarjunakonda, Attirala, Salihundam, Vijayawada, Vinukonda, Nellore.
[47:6:11] - **Pliny:** Roman gold drained to India for fine cloth (mallasella, muslin) – about 12.5 million denarii a year.
[47:6:12] - **Arikamedu:** the Periplus' "market street of the Romans" (near Puducherry).
[47:6:13] - **Exports / imports:** muslin, spices, pearls, diamonds, ivory out; gold (Malaya, Sumatra), wine (Italy, Arabia), silk and camphor (China) in.
[47:6:14] - **Inland route:** Ujjain → Bharuch via **Paithan and Tagara**; the Satavahanas were famed road builders ("Mahapatha nirmatalu").
[47:6:15] - **Reach:** Rome, and the eastern islands – Siam, Java, Borneo.
[47:6:16] > A-R angle (G2 PYQ): "Trade with Rome flourished after the Satavahanas" ✗ (it peaked under them and declined); "no ruler issued ship-motif coins after them" ✓.
[47:6:17] - **Products of Andhra centres:** Palnadu – diamonds; Guduru – fine cotton; Vinukonda – metal; **Guntupalli – copper and iron** (not gold).
[47:6:18] - **Kalyan and the Sakas:** per the Periplus, Kalyan was ruined by the Sakas (Kshatrapas) – the answer for "port destroyed by the Sakas".
[47:6:19] - **West coast into the Deccan:** Kalyan → **Naneghat pass** → Junnar → Paithan.
[47:6:20] - **Vengipuram:** = **Pedavegi** (near Eluru).
[47:6:21] - **Constantine gold coin:** found at **Kudali Sangameswaram** (Alampur) – of a later period.
[47:6:22] - **Egypt (Feb 2026):** about **30 Indian inscriptions** of the Indo-Roman phase (Tamil-Brahmi, Prakrit, Sanskrit) reported from tombs of the Theban necropolis, Luxor.
[47:6:23] - **Significance:** land grants, guild banking and Roman trade laid the base of **Deccan urbanisation**.
[47:6:24] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.3-4, p.19-21; Rocket AP History p.13-14, p.41; app notes 1:47 (sub 5, 6); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalyan; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motupalli
## SUB 7 | Land Revenue, Taxes and Tax-free Grants
[47:7:0] - **Bhaga:** land revenue = king's share of **1/6** of the produce (JA NTR UHS) – the chief income.
[47:7:1] - **First tax-free land grants:** to **Brahmanas and Buddhist monks** – by the **Satavahanas** (Deputy screening 2023; Welfare Officers) – not Parthians, Kushanas, Shakas, Guptas, Mauryas or Ikshvakus.
[47:7:2] - **Satakarni I:** gave tax-free land, cows and gold to Brahmanas (Naneghat); granted land could not be entered by royal officers.
[47:7:3] - **Other dues:** Karukara (artisans' and professionals' tax), Kara, Sulka (water tax), Deya-meya (king's share in kind).
[47:7:4] - **Vetti:** forced unpaid labour; with hereditary village headships it fed the growth of **feudalism**; also the term for the exploitation of village servant castes by **feudal lords in Telangana** (Social Structure 2016).
[47:7:5] - **⚠ Trap:** **Moturpha** was a **British** tax on trades and occupations (looms) in Andhra, not Satavahana; and the British salt monopoly did apply in Andhra (A ✓, R ✗; Welfare Officers).
[47:7:6] - **Nivartana:** land unit, about 1.5 acres.
[47:7:7] - **Spread of cultivation:** mainly in the **Krishna-Godavari** basin; paddy transplantation; chief crops rice and cotton.
[47:7:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.7, p.16-17; Rocket AP History p.48; app notes 1:47 (sub 3)
## SUB 8 | Society and Women
[47:8:0] - **G2 2008 statement:** kings followed Hinduism (Vedic), some queens patronised Buddhism ✓; **chaturvarna** existed ✓; shipping developed ✓; "**women were looked down upon**" ✗.
[47:8:1] - **Women respected:** matronymics; joined festivals, donated to viharas, issued inscriptions; titles Maharathini, Mahabhoji, Mahasenapatni.
[47:8:2] - **Patriarchal:** **both family and kingship** were patriarchal (G2 2011; APPSC PYQ); joint families.
[47:8:3] # Four status classes
[47:8:4] TABLE head: Class | Members
  [47:8:4.0] 1st | Feudal nobility – Maharathis, Mahabhojas, Mahasenapatis
  [47:8:4.1] 2nd | Officials – Amatyas, Mahamatras, Bhandagarikas
  [47:8:4.2] 3rd | Professionals – Vaidya, Lekhaka, Suvarnakara, Gandhika, Halakiya
  [47:8:4.3] 4th | Artisans and petty traders – Malakara, Vadhaki, Lohavanija
[47:8:5] - **Order question:** Maharathas → Mahamatras → Gandhikas → Lohavanijas (Sachivalayam).
[47:8:6] - **Third class:** Suvarnakara and Gandhika ("1 and 5") (Welfare Officers); ⚠ some lists put the Lekhaka in the 2nd class.
[47:8:7] - **Others:** Sakas and Yavanas absorbed with Indian names; slavery (Brihatkatha, Kamasutra); a sati statue at Nagarjunakonda.
[47:8:8] - **Vetti by women:** recorded in the **Kamasutra**.
[47:8:9] - **Independent donors:** women made gifts at **Bharhut, Sanchi and Amaravati** without naming husbands or fathers.
[47:8:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.14-16; Rocket AP History p.56; app notes 1:47 (sub 9); V.D. Mahajan, Ancient India (four classes)
## SUB 9 | Feudatories and Military Camps
[47:9:0] - **Not strongly centralised:** many vassal janapadas run by local kings, supervised by **Mahabhojas** and **Maharathas**.
[47:9:1] > A-R angle (Welfare Officers): "Semi-autonomous Bhojas and Maharathis made the polity decentralised" ✓; "the centre discouraged local leaders and ruled all areas directly" ✗.
[47:9:2] TABLE head: Feudatory | Feature
  [47:9:2.0] Maharathas | Hereditary; collected (and could remit) taxes
  [47:9:2.1] Mahabhojas | Hereditary; inscriptions omit the emperor → near-independent
  [47:9:2.2] Mahasenapatis / Mahasenadhipatis, Mahatalavaras | Commanders of border provinces against the Sakas
[47:9:3] - **⚠ Trap:** **Mahajanapadas** were NOT Satavahana feudal chiefs (Social & Cultural History).
[47:9:4] - **Kataka:** permanent garrison; **Skandhavara:** temporary camp.
[47:9:5] - **Meaning together:** **military camps and settlements** that served as **administrative centres** when the king was present (G1 2024; JA NTR UHS); not monks' tax-free villages, rock-cut areas or paddy lands.
[47:9:6] - **Army:** chaturanga bala (Hathigumpha); Amaravati sculptures show infantry in front, cavalry and elephants on the flanks, archers at the rear.
[47:9:7] - **Highest feudatory:** the **Raja**, who could issue coins; grading Raja > Mahabhoja > Senapati.
[47:9:8] - **Maharathis:** hereditary tax-collecting feudatories, mainly of the **western Deccan**.
[47:9:9] - **Mahabhojas:** powerful local chiefs of the **Konkan** – not Eastern Bengal.
[47:9:10] - **Samanta rajyas:** Chutus – Mysore; Kuras – Kolhapur; Ikshvakus – Vijayapuri; they paid tribute and sent troops.
[47:9:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.12-14; app notes 1:47 (sub 2)

=== NOTES 1:48 | Satavahana Art and Architecture – Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda and Rock-cut Caves
## SUB 0 | Amaravati Mahachaitya
[48:0:0] - **Where:** ancient **Dhanyakataka** (Amaravati–Dharanikota) on the **Krishna**, Andhra Pradesh (UPSC 2006 match); old Guntur district (now Palnadu district).
[48:0:1] - **Built under:** the **Satavahanas** (APPSC PYQ) – not Vengi Chalukyas, Ikshvakus or Salankayanas; NextGen dates the main building to **Pulomavi II**.
[48:0:2] - **Enlarged, with the stone railing round the Mahachaitya:** in the reign of **Yajnasri Satakarni**, by his contemporary **Acharya Nagarjuna** (G2 2001; Sachivalayam ×2; G2 PYQ; APPSC PYQ).
[48:0:3]   - Options printed "Gautamiputra Yagnasri" = Yajnasri Satakarni. When the question asks for the king, do not mark Nagarjuna.
[48:0:4] - **⚠ Trap:** Vasishthiputra Satakarni (earlier vedika sculptures), Vasishthiputra Pulomavi, Gautamiputra and Srimukha are distractors; final enlargement under the Ikshvakus.
[48:0:5] - **Origin:** Ashokan age – **Mahadeva Bhikshu**, first Buddhist teacher in Andhra, enshrined the Buddha's relics; Naga king **Nagashoka** helped build it at Dharanikota.
[48:0:6] # Size
[48:0:7] - **Biggest stupa in Andhra Pradesh:** Amaravati (G2 2019 prelims; G2 PYQ) and the **largest in South India** (Welfare Officers 2017); Bhattiprolu is the **oldest**.
[48:0:8] - **Larger and more artistic:** than Sanchi and Bharhut (Welfare Officers 2017).
[48:0:9] - **⚠ Sources differ:** NextGen calls Sanchi "the largest stupa in India".
[48:0:10]   - Settled: Amaravati's railing was ~59 m across vs Sanchi's 36.6 m dome, so Amaravati was larger (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaravati_Stupa; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanchi).
[48:0:11] # Ayaka platform
[48:0:12] - **Platform with ayaka (Aryaka) pillars:** hallmark of the **Amaravati** stupa (UPPCS 2022); unique to Andhra stupas.
[48:0:13] - **Layout:** 4 ayaka platforms at the cardinal points × 5 pillars = five events of the Buddha's life.
[48:0:14] TABLE head: Event | Symbol
  [48:0:14.0] Birth | Lotus
  [48:0:14.1] Great Departure | Horse
  [48:0:14.2] Enlightenment | Bodhi (peepal) tree
  [48:0:14.3] First sermon | Wheel
  [48:0:14.4] Mahaparinirvana | Stupa
[48:0:15] # Discovery and the Amaravati school
[48:0:16] - **Identified:** Col. **Colin Mackenzie**, 1797; excavated by Robert Sewell, 1877; James **Fergusson** (Tree and Serpent Worship): "epitome of Indian architecture".
[48:0:17] - **Ayaka gift:** the artisan **Siddhattha** gave five ayaka pillars at the eastern gate.
[48:0:18] - **Amaravati school:** white **Palnadu limestone**; narrative Jataka reliefs; early aniconic Buddha (tree, throne, footprints), later human form.
[48:0:19] - **Sculptures today:** British Museum (London), Government Museum (Chennai), Amaravati site museum.
[48:0:20] - **Birth symbol in full:** **lotus and bull**.
[48:0:21] - **Amaravati style:** marked by **movement and emotional expression**; its Jataka and Buddha-life subjects do not explain the style.
[48:0:22] - **Colin Mackenzie:** the first **Surveyor General of India**.
[48:0:23] - **UNESCO tentative list:** **Lepakshi Veerabhadra Temple** (monolithic Nandi) was added in 2022.
[48:0:24] - **Amaravati and UNESCO:** the app key puts the **Amaravati Buddhist Stupa** on India's UNESCO tentative list.
[48:0:25] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.10, p.21-22, p.29-30; Rocket AP History p.25, p.34; app notes 1:48 (sub 1, 2, 10); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaravati_Stupa
## SUB 1 | Stupa, Chaitya, Vihara – Terms
[48:1:0] - **Chaitya:** **prayer hall / place of worship** (Chaitya-shala, Chaitya-griha); rectangular, ending in an **apse (horseshoe plan)** with the stupa; horseshoe **chaitya window** on the facade.
[48:1:1] - **Vihara:** **monastery – dwelling of the monks**; square, cells round a central hall (**Madhyashala**).
[48:1:2] > Most-asked angle (UPSC 2013; IAS 2013; UP 2001; APPSC PYQ): "Chaitya = place of worship, Vihara = dwelling of monks".
[48:1:3] - **Stupa, chaitya and vihara:** all **Buddhist** structures (State PSC) – not Ajivika, Vaishnava or Shaiva.
[48:1:4] - **Stupa:** a **mound**, generally a **repository of relics**, and a **votive and commemorative** structure.
[48:1:5] - **⚠ Trap:** the stupa concept is **not Buddhist in origin** – it predates Buddhism (UPSC 2023: only two of three statements correct).
[48:1:6] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [48:1:6.0] Stupa | Mound
  [48:1:6.1] Garbhagriha | Place where the deity's image is installed
  [48:1:6.2] Mandapa | Place in temples where people assemble
  [48:1:6.3] Pradakshina patha | Circular path around the stupa
[48:1:7] > Match angle (APPSC): 1-(b), 2-(a), 3-(d), 4-(c).
[48:1:8] - **Arama:** stupa + vihara + chaitya together (e.g. Guntupalli).
[48:1:9] - **Stupa types:** Dhatugarbha (bodily relics), Paribhogika (objects used by the Buddha), Uddeshika (symbolic).
[48:1:10] - **Uposatha:** monks' meeting in the vihara's central hall every **15 days**.
[48:1:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.22; app notes 1:48 (sub 0)
## SUB 2 | Relic Stupas and Other Andhra Buddhist Sites
[48:2:0] - **Built over whose relics:** the stupas at **Amaravati, Jaggayyapeta and Nagarjunakonda** – over **Gautama Buddha's** relics (G2 2002; APPSC PYQ); not Nagarjuna, Mahavira or Gomateshwara.
[48:2:1] - **Centres of Buddhism in AP:** Amaravati, Bhattiprolu, Guntupalli – "all the above" (AEE 2011).
[48:2:2] TABLE head: Site | Key fact
  [48:2:2.0] Bhattiprolu (Bapatla dt, old Guntur) | Oldest stupa in AP; relic-casket inscriptions name Raja Kubiraka (3rd c. BC) and the Nigama Sabha; excavated by Alexander Rea, 1892
  [48:2:2.1] Jaggayyapeta (NTR dt, old Krishna) | Mandhata (chakravartin) sculpture with raised hand; excavated by James Burgess, 1882
  [48:2:2.2] Ghantasala (Krishna) | Stupa at the port Kantakossyla
  [48:2:2.3] Guntupalli (Eluru) | Oldest chaitya in AP; rock-cut
  [48:2:2.4] Salihundam (Srikakulam) | Relic stupa
  [48:2:2.5] Sankaram–Bojjannakonda (Anakapalli) | Rock-cut monastery on twin hills
  [48:2:2.6] Thotlakonda, Bavikonda (Visakhapatnam) | Hill-top monasteries; Thotlakonda spotted in an Indian Navy aerial survey
  [48:2:2.7] Kondapur (Sangareddy, Telangana) | Fortified Satavahana town; terracotta, beads, coins
  [48:2:2.8] Phanigiri (Suryapet, Telangana) | Life-size stucco sculpture found recently; 3,730 Ikshvaku lead coins (2024)
[48:2:3] - **Bhattiprolu ruler:** **Kubiraka** (APPSC PYQ) – not Sudarshana, Mahadeva or Ashoka.
[48:2:4] - **Mandhata sculpture:** **Jaggayyapeta** (G1 1991) – not Simhachalam, Kondapuram.
[48:2:5] - **Current link:** the rare life-size stucco sculpture came from a Buddhist site in **Telangana** (Phanigiri) (G1 PYQ).
[48:2:6] > A-R angle (Welfare Officers): "Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda became big stupa-monastery complexes" ✓ because "they lay near urban centres on trade and pilgrimage routes" ✓ – R explains A.
[48:2:7] - **House viharas:** a distinctive feature of **Guntupalli**.
[48:2:8] - **Nelakondapalli (Khammam, Telangana):** post-Satavahana mahastupa; bronze and marble Buddha images; sculptor's workshop found by **V.V. Krishna Sastry** – not the oldest stupa in Andhra.
[48:2:9] - **Thotlakonda finds:** its 1988–92 excavations found the main stupa, votive stupas and **Satavahana and Roman coins**.
[48:2:10] - **AP Buddhist International Tourism Circuit:** Amaravati, Thotlakonda-Bavikonda, Bojjannakonda-Sankaram, **Salihundam**, Ghantasala.
[48:2:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.14, p.22; Rocket AP History p.6, p.32; app notes 1:48 (sub 4, 5)

  [48:3:0.0] Purvasaila | Dhanyakataka (Amaravati)
  [48:3:0.1] Aparasaila | Sriparvata (Nagarjunakonda)
  [48:3:0.2] Uttarasaila | Jaggayyapeta
  [48:3:0.3] Rajagirika | Guntupalli
  [48:3:0.4] Siddharthika | Gudivada
[48:3:1] - **Siddharthaka chaitya:** of Buddhist literature = **Gudivada** (G2 2008; APPSC PYQ).
[48:3:2] - **Wrong pair:** **Guntupalli – Siddharthaka chaitya** (G2 2011; APPSC PYQ); Purvasaila–Dhanyakataka, Aparasaila–Sriparvata, Uttarasaila–Jaggayyapeta are right.
[48:3:3] - **Origin:** the five Chaitika sects were branches of the **Mahasanghikas**, founded by **Mahadeva Bhikshu**.

## SUB 4 | Tambaya Danamu – Kotturu
[48:4:0] - **Term:** **"Tambaya Dana(mu)"** – a donation term at the Buddhist site of **Kotturu (Dhanadibbalu)** on the **Sarada** river near Yelamanchili (G2 2017; APPSC PYQ; Police Constable 2019).
[48:4:1] - **District key:** **Visakhapatnam** (G2 2017) (now Anakapalli district).
[48:4:2] - **⚠ Outdated:** Kotturu's district was "Visakhapatnam" — now **Anakapalli district** (Rambilli mandal), after the April 2022 district reorganisation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kotturu_Dhanadibbalu).
[48:4:3] - **⚠ Trap:** Chandavaram, Amaravati, Bhattiprolu; Kurnool, Krishna, West Godavari are distractors.
[48:4:4] ~~ Sources: app notes 1:48 (sub 8); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kotturu_Dhanadibbalu
## SUB 5 | Rock-cut Caves – Karle, Guntupalli
[48:5:0] - **Karle (Pune):** the **largest and most evolved rock-cut chaitya hall of the Hinayana phase** (UPRO 2014); not Pitalkhora, Junnar or Bedsa. Bhaja is earlier.
[48:5:1] - **Guntupalli (West Godavari, now Eluru district):** its early chaityagrihas and viharas are **rock-cut** ✓ (UPPCS 2017 ×2).
[48:5:2] - **⚠ Trap:** eastern Deccan chaityas and viharas are usually **structural**, not rock-cut – Guntupalli is the exception → "only 1 is correct".
[48:5:3] - **⚠ Outdated:** "Guntupalli in West Godavari" — now **Eluru district** (Kamavarapukota mandal) after the 2022 reorganisation.
[48:5:4] - **Later imitation:** Buddhists cut the first rock-cut chaityas; Vaishnavas, Shaivas and Jainas imitated them later ✓ – at the same sites, not far away ✗ (NDA 2011).
[48:5:5] - **Western Deccan caves:** Nasik, Naneghat, Bhaja, Kanheri, Junnar, Bedsa, Pitalkhora; **Ajanta** Caves 9-10 – Shwetagaja (Chhaddanta) Jataka painting in Cave 10.
[48:5:6] - **Peak of rock-cut activity:** the **Sahyadris** of the western Deccan (Nasik, Naneghat, Karle, Bhaja, Kanheri, Junnar, Ajanta, Bedsa, Pitalkhora).
[48:5:7] - **Karle details:** **12 dance-couple** sculptures; **Pulumavi II** donated a village to it.
[48:5:8] - **Bedsa (Pune):** chaitya with **bell-capital pillars**.
[48:5:9] - **Nasik:** viharas bearing **Satavahana inscriptions**.
[48:5:10] - **Sankaram and Bagh:** Sankaram (Anakapalli) has horseshoe-shaped caves; the **Bagh** cave viharas (MP) are linked to the Satavahanas in exam keys.
[48:5:11] - **Bhairavakonda (Nellore–Prakasam border):** **8 rock-cut cave temples of Shiva** (Pallava style) – Hindu, not Buddhist.
[48:5:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.22; Rocket AP History p.8; app notes 1:48 (sub 9)
## SUB 6 | Nagarjunakonda (Ikshvaku)
[48:6:0] - **Dynasty:** the **Ikshvakus** built the stupas, viharas and temples at Nagarjunakonda, backing both Vedic and Buddhist traditions (Welfare Officers) – not Mauryas, Satavahanas or Pallavas.
[48:6:1] - **Names:** **Vijayapuri** / **Sriparvata** – the Ikshvaku capital; tutelary goddess **Hariti**.
[48:6:2] - **Monuments:** 30+ stupas, viharas, apsidal chaityas; Ikshvaku queens chief donors; a Sinhala vihara; the first structural Hindu temples of Andhra.
[48:6:3] - **Satavahana link:** **Yajnasri Satakarni** built the 1,500-room **Sriparvata Sangharama** for Nagarjuna.
[48:6:4] - **Sects:** Bahushrutiya, Aparasaila and **Mahishasaka** (the only Hinayana sect there).
[48:6:5] - **Discovery:** A.R. Saraswati, 1926; excavated by Longhurst, 1927-31; drowned by the Nagarjunasagar reservoir – monuments rebuilt on an island.
[48:6:6] - **Golden Temple (Swarna Devalayam):** of Ehuvala Chamtamula at Nagarjunakonda – bears the **first Sanskrit inscription** of Andhra and South India.
[48:6:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.10, p.30; app notes 1:48 (sub 3)
## SUB 7 | Amaravati School, Donors and Acharyas
[48:7:0] Asked only in the app's own MCQs (no PYQ yet) – one quick read.
[48:7:1] TABLE head: Feature | Gandhara | Mathura | Amaravati
  [48:7:1.0] Material | Grey-blue schist | Spotted red sandstone | White limestone
  [48:7:1.1] Influence | Greco-Roman | Indigenous | Indigenous
  [48:7:1.2] Patrons | Kushanas | Kushanas | Satavahanas, Ikshvakus
[48:7:2] - **⚠ Trap:** Amaravati shows **no** Greco-Roman influence; its influence spread to **Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia**.
[48:7:3] - **Donors:** queens and women first; merchants, guilds (**ivory workers** at Amaravati), Yavanas; leather-worker **Dimikudu** offers a **Purnakumbha** in a relief.
[48:7:4] - **Karle donors:** Bhutapala funded the great chaitya hall.
[48:7:5] TABLE head: Acharya | Association
  [48:7:5.0] Bhavaviveka | Vihara at Dhanyakataka
  [48:7:5.1] Dinnaga | Father of Buddhist logic
  [48:7:5.2] Aryasangha | Yogachara
  [48:7:5.3] Padmasambhava | From Andhra; took Vajrayana to Tibet
  [48:7:5.4] Aryadeva | Nagarjuna's disciple; Chittasuddhi Prakaranam
[48:7:6] - **Records:** oldest stupa in Andhra = Bhattiprolu; largest brick stupa = **Kesariya**; "Sakiyanam" relic casket = **Piprahwa**.
[48:7:7] - **Jain patron:** Bethanamathya (and early Kakatiya kings).
[48:7:8] - **Most ancient stupa in India (exam key):** **Bharhut**; oldest in Andhra = Bhattiprolu.
[48:7:9] - **Nannayabhattu:** patronised by the Eastern Chalukya **Rajaraja Narendra**; began the Telugu Mahabharata.
[48:7:10] - **Most mature phase:** the Amaravati school reached its final phase under the **Ikshvakus**.
[48:7:11] - **Sanchi gateway:** carved by the **ivory carvers of Vidisha**.
[48:7:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.24, p.30; Rocket AP History p.39; app notes 1:48 (sub 7, 8, 10)

=== NOTES 1:49 | Satavahana Religious Conditions – Buddhism, Brahmanism and Royal Patronage
## SUB 0 | Acharya Nagarjuna
[49:0:0] - **Who:** a **Buddhist philosopher** (AEE 2008) – not a Greek king, Vedic rishi or Jain monk; spread **Mahayana** Buddhism in Andhra.
[49:0:1] - **Titles:** **"Second Buddha"** (Junior Analyst 2011), Indian Martin Luther, Indian Einstein.
[49:0:2] - **Philosophy:** founder of the **Madhyamika** school; propounded **Sunyavada** (emptiness) (G1 2012; APPSC PYQ).
[49:0:3] - **⚠ Trap:** not Advaita, Mahadvaita or Visishtadvaita; **Syadvada** = Kundakundacharya; Asvaghosha and Somadeva Suri are distractors.
[49:0:4] TABLE head: Work | Fact
  [49:0:4.0] Suhrullekha ("friendly letter") | Letter to Yajnasri Satakarni; Itsing saw students memorise it
  [49:0:4.1] Prajnaparamita Shastra | Foundation text of Mahayana
  [49:0:4.2] Ratnavali | Advice to a Satavahana king; Rajaparikatha chapter = Shreyorajya (welfare state)
  [49:0:4.3] Yogasara | Credited to Nagarjuna (G2 2017 key)
  [49:0:4.4] Mulamadhyamakakarika | Verse treatise on Madhyamika
[49:0:5] - **Suhrullekha and Prajnaparamita:** both by **Acharya Nagarjuna** (Sachivalayam 2019); not Aryadeva, Dharmanandi, Chandramukha.
[49:0:6] - **Welfare-state doctrine:** set out by Nagarjuna in the **Ratnavali** (Welfare Officers).
[49:0:7] - **⚠ Trap:** NextGen merges Ratnavali with "Rasaratnavali/Rasaratnakara" (alchemy); exams mean the Ratnavali of advice to the king, and Harsha's play Ratnavali is a different work (https://encyclopediaofbuddhism.org/wiki/Ratnavali).
[49:0:8] - **Yogasara:** **Nagarjuna** (G2 PYQ; APPSC PYQ) – not Dhanapala, Vastupala or Kondakundacharya.
[49:0:9] - **Life:** contemporary and friend of **Yajnasri Satakarni**; lived at **Sriparvata** (Nagarjunakonda) in the 1,500-room vihara the king built; disciple **Aryadeva**.
[49:0:10] - **Works in stone:** built the railing (rampart) of the Amaravati Mahachaitya and stone mandapas at Sriparvata.
[49:0:11] - **Death legend:** Kathasaritsagara says a Satavahana prince had him killed.
[49:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.2, p.24, p.29-31; Rocket AP History p.32, p.52; app notes 1:49 (sub 6); https://encyclopediaofbuddhism.org/wiki/Ratnavali
## SUB 1 | Kings Vedic, Queens Buddhist – Patronage
[49:1:0] - **Royal religion:** the Satavahana kings followed the **Vedic religion** (APPSC PYQ); their **queens patronised Buddhism**.
[49:1:1] > Statement angle (G2 2008): "rulers followed Hinduism but some queens patronised Buddhism" ✓; fourfold caste ✓; maritime trade flourished ✓; "women were looked down upon" ✗ (the false one).
[49:1:2] - **Yajnasri Satakarni's faith:** personally Vedic (the name shows it); with no Vedic option, mark **Buddhism** – he was Nagarjuna's friend and patron (APPSC PYQ).
[49:1:3] - **Ikshvakus:** Vedic themselves but **great supporters of Buddhism** (Social & Cultural History); Virapurushadatta's reign = golden age of Buddhism.
[49:1:4] > Statement angle (Welfare Officers): Satavahanas and Ikshvakus gave to Hindu (Brahmanical) cults and to Buddhist monks ✓; both claim Shrauta (Vedic) sacrifices ✓; "Satavahanas gave only to Hindu temples" ✗ → "1 and 2".
[49:1:5] - **Donors:** queens, merchants and common people; **Gautami Balasri** gave the Nasik cave vihara to the **Bhadrayaniya** sect; Pulomavi II gave a village to Mahasanghika monks at Karle.
[49:1:6] - **Guild support:** guilds at Nasik, Junnar and Kanheri held money on deposit and paid the interest to monks.
[49:1:7] TABLE head: Patron | Religion
  [49:1:7.0] Satavahana rulers | Vedic religion
  [49:1:7.1] Satavahana queens | Buddhism
  [49:1:7.2] Salankayanas | Saivism
  [49:1:7.3] Pallavas | Rise of Brahmanism, decline of Buddhism
  [49:1:7.4] Early Kakatiya kings | Jainism
  [49:1:7.5] Reddy period | Veerasaivism
[49:1:8] - **Prakrit:** the people's language helped Buddhism become a mass movement.
[49:1:9] - **Krishna (Kanha), 2nd king:** made a Nasik cave for shramanas and appointed a **Dharma Mahamatra**.
[49:1:10] - **Alluru inscription:** of the Ikshvaku **Virapurushadatta** – records his donations to many communities and institutions (G2 2017).
[49:1:11] - **Yavana merchants:** funded caves at Karle, Bhaja, Nasik, Junnar and Kanheri.
[49:1:12] - **Chitrarathaswami:** family deity of the **Salankayanas** of Vengi (Pedavegi), usually taken as the Sun god – match "Salankayanas – Chitrarathaswami".
[49:1:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.24, p.29; Rocket AP History p.39, p.45, p.52; app notes 1:49 (sub 0, 4)
## SUB 2 | Gudimallam and Shaivism
[49:2:0] - **Oldest Shiva temple:** **Parasurameswara temple, Gudimallam** (Yerpedu mandal; Chittoor, now Tirupati district) (G2 2008; APPSC PYQ).
[49:2:1] - **⚠ Trap:** Thondawada, Renigunta, Jogulamba (Alampur) are distractors.
[49:2:2] - **Oldest Shiva linga of AP and India:** **Gudimallam** – Shiva carved standing on the linga as a hunter (G1 1991; APPSC PYQ); not Amaravati, Draksharama, Srisailam, Nagarjunakonda, Hanumakonda.
[49:2:3] - **⚠ Outdated:** Gudimallam's district "Chittoor" — now **Tirupati district** (2022 AP district reorganisation).
[49:2:4] - **Other Shaiva evidence:** 14 early Shiva temples at **Veerapuram** (Kurnool); Gathasaptasati opens with a Shiva prayer; king names Sivasri, Shivaskandha.
[49:2:5] - **Pashupata:** first branch of Shaivism, founder **Lakulisha**.
[49:2:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.23, p.26-27; Rocket AP History p.34; app notes 1:49 (sub 2)
## SUB 3 | Buddhist Sects – Rajagirika, Sri Parvataswamy
[49:3:0] - **Rajagirika centre:** **Guntupalli** (G2 2012 key) – not Gudivada, Sriparvatam or Jaggayyapeta.
[49:3:1] - **Sri Parvataswamy = the Buddha:** identification by **N. Venkataramanayya** (G2 2019 key; APPSC PYQ).
[49:3:2] - **⚠ Trap:** **Kielhorn** identified Sri Parvataswamy with Mallikarjuna of Srisailam; another key named Kielhorn – follow G2 2019.
[49:3:3] - **First Buddhist acharya in Andhra:** **Mahadeva Bhikshu**, founder of **Chaityakavada** (worship of chaityas).
[49:3:4] - **Mahasanghika:** main centre **Dhanyakataka**; followers called Mahasanghis or Chaityakas. **Bhadrayaniya** sect: Nasik.
[49:3:5] - **Arrival:** Buddhism reached Andhra in the **6th century BC**; "Andhra Buddhism" held the **Pratitya Samutpada** doctrine; Tibetan tradition – the Buddha preached at Amaravati at king Subendran's request.
[49:3:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.28-29; Rocket AP History p.8; app notes 1:49 (sub 3)
## SUB 4 | Jainism – Kundakundacharya
[49:4:0] - **Samayasara:** by **Kundakundacharya (Kondakundacharya)**, a Digambara monk (G2 2019; APPSC PYQ); not Somadeva Suri, Mahaviracharya or Pujyapada.
[49:4:1] - **Philosophy:** **Syadvada** and Anekantavada; other works Pravachanasara, Panchastikayasara, Niyamasara.
[49:4:2] - **Ashram:** **Konakondla** (Anantapur district), where he practised yoga in a cave.
[49:4:3] - **Jain tradition on the Satavahanas:** Simuka was first a Jain (guru Kalakasuri); Ashoka's grandson **Samprati** spread Jainism in Andhra; Guntupalli was first a Jain site.
[49:4:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.27-28; Rocket AP History p.46, p.52; app notes 1:49 (sub 7)
## SUB 5 | Vedic Sacrifices and Bhagavata Religion
[49:5:0] - **Naneghat (Devi Naganika):** Satakarni I performed **2 Ashvamedhas** and a **Rajasuya**; gave cows, land and gold to Brahmanas.
[49:5:1] - **Deities invoked at Naneghat:** Indra, Vasudeva, Sankarshana, Surya, Chandra, Yama, Varuna (NextGen p.24 also lists Agni).
[49:5:2] - **Yajna-performing kings:** Satakarni I, Satakarni II, Gautamiputra, Yajnasri; the names **Vedasri** and **Yajnasri** show Vedic faith.
[49:5:3] > A-R angle (Welfare Officers): "Satavahanas performed the Ashvamedha to legitimise power" ✓; "they patronised both Brahmanas and Buddhists" ✓ – but R does not explain A.
[49:5:4] - **Bhagavata religion:** founded on Krishna-Vasudeva (a Vrishni of Mathura; disciple of **Ghor Angirasa** in the Chhandogya Upanishad); entered Andhra under **Kanha (Krishna)**, the 2nd king; called the "Vasudeva religion" by Hala's time.
[49:5:5] - **Symbols:** Bhagavata symbols on Gautamiputra's inscriptions; Nasik calls him **Agama-nilaya**.
[49:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.7-8, p.24-25; app notes 1:49 (sub 1, 2)
