=== NOTES 1:50 | Ikshvakus – Political History, Vasishthiputra Chamtamula and Virapurushadatta
## SUB 0 | Capital Vijayapuri and the Dynasty at a Glance
[50:0:0] # Capital
[50:0:1] - **Capital:** **Vijayapuri** = modern **Nagarjunakonda**, in the Nagarjuna Sagar valley, now **Palnadu** district (asked 7 times: G2 2008 ×3, G2 2011 ×3, G2 2012).
[50:0:2] - **⚠ Trap:** not **Amaravati** (Dhanyakataka, a Satavahana centre), not Vengi (Salankayanas), not Vemulawada, Srikakulam or Pithunda.
[50:0:3] - **⚠ Option clash (G2 2012):** "Vijayapuri" and "Nagarjunakonda" both appear – the exam key is **Vijayapuri**, the ancient name of the capital.
[50:0:4] - **Name:** Vijayapuri is thought to be named after Satavahana **Vijaya Satakarni**; the hill was **Sriparvata**.
[50:0:5] - **Excavated** at Nagarjunakonda by the Andhra archaeologist **R. Subrahmanyam** (1954–60 rescue dig).
[50:0:6] - **Sites and ports:** **Ghantasala (Kantakasala)** and **Motupalli** = ports of the Ikshvaku period; Phanigiri (Suryapet, Telangana) – a pot of **3,730 lead coins** of the Ikshvaku period found in **2024**.
[50:0:7] # The dynasty in one look
[50:0:8] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [50:0:8.0] Successors of | Satavahanas in the Krishna valley (3rd c. CE); first their feudatories (Mahatalavaras)
  [50:0:8.1] Period | About 75 years, c. AD 225–300 (3rd century CE)
  [50:0:8.2] Kings | Puranas: 7; inscriptions confirm 4
  [50:0:8.3] Symbol / court language | Lion / Prakrit
  [50:0:8.4] Official religion | Vedic-Brahmanical (Shaivism); Buddhism patronised by the queens
[50:0:9] - **Immediate successors of the Satavahanas** in the Krishna valley = **Ikshvakus**, not the Pallavas or Vishnukundins.
[50:0:10] - **Bridge dynasty:** carried the **Amaravati school to its peak**, built the **first temples** and moved Andhra towards an **agrarian, Puranic order**; they did **not** replace Buddhism with Jainism.
[50:0:11] - **Deccan dynasty that promoted Buddhism** (G2 2000 backlog): the **Ikshvakus** – their period is the golden age of Buddhism in Andhra.
[50:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Ikshvakus p.1, p.7-8; Rocket AP History sheet #31, #43 (capitals); NextGen Previous Papers p.50-51; app notes 1:50 (sub 0, 1, 3)
## SUB 1 | Rulers – Founder to Last King
[50:1:0] TABLE head: No. | King | Exam fact
  [50:1:0.0] 1 | Vasishthiputra Sri Santamula (Chamtamula, Shantamula I) | Founder; overthrew the last Satavahana Pulomavi III; Vedic sacrifices
  [50:1:0.1] 2 | Mathariputra Virapurushadatta | Greatest king; golden age of Buddhism; Sri Parvatadhipati, "Ashoka of the South"
  [50:1:0.2] 3 | Ehuvala Santamula (Shantamula II) | Son of Virapurushadatta and Bhatti Mahadevi; ruled about 24 years; first Sanskrit inscriptions
  [50:1:0.3] 4 | Rudrapurushadatta | Last king; Gurajala (Gurazala) inscription
[50:1:1] - **Founder:** **Vasishthiputra Santamula** (ASO 2011) – not Vishnuvardhana, Satakarni or Ganapatideva.
[50:1:2] - **Lineage:** **Veera Purushadatta** belongs to the **Ikshvakus** (G1 1995) – not the Rashtrakutas, Vemulawada Chalukyas or Salankayanas.
[50:1:3] - **Last king:** **Rudrapurushadatta** (G2 2019 ×2); Sri Chantamula, Virapurushadatta, Ehuvala are distractors.
[50:1:4] - **Gurajala (Gurazala) inscription:** issued by **Rudrapurushadatta** (APPSC PYQ ×2) – Jaggayyapeta belongs to Virapurushadatta.
[50:1:5] # Vasishthiputra Santamula – Vedic king and agrarian patron
[50:1:6] - **Sacrifices:** **Ashvamedha, Vajapeya, Agnishtoma, Agnihotra, Rajasuya**; evidence = the **Ashvamedha platform** found at **Nagarjunakonda**.
[50:1:7] - **Intelligentsia in farming:** **Sri Chantamula** tried to make the **intelligentsia partners in agricultural development** (G2 2012 ×2) – gifts of land, ploughs, bullocks and cows to Brahmins.
[50:1:8] - **Titles:** **Gosatasahasra**, **Halasatasahasra** (Satasahasrahalaka), **Mahadanapati** – giver of lakhs of cows and ploughs; crores of gold coins.
[50:1:9] - **Inscriptions:** Rentala, Kesanapalli, Dechepalli.
[50:1:10] # Virapurushadatta
[50:1:11] - **Sri Parvatadhipati** (lord of Sriparvata) = **Virapurushadatta** (APPSC PYQ ×2) – not Shantamula I or II or Rudrapurushadatta.
[50:1:12] - Only Ikshvaku king to turn to **Buddhism**; his queens and aunts were great Buddhist donors.
[50:1:13] # Ehuvala Santamula and Rudrapurushadatta
[50:1:14] - **Ehuvala** was named after his **grandfather** (Santamula) – an Ikshvaku naming custom; under him **Sanskrit** entered the records and Brahmanical temples rose beside Buddhist ones.
[50:1:15] - **Gummadidurru** inscription = Ehuvala Santamula.
[50:1:16] - **Rudrapurushadatta:** Gurajala record (land grant to **Halampuraswami**, i.e. Nagulapuram, Palnadu); defeated by Pallava **Simhavarman** (Manchikallu).
[50:1:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Ikshvakus p.1, p.4, p.10-14; Rocket AP History sheet "Inscriptions" (Gurazala), #16 (founders); NextGen Previous Papers p.8, p.13, p.28; app notes 1:50 (sub 4)
## SUB 2 | Puranic Names, Origin Theories and the Ayodhya Claim
[50:2:0] # Puranic names
[50:2:1] - **Sriparvatiyas (Sri Parvatiya Andhras):** the **Puranas** call the Ikshvakus "Sriparvatiyas" (UPPCS 2020) – not the Vakatakas, Sakas or Kharavela.
[50:2:2] - They are also called **Andhrabhrityas** – a Puranic name of the dynasty, not a title of Ehuvala Santamula.
[50:2:3] # Origin theories
[50:2:4] TABLE head: Theory | Proponent
  [50:2:4.0] Andhra / Telugu people | Bishop Caldwell (G2 2011 ×2) – the accepted view
  [50:2:4.1] Tamil | K. Gopalachari
  [50:2:4.2] Kannada | Vogel
  [50:2:4.3] North Indian | Rapson, Buhler
  [50:2:4.4] Name from ikshu (sugarcane, their tribal symbol) | B.S.L. Hanumantha Rao
[50:2:5] - **Proof of Andhra origin:** southern names (Bapi, Adavi, Chelike) + the southern custom of marrying the **maternal uncle's daughter** (cross-cousin marriage).
[50:2:6] - **⚠ Trap:** V.A. Smith and Oldenberg are distractors; Gopalachari = Tamil, not Telugu.
[50:2:7] # The Ayodhya claim (G2 Mains 2025)
[50:2:8] - **Incorrect statement (official final key):** "In their inscriptions, the Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri described themselves as descendants of the **Ikshvakus of Ayodhya**."
[50:2:9] - **True statements in the same question:** Puranas call them **Sri Parvathiyas**; matrimonial ties with the **Sakas / Western Satraps of Ujjain**; **Virapurushadatta's** reign = golden age of Buddhism in Andhra.
[50:2:10] - The **Ayodhya** link comes from texts (Ramayana, Puranas, the Kannada Jain *Dharmamrita* of Nyayasena); the Vijayapuri records use the Ikshvaku name (a record of Ehuvala traces him to the legendary Ikshvakus) but do not name Ayodhya – hence the key.
[50:2:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Ikshvakus p.1, p.8, p.10; APPSC G2 Mains 2025 Paper 1 final key (Q3, Series A, https://bloomappsc.com/documents/G2_MAINS_2025_P1_SeriesA_FINAL_KEY.pdf); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andhra_Ikshvaku
## SUB 3 | Marriage Alliances
[50:3:0] - **Princess of Ujjain:** **Virapurushadatta** married **Rudradhara Bhattarika**, daughter of the Saka (Western Kshatrapa) ruler of **Ujjain** (Rudrasena II) → tie with the **Sakas / Western Kshatrapas** (APPSC PYQ).
[50:3:1] - **⚠ Trap:** she came from Ujjain (Sakas), not from the Pallavas; not the wife of Santamula or Ehuvala.
[50:3:2] - **Santamula's sister Santisri** married **Skandasri of the Pugiya** family; his daughter **Adavi Santisri** married **Skanda Visakha of the Dhanika** family.
[50:3:3] - **Virapurushadatta's daughter Kodabalisri** married **Vishnurudra Sivalananda Satakarni of the Chutus**.
[50:3:4] - **Cross-cousin marriage** (maternal uncle's daughter) was practised – Virapurushadatta married his aunt's daughters **Bapisri** and **Shastisri**.
[50:3:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Ikshvakus p.4, p.11-13; Powerplay #1 Part 8 (Drive 1LGVBeIeFhUUw_ZzIC5_DW5cRtd3H05y2); app notes 1:50 (sub 6)
## SUB 4 | Inscriptions and the End of the Dynasty
[50:4:0] TABLE head: Inscription | Issuer | What it shows
  [50:4:0.0] Alluru | Virapurushadatta (NextGen; Rocket names Ehuvala) | Gifts to many sections and institutions; Ikshvakus as Satavahana vassals
  [50:4:0.1] Nagarjunakonda | Virapurushadatta and royal women | Founding of the kingdom at Vijayapuri by Santamula; Buddhist gifts (ayaka pillars)
  [50:4:0.2] Jaggayyapeta | Virapurushadatta | Ikshvaku rule in the lower Krishna
  [50:4:0.3] Gummadidurru | Ehuvala Santamula | Later Ikshvaku rule
  [50:4:0.4] Gurajala | Rudrapurushadatta | Last Ikshvaku king
  [50:4:0.5] Manchikallu | Pallava Simhavarman | Found near Vijayapuri; Rudrapurushadatta defeated → Pallava rule
  [50:4:0.6] Mayidavolu plates | Sivaskandavarman (crown prince, from Kanchi) | Grant concerning Dhanyakataka → Pallava hold on the Krishna–Guntur region
[50:4:1] - **Who ended the Ikshvakus:** **D.C. Sircar** – Simhavarman helped bring them down (end of the 3rd c. CE); **T.V. Mahalingam** – Simhavarman bore no royal title, **Sivaskandavarman I** completed the takeover.
[50:4:2] - An **Abhira** inscription at the capital is read by some as an Abhira occupation; by the mid-4th century the **Pallavas** held the region south of the Krishna, the **Brihatphalayanas** the north.
[50:4:3] - **Firsts:** first dated inscriptions (year, month, day) and first sculptors' names; first structural Hindu temples (Pushpabhadraswami, Ashtabhuja Narayana at Nagarjunakonda).
[50:4:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Ikshvakus p.8-9, p.14; Rocket AP History sheet "Inscriptions" (Manchikallu, Alluru); Powerplay #1 Part 8; app notes 1:50 (sub 7, 8)

=== NOTES 1:51 | Ikshvaku Socio-economic Conditions and Royal Women Donors
## SUB 0 | Royal Women Donors
[51:0:0] - **Dual pattern:** kings were **Vedic**; **royal women** were the main patrons of Buddhism at Nagarjunakonda, giving **without male intervention** – a trend of women endowing Buddhism while the men patronised Hindu cults (Tribal Welfare Officer PYQ: statements 1 and 2 true, "women took no part in donations" false).
[51:0:1] - **Nagarjunakonda inscriptions** record gifts by the Ikshvaku family both to **Hindu temples** and to **Buddhist monks**.
[51:0:2] - **Santisri (Chamtisri) and Harmyasri** = **sisters of Vasishthiputra Santamula (Chantamula I)** (Welfare Officers 2017; APPSC PYQ) – not of Virapurushadatta or Ehuvala.
[51:0:3] TABLE head: Donor | Relation | Gift
  [51:0:3.0] Chamtisri (Santisri) | Sister of Santamula; paternal aunt of Virapurushadatta | First woman donor; rebuilt the Maha Chaitya in Virapurushadatta's 6th regnal year; 9 ayaka pillars; 170 dinari-masakas
  [51:0:3.1] Harmyasri | Sister of Santamula | Pillar for her mother at the Aparamahavinaseliya chaitya; daughter Chathasri also gave
  [51:0:3.2] Adavi Chamtisri | Sister of Virapurushadatta (daughter of Santamula) | Ayaka pillar, Maha Chaitya
  [51:0:3.3] Bapisri, Chatisri | Queens of Virapurushadatta (his aunt's daughters) | Pillars at the Mahachaitya
  [51:0:3.4] Rudradhara Bhattarika | Queen; daughter of Rudrasena of Ujjain | Ayaka pillar
  [51:0:3.5] Kodabalisri | Daughter of Virapurushadatta | Vihara for Mahishasaka monks
  [51:0:3.6] Bhatti Mahadevi | Chief queen; mother of Ehuvala | Vihara for the Bahushrutiya
  [51:0:3.7] Upasika Bodhisri | Non-royal; daughter of Revanta of Amaravati | Sinhala Vihara; viharas for foreign monks; ranked first among women donors
[51:0:4] - **⚠ Trap:** Bodhisri did not build a vihara for the Aparamahavinaseliya sect; Harmyasri did not build the Mahishasaka vihara.
[51:0:5] # Donative inscriptions
[51:0:6] - Mostly **Prakrit ayaka-pillar** records of Virapurushadatta's **6th regnal year**; each names the donor by her tie to the king.
[51:0:7] - Ikshvakus were the **first to date** records by **year, month and day**; Bodhisri's record = evidence of **non-royal** patronage.
[51:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Ikshvakus p.2, p.11-12; Powerplay #1 Part 8 (Drive 1LGVBeIeFhUUw_ZzIC5_DW5cRtd3H05y2); app notes 1:51 (sub 0, 1)
## SUB 1 | Agrarian Economy and Agraharas
[51:1:0] - **Sri Chantamula (Vasishthiputra Santamula)** tried to make the **intelligentsia partners in agricultural development** (G2 2012) – gave **gold, cows, ploughs and land**; brought **Brahmins from the north** and gave them **agraharas**.
[51:1:1] - **Agraharas** = grants of land and its royal income, mostly to **Brahmins** (JA Panchayat Raj 2012; NTR Univ. JA) – not to Shudras, Kshatriyas, leaders, goldsmiths or widows.
[51:1:2] - He performed **Ashvamedha, Vajapeya, Agnistoma** – altar found at **Nagarjunakonda**.
[51:1:3] - **Revenue split four ways:** administration + army; temples + festivals; poets + scholars; gifts to religious bodies; some on **tanks and canals** – not on overseas colonies.
[51:1:4] - **Shift:** from the Satavahana **trade economy** to an **agrarian, agrahara-based** early medieval order.
[51:1:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Ikshvakus p.1, p.4, p.15; NextGen Previous Papers p.28; app notes 1:51 (sub 2)
## SUB 2 | Taxes, Guilds, Trade and Coins
[51:2:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [51:2:0.0] Bhaga | Land tax, 1/6 of produce
  [51:2:0.1] Hiranya / Meya | Tax in money / in grain
  [51:2:0.2] Kara | Tax on industries, professions and trade
  [51:2:0.3] Halikas | Farmers
  [51:2:0.4] Nigamalu (Negimalu) | Guilds; continued the Satavahana sreni tradition
  [51:2:0.5] Parnika Sreni | Betel-leaf traders
  [51:2:0.6] Poosika Sreni | Sweetmeat traders
  [51:2:0.7] Sale / Telika / Kammaru | Weavers / oil pressers / blacksmiths
[51:2:1] - **Roman trade** was **lower than under the Satavahanas**; **Roman gold and silver coins** at Nagarjunakonda and a **Roman-style amphitheatre** at **Vijayapuri**.
[51:2:2] TABLE head: Exports | Imports
  [51:2:2.0] Spices, iron, coconuts, cotton textiles | Gold, silver, wine, glassware
[51:2:3] - **Coins:** of **lead and copper**; symbols **Ujjain symbol, elephant, lion**; found in Guntur, Krishna and Godavari districts.
[51:2:4] - **Ports:** Ghantasala (Ptolemy's Kantakossyla), Motupalli.
[51:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Ikshvakus p.15-17; Rocket AP History sheet "Ports" and "Guilds"; app notes 1:51 (sub 3, 4)
## SUB 3 | Society
[51:3:0] - **Shudras** were the majority; Brahmins rose through **Brahmadeya** grants (exempt from **18 taxes**) – a new **landlord class**.
[51:3:1] - **Cross-cousin marriage** began with the Ikshvakus; alliances with the **Kshatrapas of Ujjain** and the **Chutus** (Kodabalisri married Vishnurudra Sivalananda Satakarni).
[51:3:2] - Records show **matronymics** (Vasishthiputra, Mathariputra), naming after the **grandfather** (Ehuvala Santamula) and **sati** (Satisahagamanam).
[51:3:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Ikshvakus p.3, p.16, p.19; app notes 1:51 (sub 5)

=== NOTES 1:52 | Ikshvaku Religious Conditions – Buddhism at Nagarjunakonda and Brahmanical Temples
## SUB 0 | Golden Age of Buddhism – Virapurushadatta
[52:0:0] - **Golden age of Buddhism in Andhra** = the **Ikshvaku period** (APPSC PYQ) – not the Satavahana, Vishnukundin or Chalukya period.
[52:0:1] - **Greatest patronage to Buddhism** in the Ikshvaku kingdom: reign of **Virapurushadatta** (G2 2008 ×2; APPSC PYQ) – not Sri Chantamula, Ehuvala Chantamula or Rudrapurushadatta.
[52:0:2] - **Women patronised Buddhism** most under the Ikshvakus (APPSC PYQ); queens, princesses and rich lay women funded stupas and viharas.
[52:0:3] - **Upasika Bodhisri** served Buddhism in the reign of **Virapurushadatta** (her Chula-Dhammagiri record is dated in his **14th** regnal year) (G2 2012).
[52:0:4] - **⚠ Trap:** a G2 2012 answer grid printed **Ehuvala Chantamula** for Bodhisri – wrong; NextGen, Rocket and her own inscription place her under Virapurushadatta.
[52:0:5] - **Trampled Shivalinga:** a Nagarjunakonda sculpture shows **Mathariputra Virapurushadatta** trampling a Shivalinga – a sign of his turn to Buddhism (APPSC PYQ).
[52:0:6] TABLE head: King | Religious policy
  [52:0:6.0] Vasishthiputra Sri Santamula (founder) | Vedic: Ashvamedha, Rajasuya, Vajapeya, Agnistoma; worshipped Virupakshapati (Shiva) and Mahasena (Skanda); agraharas to northern Brahmins
  [52:0:6.1] Virapurushadatta | Only Ikshvaku king to adopt Buddhism (earlier Vedic; did not wholly drop Brahmanical ties); "Ashoka of the South", Sri Parvatadhipati; rebuilt the Maha Chaitya under Acharya Bhadanta Ananda; set up the Sriparvata University
  [52:0:6.2] Ehuvala Santamula | Revived Brahmanism; first Hindu temples; first Sanskrit inscriptions; still built a vihara for the Bahushrutiyas in his mother's name
  [52:0:6.3] Rudrapurushadatta (last) | Vedic; deity Mahasena; custom of chhaya-stambhas (shadow pillars) near graves began
[52:0:7] - **Puranic Shaivism, Vaishnavism and Shakti worship** all thrived; the Ikshvakus were the **last royal Buddhist zenith** in Andhra.
[52:0:8] - **Kings** (all except Virapurushadatta) were Vedic; kings were **not** the chief patrons of stupas and viharas.
[52:0:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Ikshvakus p.2, p.4-5, p.12-13, p.17; Rocket AP History sheet "During the reign of" (Bodhisri, golden age – Virapurushadatta); NextGen Previous Papers p.13, p.19; Powerplay #1 Part 8 (Sivalingam); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andhra_Ikshvaku
## SUB 1 | Deities – Hariti and the Dynastic Gods
[52:1:0] - **Hariti (Harati)** = **tutelary deity** of the **Ikshvakus** of Vijayapuri (G2 2012; APPSC PYQ) – the protector of **children**; women offered bangles for progeny.
[52:1:1] - Installation of her image = beginning of **Shakti worship**; Hariti was also a mother goddess of the Early Chalukyas.
[52:1:2] TABLE head: Deity | Dynasty / group
  [52:1:2.0] Hariti | Ikshvakus (also Early Chalukyas)
  [52:1:2.1] Sriparvataswamy | Vishnukundins – family deity (identified with Srisaila Mallikarjuna)
  [52:1:2.2] Chitraratha Swamy (Sun) | Salankayanas – family deity
  [52:1:2.3] Bappa Bhattaraka | Salankayanas – "regarding the father as God"
  [52:1:2.4] Vishnu | Salankayana Nandivarman II – land grant in the Pedavegi inscription
  [52:1:2.5] Kakati | Kakatiyas
  [52:1:2.6] Virupaksha | Vijayanagara kings (Hampi)
  [52:1:2.7] Vasavi | Arya Vysya community – seat Penugonda
[52:1:3] - **Sri Parvataswamy** as tutelary deity = **Vishnukundins** (G2 1993) – not the Ikshvakus, Salankayanas or Anandagotrikas.
[52:1:4] - **⚠ Trap:** Hariti = Ikshvaku tutelary deity; Virupakshapati and Mahasena = gods the Ikshvaku kings worshipped; Kakati = Kakatiyas.
[52:1:5] ~~ Sources: Rocket AP History sheet #7 (Gods); NextGen Ikshvakus p.2, p.10; NextGen Vishnukundis p.10; NextGen Previous Papers p.27; app notes 1:52 (sub 2, 8)
## SUB 2 | Monasteries, Sects and Foreign Links
[52:2:0] TABLE head: Monastery / donor | Sect
  [52:2:0.0] Maha Chaitya (Chamtisri, Harmyasri) | Aparamahavinaseliya (Aparasaila) – Nagarjunakonda its main centre
  [52:2:0.1] Vihara of Bhatti Mahadevi (by Ehuvala) | Bahushrutiya
  [52:2:0.2] Kodabalisri's vihara | Mahishasaka
  [52:2:0.3] Bodhisri's Sinhala Vihara (Chuladhammagiri) | Mahaviharavasin (Theravada) – Sri Lankan monks
  [52:2:0.4] Purvasailiya | Amaravati
  [52:2:0.5] Aparasailiya | Nagarjunakonda
[52:2:1] - Mahasanghika branches / related sects: Purvasailiya, Aparasailiya, Bahushrutiya, Rajagirika, Siddharthika – **Mahaviharavasin is not one**.
[52:2:2] - **Acharya Bhadanta Ananda** (Aparamahavinaseliya) knew the **Digha and Majjhima Nikayas** by heart.
[52:2:3] # Maha Chaitya and Bodhisri
[52:2:4] - A **Dhatugarbha** stupa over the Buddha's bodily relics: "**Samma Sambudhasa dhatuvara parigahita**".
[52:2:5] - Earlier **Paravata Mahachaitya** built by **Yajnasri Satakarni** for **Acharya Nagarjuna**; rebuilt by **Chamtisri** with **9 ayaka pillars**.
[52:2:6] - **Bodhisri's** works: stone mandapa at the eastern gateway of the Maha Chaitya at **Kantakasala (Ghantasala)**; **seven viharas at Papili**.
[52:2:7] # Foreign links
[52:2:8] - Bodhisri's inscription names lands that received the Dhamma: **Kashmir, Gandhara, China, Chilata, Tosali, Aparanta, Vanga, Vanavasi, Yavana, Damila, Palura** (not Magadha).
[52:2:9] - **Ceylonese monks** made Nagarjunakonda their **Hinayana** base; **Mahadeva Bhikshu** took Buddhism from the **Pallava-bhoga** region to Sri Lanka (Mahavamsa).
[52:2:10] - **Suhrllekha:** the Chinese pilgrim **Itsing** (I-tsing, in India 671–695 CE) saw Indian students memorising Nagarjuna's *Suhrllekha*, a letter to **Yajnasri Satakarni** (G2 2012) – not Fa-hien or Hiuen Tsang.
[52:2:11] - **Hiuen Tsang (7th c.)** found the **Sriparvata vihara neglected**.
[52:2:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Ikshvakus p.2, p.5-6, p.12-14; Rocket AP History sheet #23 (Itsing); app notes 1:52 (sub 3, 4, 5)
## SUB 3 | Brahmanical Temples at Nagarjunakonda
[52:3:0] - The Ikshvakus built **India's first structural Hindu temples**: **9 Shaiva + 1 Vaishnava** at Nagarjunakonda.
[52:3:1] - Temples found in excavations: **Harati, Mahajana, Kumara Swami, Pushpabhadra Swami, Ashtabhuja Narayana Swami**; also Nandikeshwara and Navagraha.
[52:3:2] TABLE head: Temple | Builder / deity
  [52:3:2.0] Pushpabhadraswami | Started by Virapurushadatta, completed by Ehuvala Santamula; Shiva; Gajaprishtha (elephant-back) plan
  [52:3:2.1] Sarvadevadhivasam | Commander Elisiri (of Ehuvala); for Kumara Swami (Kartikeya); Sanskrit record
  [52:3:2.2] Ashtabhuja Narayanaswami | Shivasena, commander of the Abhira king Vasusena; first Vaishnava temple in Andhra
[52:3:3] - Inscriptions of Vasishthiputra Santamula were found at **Rentala** and Kesanapalli near Nagarjunakonda.
[52:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Ikshvakus p.2, p.13-14, p.19; Rocket AP History sheet #4 (temples), #7; app notes 1:52 (sub 7)
## SUB 4 | Acharya Nagarjuna and Sriparvata
[52:4:0] - **Nagarjuna** = **Madhyamika** philosopher; **Sriparvata = Nagarjunakonda / Vijayapuri**, named after him.
[52:4:1] - **Yajnasri Satakarni** built viharas and chaityas at Sriparvata for him; **Virapurushadatta** set up the **Sriparvata University**.
[52:4:2] - Sriparvata = "**Dakshina Gaya**", sacred to **Mahayana**, while **Bodh Gaya** is sacred to **Hinayana**.
[52:4:3] - **Sri Parvataswamy = Buddha:** identified by **N. Venkataramanayya** (G2 2019); do not confuse with **Sriparvataswami**, the Vishnukundin family deity (Srisaila Mallikarjuna).
[52:4:4] - **In news (May 2025):** Miss World contestants visited **Buddhavanam** next to Nagarjunakonda (Buddhist circuit).
[52:4:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Ikshvakus p.13; Rocket AP History sheet #7; NextGen Previous Papers p.13; app notes 1:52 (sub 6, 9)

=== NOTES 1:53 | Ikshvaku Art, Architecture and Literature
## SUB 0 | Discovery, Excavation and the Nagarjuna Sagar Dam
[53:0:0] TABLE head: Year | Person / event
  [53:0:0.0] 1926 | Site discovered by A.R. Saraswati (A. Rangaswami Sarasvati, Telugu Assistant, Madras epigraphy office)
  [53:0:0.1] 1927–31 | Excavated by A.H. Longhurst (ASI)
  [53:0:0.2] 1938 | Re-excavated by T.N. Ramachandran
  [53:0:0.3] 1954–60 | Large rescue excavation before submergence; R. Subrahmanyam among the excavators; palace complex and brick Brahmanical temples
[53:0:1] - **Discoverer of Nagarjunakonda (Nagarjuna Hill):** **A.R. Saraswati** (Welfare Officers 2017 ×2; APPSC PYQ) – Longhurst and Ramachandran excavated later; R. Subrahmanyam led the 1950s dig.
[53:0:2] - **Nagarjuna Sagar Project:** **Nehru** laid the foundation stone on **10 December 1955** at Nandikonda (construction 1955–67); the valley was submerged after **1960**.
[53:0:3] - **⚠ Trap:** 29 Dec 1955, 23 Mar 1955, 1 Nov 1955 and 29 Dec 1956 are all wrong dates (AEE 2011 offered none of 10 Dec 1955).
[53:0:4] - **Salvage archaeology:** ASI dismantled and rebuilt monuments on higher ground at **Anupu** (Krishna bank) and on **Nagarjunakonda island** – "**transplanted monuments**"; India's only **island museum**.
[53:0:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas (src/nextgen-03-satavahanas.txt, Nagarjunakonda discovered 1926 by A.R. Saraswati); Epigraphia Indica XX (via https://jainqq.org/pagetext/Epigraphia_Indica_Vol_20/032574/12); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagarjuna_Sagar_Dam; app notes 1:53 (sub 5, 6)
## SUB 1 | Language of the Inscriptions
[53:1:0] - **Prakrit** = court language and language of the Ikshvaku inscriptions, including the Nagarjunakonda records of gifts to the great monastery (NTR Univ. JA; APPSC PYQ) – not Sanskrit, Telugu, Tamil or Paisachi.
[53:1:1] - **Ehuvala Santamula** brought **Sanskrit** into inscriptions; Sanskrit replaced Prakrit from the **4th c. CE**.
[53:1:2] TABLE head: Inscription | Language

=== NOTES 1:56 | Vishnukundin Art and Architecture – Undavalli, Mogalrajapuram and Bhairavakonda Caves
## SUB 0 | Undavalli and Mogalrajapuram – Which Dynasty
[56:0:0] - **Undavalli, Mogalrajapuram and Vijayawada (Indrakeeladri) cave temples** = **Vishnukundins** (G2 2019; G2 Mains 2025; Welfare Officers 2017 ×2; APPSC PYQ ×3) – not Ikshvakus, Salankayanas, Pallavas, Rashtrakutas, Cholas, Chalukyas, Kakatiyas or Reddi kings.
[56:0:1] - **Brahmanical (Hindu) caves** of Mogalrajapuram and Undavalli are assigned to the Vishnukundins; **Madhava Varma I** is credited with Undavalli, Bhairavakonda and Mogalrajapuram.
[56:0:2] - **Vishnukundins** = **first Hindu cave temples in the Telugu states**; **Guptas** = earliest Hindu cave temples in India (**Udayagiri**, Madhya Pradesh).
[56:0:3] TABLE head: Cave | Dynasty | Deity / sect | Location
  [56:0:3.0] Undavalli | Vishnukundins | Ananta Padmanabha Swamy (Vishnu); earlier Jain, Buddhist | Tadepalli mandal, Guntur district; south bank of the Krishna near Vijayawada
  [56:0:3.1] Mogalrajapuram | Vishnukundins | Trimurti, Durga, Nataraja; mainly Shaiva | Vijayawada (NTR district)
  [56:0:3.2] Bhairavakonda | Vishnukundin (MV I) or Pallava | Shiva, Kapalika sect | Nallamala hills, Nellore–Prakasam border
  [56:0:3.3] Akkanna-Madanna | Vishnukundins | Shaiva | Indrakeeladri, Vijayawada
  [56:0:3.4] Bojjannakonda | – | Buddhist | Visakhapatnam
[56:0:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Vishnukundis p.9, p.12, p.15; Rocket AP History sheet "Art"; app notes 1:56 (sub 0)
## SUB 1 | Undavalli Caves
[56:1:0] - **District:** **Guntur** (Endowment EO 2022) – not Krishna, NTR or Prakasam; the caves face **Vijayawada** across the Krishna (Boilers 2019: "near Vijayawada").
[56:1:1] - **Four storeys**, **three main caves**; carved **top-down** – upper levels finely finished, ground floor **crude and unfinished**.
[56:1:2] - Centrepiece: **monolithic reclining Vishnu** (**Ananta Padmanabha Swamy**), about 5 m; a Buddha in padmasana was later turned into Vishnu; **Purnakumbha** motif.
[56:1:3] - **Changing use:** **Jain abode → Buddhist monks → Hindu temple**.
[56:1:4] - **⚠ Trap:** on the **Krishna**, not the Godavari; "built by the Cholas as a Hindu temple, later Buddhist" is false.
[56:1:5] - **In news:** AP's two-day **Telugu Mahotsavam** at Undavalli Caves, **25–26 July 2026**.
[56:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Vishnukundis p.15; app notes 1:56 (sub 1)
## SUB 2 | Mogalrajapuram Caves
[56:2:0] TABLE head: Cave | Feature
  [56:2:0.0] Caves 1–3 | Sanctums behind a pillared mandapa for the Trimurti
  [56:2:0.1] Cave 4 | Durga cave; Ardhanarishvara on the back wall
  [56:2:0.2] Cave 5 (largest) | Shiva Tandava Nataraja
[56:2:1] - **Five caves** in all, in Vijayawada (NTR district); Trimurti figures on the **kapota** (eave) above the pillar capitals.
[56:2:2] ~~ Sources: NextGen Vishnukundis p.15; app notes 1:56 (sub 2)
## SUB 3 | Bhairavakonda Caves
[56:3:0] - **Eight rock-cut caves**, all dedicated to **Shiva** (G2 2012) – not 4, 9 or 12; a centre of **Shaivism** (Kapalika sect).
[56:3:1] - **Location:** listed under **Nellore** district in NextGen/Rocket and the G2 2012 stem; on the ground in the **Nallamala hills** on the Nellore–Prakasam border.
[56:3:2] - **Attribution debate:** Madhava Varma I (Vishnukundin) vs **Pallava period (7th–8th c.)**; closely resembles the early Pallava caves of **Mahabalipuram**.
[56:3:3] - Pillars: **lion-based** with **kumbha (pot) capitals**.
[56:3:4] > Number angle: 4 storeys = Undavalli | 5 caves = Mogalrajapuram | 8 caves = Bhairavakonda.
[56:3:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Vishnukundis p.9, p.15; Rocket AP History sheet #4, "Art" (Bhairavakonda – eight caves); NextGen Previous Papers p.28; app notes 1:56 (sub 3)
## SUB 4 | Features and the Pallava Comparison
[56:4:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [56:4:0.0] Pillared mandapa | Hall in front of rock-cut garbhagriha cells – the usual Vishnukundin plan
  [56:4:0.1] Kumbha capitals | Pot capitals on lion-based pillars (Bhairavakonda)
  [56:4:0.2] Kapota | Decorated eave above capitals (Mogalrajapuram)
  [56:4:0.3] Dwarapalas | Door guardians
[56:4:1] - Style: mix of **Ikshvaku and Vakataka** traditions with **Pallava** borrowings; dated **4th–6th c. CE**.
[56:4:2] - **Brick structural temples** with garbhagriha, antarala-mandapa, mukhamandapa at **Keesaragutta**.
[56:4:3] - **Lost-wax (cire perdue):** early multi-armed metal images credited to the **Vishnukundin** age.
[56:4:4] - **Pallava caves** of **Mahendravarman I** (7th c. CE) – lion-based pillars – later taken up by the **Telugu Chodas and Eastern Chalukyas**.
[56:4:5] - **⚠ Trap:** the storeyed cave is **Undavalli**, not Bhairavakonda.
[56:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Vishnukundis p.8, p.15; app notes 1:56 (sub 4, 5)

=== NOTES 1:57 | Andhra Society and Culture in the Early Period – Varna, Women, Education and Festivals
## SUB 0 | Ikshvaku Women Patrons – Bodhisiri and Chantisiri
[57:0:0] # The women donors of Nagarjunakonda
[57:0:1] TABLE head: Woman | Dynasty | Patronage
  [57:0:1.0] Bodhisiri (Bodhisri) | Ikshvaku (Virapurushadatta's time) | Upasika (lay devotee); built viharas and chaityas at Nagarjunakonda; sent monks to Kashmir and Tibet; daughter of Revanta of Amaravati
  [57:0:1.1] Chantisiri (Santisiri, Chamtisiri) | Ikshvaku | Sister of Vasishthiputra Chamtamula; built the Mahachaitya at Nagarjunakonda over the Buddha's relics
  [57:0:1.2] Adavi Chantisiri | Ikshvaku | Daughter of Chamtamula; another royal donor
  [57:0:1.3] Gautami Balasri | Satavahana | Funded the cave-vihara at Nasik; not a Gathasaptasati poet
[57:0:2] - **Woman who gave the greatest service to Buddhism in the Ikshvaku period:** **Bodhisiri** (G2 2012, G2 2019, APPSC PYQ).
[57:0:3] - **Mahachaitya at Nagarjunakonda:** **Chantisiri** (APPSC Tribal Welfare Officer).
[57:0:4] - **⚠ Trap:** Bodhisiri and Chantisiri are **Ikshvaku**, not Satavahana; **Rudramadevi** (Kakatiya) and Vasavadatta are distractors; "Bapisiri" is a made-up option.
[57:0:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Ikshvakus p.2, p.4; NextGen AP History Previous Papers p.13, p.27; app notes 1:57 (sub 2)
## SUB 1 | Gathasaptasati – the Chief Source of Satavahana Society
[57:1:0] # Hala's anthology
[57:1:1] - **Author:** Satavahana king **Hala**; about **700 verses (gathas)** in **Maharashtri Prakrit** on love, village and family life.
[57:1:2] - **Chief literary source** of Satavahana social and cultural history (G2 Prelims 2019; APPSC PYQ) – not the Aitareya Brahmana, Dharmasutras or Puranas.
[57:1:3] - **Opening:** begins with a prayer to **Shiva (Pasupati)** and ends with a prayer to **Gauri** (APPSC PYQ); Saiva names Pashupati, Rudra, Gauri, Ganapati appear.
[57:1:4] - **Women poets in it:** **Madhavi, Revati, Anupamalabdha, Anulakshmi**.
[57:1:5] - **Telugu words in it:** atta, addam, potta, pilla, padi.
[57:1:6] > Exam angle: "most important source of Satavahana society" = **Gathasaptasati of Hala**; opening prayer = **Shiva**.
[57:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.1-2, p.14, p.23-26; app notes 1:57 (sub 5)
## SUB 2 | Dress, Cosmetics and Amusements
[57:2:0] # Dancers and dress
[57:2:1] - **Foundation cream of Satavahana dancers:** **Aradalam** – in Telugu "**maipoota / Maiputa**" (body coating) (G2 Mains 2019 and G2 2019).
[57:2:2]   - **⚠ Settled:** "Maiputa = Kusuma Lepanam" (old app key) is wrong – Maiputa is the Telugu word for the foundation cream, which NextGen and Rocket name **Aradalam**; Kusuma Lepanam, Mukhateji and Meni-kanti are distractors.
[57:2:3] - **Reliefs (Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda):** **men** – lower cloth and **turban**; **women** – heavy **anklets, bangles, girdles, necklaces**.
[57:2:4] - **Amphitheatre at Nagarjunakonda (Vijayapuri):** for **performances and games**, not Vedic sacrifices.
[57:2:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen AP History Previous Papers p.13; Rocket AP History (Foundation cream = Aradalam); app notes 1:57 (sub 5)
## SUB 3 | Varna and Caste
[57:3:0] # Varna in early Andhra
[57:3:1] - **Caste of the Satavahanas:** **Brahmins** – Gautamiputra Satakarni is called **Ekabrahmana** (Eka Brahmin) and **Agama Nilaya** in the Nasik prasasti; kings upheld **varna-dharma**.
[57:3:2] - **Nanaghat inscription:** Brahmins trained in Vedic learning and ritual; Brahmins got **tax-free villages**.
[57:3:3] - **Kshatriya status by assimilation:** **Greeks, Sakas, Pahlavas, Kushanas** took Indian names and faiths – e.g. Nahapana's daughter **Dakshamitra**, son-in-law Rishabhadatta.
[57:3:4] - **Vishnukundins:** followed varnasramadharma; **farmers = "the backbone"**, got land grants.
[57:3:5] TABLE head: Term | Occupation
  [57:3:5.0] Halikas | Farmers
  [57:3:5.1] Sethis | Merchants
  [57:3:5.2] Selavaddikas | Stone sculptors / masons
  [57:3:5.3] Swarnakaras | Goldsmiths
[57:3:6] - **Samayamu** = caste associations of the **Kakatiya** period (later term).
[57:3:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.15, p.25; app notes 1:57 (sub 0)
## SUB 4 | Position of Women and Marriage
[57:4:0] # Women
[57:4:1] - **Patriarchal joint family**, yet women had **respect and freedom** – joined men in festivals and gatherings and **donated generously** to viharas and chaityas.
[57:4:2] - **Matronymics:** kings bore their mothers' names – **Gautamiputra** Satakarni, **Vasishthiputra** Pulumavi.
[57:4:3] - **Titles from husbands:** **Mahasenapatni, Mahabhojaki, Maharathi**.
[57:4:4] - **Sati:** a **Nagarjunakonda sculpture** and the Greek writer **Strabo**.
[57:4:5] - **Polygamy** was practised in the **upper classes**; widows observed **celibacy**; marriage was **sacred**.
[57:4:6]   - **⚠ Settled:** the PYQ "what inscriptions tell us about women" has three true options (prominence, lavish donations, matronymics) and no "all of these" – left unkeyed; "no polygamy among princes" is false.
[57:4:7] # Marriage
[57:4:8] TABLE head: Type | Union | Children
  [57:4:8.0] Anuloma | Higher-caste man + lower-caste woman | Ugra
  [57:4:8.1] Viloma (Pratiloma) | Lower-caste man + higher-caste woman | Chandala
[57:4:9] - **Kathasaritsagara** mentions inter-caste marriages – caste not fully rigid.
[57:4:10] TABLE head: King | Married
  [57:4:10.0] Hala | Sri Lankan princess Lilavati
  [57:4:10.1] Satakarni I | Naganika, daughter of Maharathi Tranakayira
  [57:4:10.2] Vasishthiputra Satakarni | Daughter of Saka Rudradaman
[57:4:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Satavahanas p.15; https://kpiasacademy.com/satavahana-deccan-social-structure/; app notes 1:57 (sub 1, 2)
## SUB 5 | Education and Popular Religion
[57:5:0] # Education
[57:5:1] TABLE head: Centre | Nature
  [57:5:1.0] Viharas | Buddhist monastic learning (Nagarjunakonda a leading centre)
  [57:5:1.1] Ghatikasthanas | Vedic colleges (Vishnukundins)
  [57:5:1.2] Agraharas | Land grants to Vedic Brahmins
[57:5:2] - **Indrabhattaraka Varma** (Vishnukundin) – "**Ghatika Vapta punyasancharya**"; credited with founding ghatikas.
[57:5:3] # Religion and folk cults
[57:5:4] - **Amaravati reliefs:** worship of **nagas, yakshas and sacred trees** beside Buddhist symbols.
[57:5:5] - **Ikshvaku kings** performed **Vedic sacrifices** (**Vasishthiputra Chamtamula**: Asvamedha, Vajapeya); **queens** patronised Buddhism; Brahmanical shrines such as **Pushpabhadraswami** stood at Nagarjunakonda.
[57:5:6] - **Vishnukundins:** family deity **Sriparvataswamy**; titles **Paramamaheswara, Parama Brahmanya**.
[57:5:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Vishnukundins; NextGen Ikshvakus p.10; app notes 1:57 (sub 3, 4)

  x: Viloma, a lower-caste man with a higher-caste woman, produced offspring termed Chandala; Anuloma offspring were termed Ugra.

=== NOTES 1:61 | Gupta Empire – Sources, Chandragupta I, Samudragupta and the Allahabad Prasasti (harishena)
## SUB 0 | Allahabad Prasasti – Harisena, the Pillar and Its Inscriptions
[61:0:0] # The prashasti
[61:0:1] - **Allahabad Pillar inscription (Prayaga Prashasti)** = the chief source for **Samudragupta**: his conquests and personality (UPSC 2006 ×2; UP Lower 2004; SSC 2019; APPSC Draughtsman).
[61:0:2] - **Composer:** **Harisena**, court poet, who was at once **Kumaramatya, Sandhivigrahika** (minister of peace and war) and **Mahadandanayaka** (SI Mains 2017) – not Ravikirti (Aihole, Pulakesin II).
[61:0:3] - **Form:** classical **Sanskrit**, **champu** style (prose + verse), Gupta **Brahmi** script, **33 lines**.
[61:0:4] - Harisena of the prashasti is **not** the later Jain Harisena of the **Brihatkatha Kosha**.
[61:0:5] # The pillar
[61:0:6] - An **Ashokan** pillar first set up at **Kaushambi**; **Akbar** moved it to the Allahabad (Prayagraj) fort.
[61:0:7] TABLE head: Inscription on the pillar | Fact
  [61:0:7.0] Ashoka's edicts | Brahmi; dhamma
  [61:0:7.1] Queen's Edict | Queen Karuvaki
  [61:0:7.2] Samudragupta's prashasti | By Harisena; glorifies war
  [61:0:7.3] Jahangir's record | Persian
[61:0:8] - **Not on the pillar:** **Kumaragupta** (and no Shahjahan, Aurangzeb or Dara Shikoh).
[61:0:9] - **Mehrauli Iron Pillar** = **Chandragupta II** ("Chandra"), not Samudragupta.
[61:0:10] # Reading the prashasti (CAPF 2017)
[61:0:11] - Upinder Singh: the prashasti presents the Gupta empire as the **epicentre of a complex web of varied political relationships** – the line-number options in that PYQ are misquoted.
[61:0:12] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval India Part 3 p.55, p.57-58; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 3 p.3; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India; app notes 1:61 (sub 0, 5)
## SUB 1 | Samudragupta's Southern Campaign – Andhra Kings
[61:1:0] # Policy
[61:1:1] TABLE head: Group | Treatment | Regions
  [61:1:1.0] North (Aryavarta) | Rulers slain, kingdoms annexed | Ganga–Yamuna region
  [61:1:1.1] Atavika rajyas | Subdued | Forest kingdoms of central India
  [61:1:1.2] Frontier kings | Paid tribute | Assam, Nepal, Bengal
  [61:1:1.3] South (Dakshinapatha) | Captured and released – reinstated as tributaries | 12 kings from Kosala to Kanchi
  [61:1:1.4] Distant kings | Homage | Kushanas, Sakas, Sri Lanka
[61:1:2] - Southern policy = **grahana-moksha-anugraha** → **no permanent annexation** in the south (APPSC G1 statement II true).
[61:1:3] # The twelve southern kings
[61:1:4] TABLE head: King | Kingdom (present area)
  [61:1:4.0] Mahendra | Kosala (Mahanadi region)
  [61:1:4.1] Vyaghraraja | Mahakantara
  [61:1:4.2] Mantaraja | Kurala / Kaurala – identified with the Kolleru lake region (Kielhorn)
  [61:1:4.3] Mahendragiri | Pishtapura (Pithapuram, Kakinada)
  [61:1:4.4] Swamidatta | Kottura
  [61:1:4.5] Damana | Erandapalle (Srikakulam)
  [61:1:4.6] Vishnugopa | Kanchi (Pallava)
  [61:1:4.7] Nilaraja | Avamukta (Guntur)
  [61:1:4.8] Hastivarman (Salankayana) | Vengi (Pedavegi, near Eluru)
  [61:1:4.9] Ugrasena | Palakka (Nellore area)
  [61:1:4.10] Kubera | Devarashtra – Yelamanchili area, Visakhapatnam
  [61:1:4.11] Dhananjaya | Kusthalapura (Arcot)
[61:1:5] - **Ruler of Vengi** during the campaign = **Hastivarman** (SI 2019; APPSC PYQ) – not Damana, Mahendra or Vishnugopa.
[61:1:6] - **Pallava king defeated** = **Vishnugopa** of Kanchi (G2 1993) – not Vishnugupta, Nandivarman or Kubja Vishnuvardhana.
[61:1:7] - **Kosala's king** = **Mahendra**; Pishtapura's = **Mahendragiri**.
[61:1:8]   - **⚠ Settled:** Devarashtra = **Yelamanchili** (Visakhapatnam) per NextGen; the old app note "S. Kota, Vizianagaram" is dropped. **Kaurala** is disputed (Bhandarkar: Kolleru lay inside Vengi; others Ganjam or Korada), but among the options Kolleru is the accepted answer.
[61:1:9] # AP angle
[61:1:10] - The campaign hit **coastal Andhra**: Pishtapura, **Vengi, Avamukta, Devarashtra**, Erandapalle, Palakka – the Allahabad Pillar is the **chief source for 4th-century Andhra** kings.
[61:1:11] - A Samudragupta-period record is found at **Sankaram** (Visakhapatnam).
[61:1:12] - Empire stretched from Nepal and Punjab to Kanchi; influence reached **Simhala** – not confined to Magadha.
[61:1:13] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval India Part 3 p.58; NextGen Eastern Chalukyas (Sarvasiddhi in Yalamanchili taluka = Devarashtra); Rocket AP History (Allahabad Pillar – Hastivarma); NextGen AP History Previous Papers p.52; https://whatisindia.com/inscriptions/earlyguptakings/politicalhistory17.html; app notes 1:61 (sub 4)
## SUB 2 | Titles of Samudragupta and Other Guptas
[61:2:0] TABLE head: Ruler | Title
  [61:2:0.0] Sri Gupta, Ghatotkacha | Maharaja only
  [61:2:0.1] Chandragupta I | Maharajadhiraja (first)
  [61:2:0.2] Samudragupta | Kaviraja (king of poets); Lichchhavi-dauhitra (daughter's son of the Lichchhavis); Prithivyah Pratham Veer (first hero of the earth); Param Bhagavata (first Gupta, Nalanda and Gaya plates); after the Ashvamedha Prithivyama Pratiratha (no rival on earth)
  [61:2:0.3] Chandragupta II | Vikramaditya, Sakari, Devagupta
  [61:2:0.4] Kumaragupta I | Mahendraditya
[61:2:1] - **Napoleon of India** = **Samudragupta**, so named by **V.A. Smith** (State PSC; UP Lower 2009; SSC 2019).
[61:2:2] - **Kaviraja** = Samudragupta (G2 2011) – shown playing the veena on lyrist coins.
[61:2:3] - **Lichchhavi-dauhitra** = Samudragupta, son of the Lichchhavi princess **Kumaradevi** (CGPSC 2024).
[61:2:4] - **Param Bhagavata:** first used by **Samudragupta** (UPPCS 2009, 2015); **⚠ Settled:** the official UPPSC key gave Chandragupta II, who used it widely on coins – the Nalanda and Gaya plates put it first with Samudragupta.
[61:2:5] # Non-Gupta distractor titles
[61:2:6] TABLE head: Ruler | Title
  [61:2:6.0] Kushanas (Kanishka) | Devaputra
  [61:2:6.1] Gautamiputra Satakarni | Rajaraja
  [61:2:6.2] Rajendra I | Gangaikonda Chola
  [61:2:6.3] Pulakeshin II | Satyashraya
[61:2:7] # Kings → queens
[61:2:8] TABLE head: King | Queen
  [61:2:8.0] Chandragupta I | Kumaradevi (Lichchhavi)
  [61:2:8.1] Samudragupta | Duttadevi
  [61:2:8.2] Kumaragupta I | Anantadevi
[61:2:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval India Part 3 p.56, p.58-59; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 3 p.2-4; Rocket Indian History Part 1 (Samudragupta – Param Bhagavata); app notes 1:61 (sub 8)
## SUB 3 | Chandragupta I and the Early Guptas
[61:3:0] # Origin and order
[61:3:1] - **Sri Gupta** = **founder of the dynasty** (SSC 2015); ruled a small area of **North Bengal and South Bihar**; succeeded by **Ghatotkacha**.
[61:3:2] - **Origin** debated: Vaishya, later treated as Kshatriya; a Brahmana origin argued from the **Dharana gotra** of Prabhavatigupta – the Junagadh inscription does not settle it.
[61:3:3] - **Early territory:** Magadha, **Prayag**, eastern UP (**Vayu Purana**).
[61:3:4] - **Order:** Sri Gupta → Ghatotkacha → Chandragupta I → Samudragupta → **Ramagupta** → Chandragupta II → Kumaragupta I → Skandagupta.
[61:3:5] # Chandragupta I (c. 319–335 CE)
[61:3:6] - **Real founder of the empire**; capital **Pataliputra**.
[61:3:7] - **Gupta era (Gupta Samvat):** **319–320 CE** = his accession (MPPCS 1991; SSC 2006; APPSC G1) – not Sri Gupta.
[61:3:8] - **Maharajadhiraja:** the first Gupta to take it (SSC 2018).
[61:3:9] - **Marriage:** **Kumaradevi**, a **Lichchhavi** princess – gave legitimacy and power.
[61:3:10] - **First Gupta coins:** gold **king-queen type** (Chandragupta I with Kumaradevi, legend "Lichchhavayah") (UPPCS 2010) – no coins of Sri Gupta or Ghatotkacha are known.
[61:3:11]   - **⚠ Settled:** one NextGen page says Chandragupta I "defeated Saka satraps" and "first minted silver coins" – wrong: both belong to **Chandragupta II** (PMF, NextGen p.4, p.7); Chandragupta I did **not** defeat the Sakas (APPSC G1 statement I false).
[61:3:12] # Gupta coins
[61:3:13] - Mostly **gold** (dinaras): show rulers, deities and rituals. **Samudragupta's types:** **lyrist (veena)**, **Ashvamedha** (to celebrate his conquests after the horse sacrifice), **archer**; the **king-queen** type is Chandragupta I's.
[61:3:14] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval India Part 3 p.55-56, p.60; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 3 p.2, p.4, p.7, p.17; app notes 1:61 (sub 1, 2, 3, 6)
## SUB 4 | Other Gupta Inscriptions and Literary Sources
[61:4:0] # Inscriptions
[61:4:1] TABLE head: Inscription | Ruler | Key facts
  [61:4:1.0] Eran (Sagar, Madhya Pradesh), 510 CE | Bhanugupta | First inscriptional evidence of sati – wife of commander Goparaja (UPPCS 2010)
  [61:4:1.1] Mehrauli Iron Pillar | Chandragupta II | In the yard of the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, Delhi; a Vishnu Dhvaja on hill Vishnupada; conquests in the north-west and Bengal
  [61:4:1.2] Udayagiri cave | Chandragupta II | Minister Virasena
  [61:4:1.3] Mandsaur | Kumaragupta I | Feudatory Bandhuvarman; composed by Vatsabhatti; silk-weavers' Sun temple
  [61:4:1.4] Bhitari Pillar (Ghazipur, UP) | Skandagupta | War with the Hunas
  [61:4:1.5] Junagadh | Skandagupta | Governor Parnadatta repaired the Sudarshana lake
[61:4:2] # Literary sources
[61:4:3] TABLE head: Work | Author | Subject
  [61:4:3.0] Mudrarakshasa | Vishakhadatta | Chanakya and Chandragupta Maurya
  [61:4:3.1] Devichandraguptam | Vishakhadatta | Ramagupta – Dhruvadevi – Chandragupta II
[61:4:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 3 p.8, p.11; app notes 1:61 (sub 0)
## SUB 5 | Samudragupta's Foreign Contacts
[61:5:0] - **Meghavarman**, Buddhist king of **Sri Lanka**, sent a mission to **Samudragupta** for permission to build a **Buddhist monastery at Bodh Gaya** – recorded in a **Chinese source** (State PSC).
[61:5:1] - The **Kushanas and Sakas** paid homage to the Gupta ruler.
[61:5:2] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval India Part 3 p.61; NextGen Indian History APPSC Part 3 p.4; app notes 1:61 (sub 6)

=== NOTES 1:62 | Chandragupta II Vikramaditya, Kumaragupta, Skandagupta; the Hunas and Gupta Decline
## SUB 0 | Chandragupta II Vikramaditya – Saka Conquest, Silver Coins, Titles and Fa-hien
[62:0:0] # Accession – the Ramagupta episode
[62:0:1] - **Killed his elder brother:** **Chandragupta II** took the throne after killing his elder brother **Ramagupta** and married his widow **Dhruvadevi (Dhruvaswamini)** – story in **Vishakhadatta's Devichandraguptam** (State PSC).
[62:0:2]   - Ramagupta, defeated by the Sakas, had agreed to surrender Dhruvadevi to the Saka king; Chandragupta II, in disguise, killed the Saka king, then Ramagupta.
[62:0:3] - **Order:** Samudragupta → (Ramagupta, brief and disputed) → Chandragupta II, c. **380–415 CE** (NextGen 380–413; PMF 380–412).
[62:0:4] # Saka conquest and Ujjain
[62:0:5] - **Saka-conqueror (Sakari):** Chandragupta II defeated **Rudrasimha III**, the last Western Kshatrapa (Saka) ruler, and annexed **western Malwa and Gujarat** with the western sea ports (UP UDA/LDA 2010).
[62:0:6] - **Second capital:** **Ujjain (Ujjayini)** (RPSC 2008) – Malwa and Saurashtra are regions, Mehrauli the site of his iron pillar.
[62:0:7] - **Evidence:** the **Udayagiri cave** inscription of his minister **Virasena**, and above all his **silver coins**.
[62:0:8] # Silver coins – the strongest evidence
[62:0:9] - **First Gupta to issue silver coins:** **Chandragupta II**, after the Saka conquest, on the model of the Western Kshatrapa silver drachms (UP UDA/LDA Mains 2010; MPPSC 2023). Earlier Guptas issued gold.
[62:0:10]   - ⚠ NextGen Indian History 03 p.2 says "Chandragupta I was the first Gupta king to mint silver coins" – an error: PMF, the app notes and numismatic sources credit Chandragupta II.
[62:0:11] - **UPPCS 2022 statements:** the silver coins are the **strongest evidence of the Saka victory**, and they weigh about **30–33 grains** like the Saka drachms → **both** statements correct.
[62:0:12] - **Coin name:** silver = **rupaka**; gold = **dinara**. Lion-slayer coins gave the title **Simhavikrama** (his father = tiger-slayer coins).
[62:0:13] # Titles and names
[62:0:14] TABLE head: Title / name | Note
  [62:0:14.0] Vikramaditya | Linked with the Saka victory (SSC 2010); also used by Skandagupta
  [62:0:14.1] Sakari | "Destroyer of the Sakas"
  [62:0:14.2] Simhavikrama | Lion-slayer coins
  [62:0:14.3] Devagupta, Devaraja, Devashri | Devagupta in Sanchi and Vakataka records; Devaraja at Sanchi (UPPCS Mains 2007)
[62:0:15] # Marriage alliances
[62:0:16] TABLE head: Alliance | Detail
  [62:0:16.0] Vakataka | Daughter Prabhavati Gupta married Rudrasena II; she ruled the Vakataka kingdom as regent for her sons (RAS 2023; JPSC 2023) – indirect Gupta control of the Deccan
  [62:0:16.1] Naga | Married the Naga princess Kuberanaga (Prabhavati's mother)
  [62:0:16.2] Dhruvadevi | Married after killing Ramagupta
[62:0:17] # Fa-hien and the court
[62:0:18] - **Fa-hien (Faxian):** came **c. 399–412 CE**, in the reign of **Chandragupta II** (UPSC 2025; State PSC) – not Samudragupta, Kumaragupta I or Skandagupta; he **did not name the king** – his interest was Buddhism. First of the three Chinese pilgrims (later **Xuan Zang**, **I-Qing**, 7th c.).
[62:0:19] - **Navaratnas** (tradition): **Kalidasa, Amarasimha, Varahamihira**, Dhanvantari, Vararuchi, Shanku, Ghatakarpara, Kshapanaka, Vetalabhatta – Fa-hien was **not** one of them.
[62:0:20] - **Not his minister:** **Harishena** was Samudragupta's court poet (Prayag prashasti), not Chandragupta II's minister.
[62:0:21] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 03 p.2, p.4-5; PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.62-63; app notes 1:62 (sub 1)
## SUB 1 | The Hunas – Skandagupta, Toramana, Mihirakula and Yashodharman
[62:1:0] # Who the Hunas were
[62:1:1] - **Hunas = Hephthalites / White Huns** of Central Asia; strong in the **Oxus** valley, they entered India by taking **Gandhara** (mid-5th c.). **Toramana** was a **Huna** (IAS 1995) – not a Saka, Scythian or Yuezhi.
[62:1:2] # Waves of invasion
[62:1:3] TABLE head: Wave / leader | Gupta reign | Outcome
  [62:1:3.0] First attack | End of Kumaragupta I's reign | Checked by prince Skandagupta
  [62:1:3.1] Main invasion | Skandagupta (c. 455–467) | Hunas repulsed twice; title Vikramaditya
  [62:1:3.2] Toramana (second invasion) | Weak successors, late 5th c. | Conquered up to Eran; Eran boar inscription of his 1st regnal year
  [62:1:3.3] Mihirakula (Toramana's son, c. 515) | Narasimhagupta | Tyrant, persecuted Buddhists; defeated by Yashodharman
[62:1:4] - **Gupta ruler who defeated the Hunas:** **Skandagupta** (UPPSC Lower 2015; UPPCS Mains 2004; State PSC) – not Samudragupta, Chandragupta II, Ramagupta or Bhanugupta.
[62:1:5] - **Reign of the Huna invasion:** **Skandagupta** (UPPCS Mains 2006); the **Guptas** were the dynasty most troubled by the Hunas (UPPCS 1993).
[62:1:6] - **"First Huna invasion faced by" (APSC 2017):** the usual key is **Skandagupta** – PMF: Skandagupta "was the one who really faced the Hunas invasion"; NextGen adds that the first attack came when Kumaragupta I was very old and was repulsed by prince Skandagupta.
[62:1:7] # Records
[62:1:8] TABLE head: Inscription | Records
  [62:1:8.0] Bhitari pillar (Saidpur, Ghazipur, UP) | Skandagupta's victories over the Pushyamitras and Hunas (UPRO 2014) – not Allahabad, Mandsaur or Udayagiri
  [62:1:8.1] Junagadh (Girnar) | Skandagupta's governor Parnadatta repaired the Sudarshana lake
  [62:1:8.2] Eran boar (Varaha) | Huna rule over Eran in Toramana's first regnal year
  [62:1:8.3] Gwalior | Record of Mihirakula's rule, including Gwalior
  [62:1:8.4] Sondani / Mandsaur pillars | Yashodharman's victory over Mihirakula; Sondani composed by Vasula (MPPSC 2024)
[62:1:9] # Yashodharman of Mandasor
[62:1:10] - **Defeated Mihirakula:** **Yashodharman**, the **Aulikara** king of Malwa (Mandasor), in **c. 528 CE** (UPPSC 2016 ×2) – not Budhagupta, Shashanka or Prabhakaravardhana; **Narasimhagupta Baladitya** and the Maukharis also fought him.
[62:1:11] - **Victory pillars at Sondani:** c. **532 CE**; his rise **weakened** Gupta authority further.
[62:1:12] - **Skandagupta:** gold coins with **bow and arrow, Garuda standard and Lakshmi**; last great Gupta; governors became **hereditary feudatories**.
[62:1:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 03 p.5-6; PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.64, p.81-82; Rocket Indian History 01 (Bhitari → Skandagupta → Hunas); app notes 1:62 (sub 3, 4, 5)
## SUB 2 | Gupta Chronology, Kumaragupta I and Nalanda
[62:2:0] # Rulers in order
[62:2:1] TABLE head: Order | Ruler | Period / note
  [62:2:1.0] 1 | Sri Gupta | Founder, title Maharaja (c. 275 CE)
  [62:2:1.1] 2 | Ghatotkacha | Maharaja
  [62:2:1.2] 3 | Chandragupta I | 319–335; Maharajadhiraja; started the Gupta era (319–20 CE)
  [62:2:1.3] 4 | Samudragupta | c. 335–375; Prayag prashasti
  [62:2:1.4] 5 | Ramagupta | Brief, disputed
  [62:2:1.5] 6 | Chandragupta II | c. 380–415
  [62:2:1.6] 7 | Kumaragupta I | c. 415–455
  [62:2:1.7] 8 | Skandagupta | c. 455–467; last great Gupta
  [62:2:1.8] 9 | Purugupta, Budhagupta, Narasimhagupta (Baladitya), Kumaragupta III | Later main line
  [62:2:1.9] 10 | Vishnugupta | c. 540–550; last recognised king of the line (SSC CGL 2019)
[62:2:2] - **Order asked (APPSC G1):** **Samudragupta → Chandragupta II → Kumaragupta I → Skandagupta** = (iii), (i), (iv), (ii).
[62:2:3] - **"Gupta dynasty ruled" (CGPSC 2003):** **319–500 AD** is the keyed span (from Chandragupta I's era; the line actually lasted to c. 550).
[62:2:4] - **Distractors:** Bimbisara (Haryanka) and Ashoka (Maurya) were not Guptas; **Bindusara** extended Mauryan power into the Deccan.
[62:2:5] # Kumaragupta I (c. 415–455)
[62:2:6] - **Titles:** **Shakraditya, Mahendraditya**; devotee of **Kartikeya** – gold coins with the king **feeding a peacock** and Kartikeya.
[62:2:7] - **Nalanda:** founded by **Kumaragupta I** (c. 450 CE) (BPSC 2015; State PSC) – not Chandragupta Vikramaditya, Dharmapala (Pala patron of Vikramashila) or Pushyagupta.
[62:2:8]   - Site identified by **Alexander Cunningham** (1861); destroyed by **Bakhtiyar Khalji** (end of 12th c.).
[62:2:9] - **Mandsaur (Dashpur) prashasti:** records the achievements of **Kumaragupta I** and his governor **Bandhuvarman**; composed by **Vatsabhatti** (UPRO Mains 2021).
[62:2:10] - **Other records:** **Bilsad** (Gupta year 96 = 415 CE, his earliest), **Damodarpur** copper plates (guilds as banks), Karamdanda.
[62:2:11] - **Threats late in his reign:** the **Pushyamitras** and the first Huna attack.
[62:2:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 03 p.2, p.5; PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.54-56, p.72, p.84; app notes 1:62 (sub 0, 2)
## SUB 3 | Gupta Decline and the Successor States
[62:3:0] # Causes of decline
[62:3:1] TABLE head: Factor | Effect
  [62:3:1.0] Huna invasions | Drained treasury and army; Hunas held Punjab, Rajasthan, Malwa by c. 485–500
  [62:3:1.1] Weak successors | After Skandagupta
  [62:3:1.2] Feudal set-up | Land grants and hereditary governors created feudatories who broke away (Yashodharman, Maitrakas)
  [62:3:1.3] Economic | Land grants cut revenue – no professional army; loss of western India cut trade income; silk weavers left Gujarat for Malwa
  [62:3:1.4] Buddhism of later Guptas | Listed as a cause in some books (pacifist policy)
[62:3:2] - **NOT a cause:** the **Arab invasion** (UKPCS 2012) – the Arabs came much later (Sindh 712 CE).
[62:3:3] - **Signs of collapse:** later gold coins had **less gold, more alloy**; coins slowly replaced by **payments in land**; no Gupta coins or inscriptions in **western Malwa and Saurashtra** after Skandagupta.
[62:3:4] # Successor states before Harsha
[62:3:5] TABLE head: Power | Seat | Exam fact
  [62:3:5.0] Later Guptas (Guptas of Magadha) | Magadha | Not the imperial line
  [62:3:5.1] Maukharis | Kannauj | Ishanavarman (Haraha), Ishvaravarman (Jaunpur), Sarvavarman
  [62:3:5.2] Maitrakas | Valabhi (Gujarat) | Rulers Dharapatta, Guhasena (APPSC 2023)
  [62:3:5.3] Pushyabhutis | Thanesar (Haryana), later Kannauj | Harsha's family
  [62:3:5.4] Aulikaras | Mandsaur | Yashodharman
[62:3:6] - **UPSC 2021:** between the Guptas and Harsha the north was held by the **Guptas of Magadha, Pushyabhutis of Thanesar, Maukharis of Kannauj and Maitrakas of Valabhi** (1, 3, 4, 6) – **not** the **Paramaras of Malwa** (9th–14th c.) or the **Yadavas of Devagiri** (12th–14th c.).
[62:3:7] # Later Gupta and Maukhari records (UPPCS 2022)
[62:3:8] TABLE head: Record | Ruler
  [62:3:8.0] Asirgarh copper seal (MP) | Maukhari Sarvavarman – so "Sarvavarman – Gaya copper plate" is the wrong pair
  [62:3:8.1] Jaunpur stone inscription | Ishvaravarman
  [62:3:8.2] Haraha stone inscription | Ishanavarman – also records his defeat of the Vishnukundin Indrabhattaraka Varma
  [62:3:8.3] Deobaranark inscription | Jivitagupta II (Later Gupta)
[62:3:9] - **Other neighbours:** **Vakatakas** (Vidarbha; Harishena patronised Ajanta), **Kadambas** of Banavasi (founded by **Mayurasharma**), **Vishnukundins** of Andhra (**Madhava Varma II**, 11 Ashvamedhas).
[62:3:10] - **Outcome:** the decline marked a transition from a single empire to **regional kingdoms and a feudal order** – not a return to Mauryan-style centralisation.
[62:3:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 03 p.6; PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.81-82; app notes 1:62 (sub 6, 7, 5)

=== NOTES 1:63 | Gupta Administration – Feudalism Debate, Land Grants, Agraharas, Revenue and Local Bodies
## SUB 0 | Revenue – Bhaga, Gupta Taxes and Vishti
[63:0:0] # The king's share
[63:0:1] - **Prescribed rate:** the law books (Dharmashastras / "Hindu law") fix the king's share (**bhaga**) at **one-sixth** of the produce (UPPCS 1992; State PSC ×2). In practice the Gupta king took **one-fourth to one-sixth**.
[63:0:2]   - ⚠ NextGen Indian History 03 p.8 gives "about 1/7" – an outlier; the same file (p.6) and PMF give 1/4–1/6, and exam keys give **1/6**.
[63:0:3] - **Tax trend:** under the Guptas **land taxes rose** while **trade and commerce taxes fell**.
[63:0:4] - **Bhaga and Bali:** **sources of revenue** (UPPCS 1996) – bhaga = king's share of produce; bali = once a voluntary offering, later compulsory. Not military departments, rituals or divisions.
[63:0:5] # Revenue terms
[63:0:6] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [63:0:6.0] Bhaga | King's share of produce – main land revenue (1/6)
  [63:0:6.1] Bhoga | Periodic supplies in kind – fruits, firewood, flowers
  [63:0:6.2] Kara | Periodic general tax
  [63:0:6.3] Udranga | New Gupta tax: land revenue in the inscriptions (nature unclear – perhaps water or police tax)
  [63:0:6.4] Uparikara | New Gupta tax, probably on temporary tenants – an additional farm tax
  [63:0:6.5] Udakabhaga | Irrigation (water) tax (UPPCS Mains 2009)
  [63:0:6.6] Halivakara | Plough tax paid by every cultivator owning a plough (SSC CGL 2019)
  [63:0:6.7] Hiranya | Tax paid in cash (gold) instead of produce
  [63:0:6.8] Sulka (Shulka) | Customs duty and tolls on merchandise
  [63:0:6.9] Sita | Revenue from crown land
  [63:0:6.10] Vata-bhuta | Cess for rites to winds and spirits
  [63:0:6.11] Uparnika / Klipta / Upaklipta / Valiam | Tax on border farmers / taxes on land sale and purchase / commodity tax
[63:0:7] # Vishti – forced labour
[63:0:8] - **Vishti:** unpaid **forced labour** for the army, officials, the state or the donee (Telugu **vetti**); it was considered **a source of income for the State, a sort of tax paid by the people** (UPSC 2019).
[63:0:9]   - It was imposed in **central and western India** (Malwa, Kathiawar – Junagadh inscription), so "totally absent in MP and Kathiawar" is wrong; it was **unpaid**, so no weekly wages; not confined to the eldest son.
[63:0:10] - **Peasants:** had to feed the royal army on the march and supply officials on tour; they sank to a **semi-servile** status.
[63:0:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian History APPSC 03 p.6-8; PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.66-67; app notes 1:63 (sub 5, 6)
## SUB 1 | Land Grants, Feudalism and the Agrarian Structure
[63:1:0] # Land grants
[63:1:1] TABLE head: Grant | Grantee | Rights
  [63:1:1.0] Agrahara | Brahmanas (religious functionaries) | Tax-free, hereditary; right to collect dues from peasants
  [63:1:1.1] Brahmadeya | Brahmanas, singly or jointly | Tax exemption + administrative rights
  [63:1:1.2] Devagrahara / Devadana | Temples and monasteries | Revenue for worship
  [63:1:1.3] Secular grants | Officials, samantas | Revenue in lieu of salary
[63:1:2] - **Tax-free agrarian land** went to the **Brahmins** (MPPSC 2014) – not to military or civil officials or court scholars.
[63:1:3] - **Most villages donated to temples and Brahmins:** the **Guptas** (State PSC key).
[63:1:4] - **Earliest land grants:** the **Satavahanas** (Deccan, early centuries CE); the practice became common under the Guptas.
[63:1:5] - **Effects:** royal officials barred from entering granted villages; grantees could punish criminals; **sub-infeudation**; grants in **tribal frontiers** brought virgin land under cultivation and turned tribes into **sub-castes**.
[63:1:6] # Post-Gupta agrarian structure (AP recruitment papers)
[63:1:7] - **TRUE:** land grants in tribal frontiers brought **virgin land under cultivation**; post-Gupta **copper-plate charters describe various types of land**; the **Smritis** speak of graded rights in the same land – **Mahipati** (king), **Kshetrasvamin** (owner), **Karshaka** (cultivator) and **sub-tenant**.
[63:1:8] - **FALSE:** "Pallava records specify 10 to 15 kinds of taxes" – the Pallava grants mention **18 types of taxes** exempted for donated villages.
[63:1:9] - **Early medieval features:** hierarchical **land intermediaries** with feudal titles and military obligations, prevalence of **vishti**, and a relatively **closed village economy** – all three.
[63:1:10] # The feudalism debate
[63:1:11] - **Essential elements (UPSC 2015):** an administrative structure based on **control and possession of land**, and a **lord–vassal** relationship – a **strong central authority** with weak local power is **not** feudal (it is the opposite).
[63:1:12] - **Post-Gupta feudalism (UPPCS Mains 2004 A–R):** the main feature of the post-Gupta agrarian structure was **feudalism** **because** a **landowning intermediate class** and a **dependent peasantry** arose – A and R true, R explains A.
[63:1:13] TABLE head: Historian | Position
  [63:1:13.0] R.S. Sharma | Proponent – land grants, sub-infeudation, vishti, decline of trade, urban decay, fewer gold coins
  [63:1:13.1] D.C. Sircar | Critic – grants transferred revenue rights, not ownership
  [63:1:13.2] Harbans Mukhia | Critic – "Was there feudalism in Indian history?"; free peasantry, no serfdom
  [63:1:13.3] B.D. Chattopadhyaya | Integrative model – grants spread state society into new areas
[63:1:14] - **Evidence cited (7th c.):** decline of long-distance trade and **gold coinage**, shrinking towns.
[63:1:15] - **Satavahana land measure:** **nivartana** ≈ **1.5 acres** (100 nivartanas granted to monks).
[63:1:16] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.66-67; NextGen Ikshvakus p.16 (Pallava – 18 taxes exempted); NextGen Indian History APPSC 03 p.8; app notes 1:63 (sub 8, 9)
## SUB 2 | Land Types and Measures
[63:2:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [63:2:0.0] Kshetra | Cultivated land
  [63:2:0.1] Khila | Untilled / uncultivable waste land
  [63:2:0.2] Aprahata | Uncultivated forest (jungle) land (BPSC 2017)
  [63:2:0.3] Vastu (Vasti) | Habitable / house-site land
  [63:2:0.4] Gopata Sarah | Pasture land
  [63:2:0.5] Kulyavapa, Dronavapa | Units of land measurement in Bengal inscriptions – area sown with one kulya / one drona of seed (UPSC 2020)
  [63:2:0.6] Nivartana | Land measure used in other regions
[63:2:1] - **Aprahata:** keyed as "uncultivated forest land", not dense forest, irrigated or cultivated land; NextGen 03 p.15 glosses it "cultivable wasteland" – same idea of land not yet tilled.
[63:2:2] - **Kulyavapa / dronavapa** are **not** coins, urban land classes or rituals.
[63:2:3] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.138 (kulyavapa); NextGen Indian History APPSC 03 p.15; app notes 1:63 (sub 7)
## SUB 3 | Kingship, Officials and Local Bodies
[63:3:0] # Kingship
[63:3:1] - **Monarchy:** Gupta rule was **kingship** (CDS 2008) – hereditary, with divine claims, not republican or democratic; **primogeniture was not firm**.
[63:3:2] - **Titles:** **Maharajadhiraja, Parameshvara, Paramabhattaraka**; kings likened to **Vishnu**; **Samudragupta** equated with **Kubera (Dhanada), Varuna, Indra and Yama (Antaka)**.
[63:3:3] - **Decentralised:** unlike the Mauryas, much of the empire was held by **feudatories (samantas)** – **Samudragupta** reinstated defeated kings; officials often paid in **land or kind**.
[63:3:4] # Officials
[63:3:5] TABLE head: Official | Function
  [63:3:5.0] Kumaramatya | Most important officers, appointed by the king in the home provinces; ministers and commanders chosen from them
  [63:3:5.1] Sandhivigrahika | Minister of peace and war
  [63:3:5.2] Mahadandanayaka | Chief judicial / military officer
  [63:3:5.3] Mahabaladhikrita | Commander-in-chief
  [63:3:5.4] Dandapashika | District police officer
  [63:3:5.5] Akshapataladhikrita | Keeper of royal records
  [63:3:5.6] Pustapala | Keeper of land-transfer records
  [63:3:5.7] Dutaka | Spy / messenger
[63:3:6] # Units
[63:3:7] TABLE head: Unit | Level | Head
  [63:3:7.0] Bhukti (desha) | Province | Uparika
  [63:3:7.1] Vishaya | District | Vishayapati
  [63:3:7.2] Vithi (eastern India) | Group of villages | Ayuktaka
  [63:3:7.3] Grama | Village | Gramika / Gramadhyaksha with mahattaras
[63:3:8] - **Village headman (CDS 2012):** he became **more important** in Gupta times, and **no land transaction could be effected without his consent** – so "lost importance" is wrong; "Kumaramatyas were the most important officers appointed by the king in home provinces" is right → **only I**.
[63:3:9] - **Mahattara and Pattakila:** designations of the **village headman** (UPSC 2014) – not military officers, Vedic ritualists or guild chiefs.
[63:3:10] # Town board and courts
[63:3:11] - **Adhikarana (Kotivarsha, Damodarpur plates):** **Nagarashreshthi** (chair, chief banker), **Sarthavaha** (chief caravan trader), **Prathama kulika** (chief artisan), **Prathama kayastha** (chief scribe); a **district council** helped the district officer.
[63:3:12] - **Law:** civil and criminal law first clearly demarcated – **property disputes = civil**, theft and adultery = criminal; **Narada smriti** (survives complete, civil law), Brihaspati and Katyayana (fragments).
[63:3:13] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.64-67; NextGen Indian History APPSC 03 p.7, p.14-15; app notes 1:63 (sub 0-4)

=== NOTES 1:64 | Gupta Society and Economy – Varna and Jati, Position of Women, Fa-hien's Account, Trade Decline
## SUB 0 | Ports, Trade and Crafts of the Gupta Age
[64:0:0] # Ports
[64:0:1] TABLE head: Port | Region | Exam fact
  [64:0:1.0] Tamralipti (Tamluk) | Bengal, east coast | The port that handled North Indian trade (UPSC 1999 ×2, 2011) – with SE Asia, China, Lanka, Java, Sumatra
  [64:0:1.1] Bhrigukachchha (Broach / Bharuch / Bhadoch / Barygaza) | Gujarat, mouth of the Narmada | Largest west-coast port – trade with the West
  [64:0:1.2] Kalyan, Chaul | Maharashtra (Konkan) coast | Chaul ~23 miles south of Mumbai
  [64:0:1.3] Ghantasala (Kontakossylla), Kadura (Koddura) | Krishna district, Andhra | East-coast ports
  [64:0:1.4] Sopara, Cambay | Western India | Western ports
  [64:0:1.5] Arikamedu, Kaveripattanam, Muziris | South India | International (incl. Roman) trade
[64:0:2] - **UPSC 2020:** **Ghantasala, Kadura and Chaul** were **ports handling foreign trade** – not capitals, art sites or Buddhist pilgrim centres.
[64:0:3] - **⚠ Trap:** Broach, Kalyan and Cambay are **western** ports; North India's trade went out through **Tamralipti**.
[64:0:4] # Crafts and exports
[64:0:5] - **Textiles:** centres in **Gujarat (Lata), Bengal, the Deccan and the Tamil country** were known for **textile manufacture** (RAS 2010) – textiles were the main export; silk weavers of Lata later moved to Mandsaur.
[64:0:6] - **Exports:** textiles, **gems, spices**; **import:** silk from China (**Chinansuka** = Chinese silk); **Vidisha** – cloth and ivory work.
[64:0:7] # Coinage
[64:0:8] TABLE head: Metal | Name | Note
  [64:0:8.0] Gold | Dinara | Issued in the largest numbers; later ones had less gold
  [64:0:8.1] Silver | Rupaka | After the conquest of the Western Satraps; local exchange
  [64:0:8.2] Copper | – | Very few
  [64:0:8.3] Cowries | – | Daily exchange (Fa-hien)
[64:0:9] - **AP angle:** **Motupalli and Koduru** served SE Asian trade under the **Vishnukundins**; Satavahana weavers' guild = **Kolika Shreni**.
[64:0:10] - **Sudarshana lake (Girnar):** built by **Pushyagupta**, Chandragupta Maurya's governor; repaired by Rudradaman and again by **Parnadatta**, Skandagupta's governor (Junagadh inscription).
[64:0:11] ~~ Sources: Rocket Indian History 01 p.64, p.66, p.99; PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.68; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.142; NextGen Indian History APPSC 03 p.6; app notes 1:64 (sub 4, 6, 7)
## SUB 1 | Trade Decline and Urban Decay
[64:1:0] # Causes of trade decline
[64:1:1] TABLE head: Factor | Effect
  [64:1:1.0] Fall of the West Roman Empire (476 CE) | The standard cause of the decline of North Indian trade, 7th–10th c. (APPSC G2 2017) – not the collapse of China or SE Asia or loss of artisan skills
  [64:1:1.1] Eastern Roman (Byzantine) trade | Silk and spices till c. 550 CE; fell when the Romans learnt to rear silkworms
  [64:1:1.2] Hunas | Blocked the north-western route; loss of western India cut the inflow of gold and silver
  [64:1:1.3] Sassanid decline | After the rise of Islam – hurt overland trade
[64:1:2] - **New direction:** as the Roman market was lost, Indian merchants relied more on **South-East Asian trade** (UPSC 1999) – it did not revive the northern economy.
[64:1:3] - **Silk weavers:** a guild left Lata (Gujarat) for **Mandsaur** (mid-5th c.) and took up other professions – falling silk demand.
[64:1:4] # Urban decay
[64:1:5] - **Gradual decline of towns:** a feature of the **Gupta period** (State PSC; BPSC 1995) – not the Pratihara, Rashtrakuta or Satavahana eras; **Pataliputra** had become a village when Hiuen-Tsang came.
[64:1:6] - **Post-Gupta decline of trade (AP recruitment):** **TRUE** – towns such as **Sanghol, Hastinapur, Mathura, Shravasti, Kaushambi** declined, and there is a **paucity of coins**; **FALSE** – that it "became more pronounced only by the middle of the 9th century" (it was marked from the 6th–7th c.).
[64:1:7] - **R.S. Sharma's view:** shrinking towns, self-reliant villages, few gold coins – the basis of the **urban decay and feudalism** thesis; critics note coins still appear in texts and inscriptions.
[64:1:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.68, p.82; NextGen Indian History APPSC 03 p.6-7; app notes 1:64 (sub 8)
## SUB 2 | Varna, Jati, Women and Post-Gupta Society
[64:2:0] # Caste
[64:2:1] - **Proliferation of jatis:** castes multiplied into sub-castes by absorbing **foreigners** (Hunas → Rajput clans) and **tribes** (through land grants).
[64:2:2] - **Post-Gupta caste (AP recruitment):** the **Abhira** tribe split into Abhira Brahmanas, Kshatriyas and Shudras; **peasants** were placed in the **Shudra** varna; **Kayasthas** worked as record-keepers and scribes – all true; but Brahmanas **were** divided into many sub-castes, so (b) is false → **a, c, d**.
[64:2:3] - **Kayastha = scribes** (APPSC G2 2012): a new caste of scribes and accountants from the land-grant bureaucracy; **prathama kayastha** sat on town boards.
[64:2:4] - **Jajmani system:** hereditary service castes serving landowning patrons (**jajmans**) for a share of produce – became prevalent in the **post-Gupta** period (APPSC G1 2010).
[64:2:5] - **Medhatithi:** the post-Gupta commentator on Manu who declared that **Shudras were not slaves by nature** (MPPSC 2010) – not Vijnaneshvara, Narada or Jimutavahana.
[64:2:6] - **Shudras and untouchables:** Shudras' position improved (seen as agriculturists by the 7th c.; could hear the epics), but **untouchability** grew – **chandalas** lived outside villages; **Narada Smriti** lists **15 types of slaves**.
[64:2:7] # Women
[64:2:8] - **Marriage:** pre-puberty marriage advised; **svayamvara** gave way to marriages arranged by parents; widows to stay celibate.
[64:2:9] - **Property:** no general property rights, but control over **stridhana** (marriage gifts); Katyayana let women sell their stridhana.
[64:2:10] - **Earliest sati record:** **Eran, 510 CE** – wife of **Goparaja**, a general/friend of Bhanugupta; sati was still rare.
[64:2:11] - **Land:** Amarasimha's **Amarakosha** lists **12 types of land** (urvara = fertile, usara = barren, maru = desert).
[64:2:12] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.69-70; PMF Ancient & Medieval 04 p.10 (Kayasthas); NextGen Indian History APPSC 03 p.8; app notes 1:64 (sub 1, 2, 3)
## SUB 3 | Guilds and the Dashpur (Mandsaur) Inscription
[64:3:0] # Guilds (shrenis)
[64:3:1] - **Autonomous bodies** of artisans and merchants with their own rules, seals and **judicial powers**; some maintained their **own armed bodies**; they took deposits and lent money (**banks**).
[64:3:2] - **NOT a feature (APPSC G1 2023):** "**non-autonomous bodies**" – the guilds were autonomous.
[64:3:3] - **Head:** **Sreshthi / Setti**; caravan trader = **Sarthavaha**.
[64:3:4] # Dashpur (Mandsaur) inscription
[64:3:5] - **Silk weavers' guild:** the **Dashpur inscription** of Kumaragupta I and his governor **Bandhuvarman** records the guild of **silk weavers** (from Lata) who built a **Sun temple** (436–37 CE) and repaired it (473 CE) (MPPSC 2019) – not the Prayag, Eran or Hathigumpha records.
[64:3:6] - **"First advertisement":** its praise of silk cloth makes it the **oldest example of advertisement** in India / "the world's first advertisement" (MPPSC 2021).
[64:3:7] - **Composer:** **Vatsabhatti** – NOT **Bhavabhuti** (MPPSC 2024); it calls Dashpur **Pashchimapur**.
[64:3:8] TABLE head: Record | Guild fact
  [64:3:8.0] Dashpur / Mandsaur (Kumaragupta I) | Silk weavers; Sun temple
  [64:3:8.1] Indore copper plate (Skandagupta) | Guild of oil-men – lamp in a Sun temple
  [64:3:8.2] Damodarpur copper plates (Kumaragupta I) | Guilds as banks; town board
[64:3:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.66-67; Rocket Indian History 01 p.10, p.85, p.100; app notes 1:64 (sub 5)
## SUB 4 | Fa-hien's Account
[64:4:0] - **Mission:** to **visit Buddhist institutions and collect copies of Buddhist manuscripts** (CDS 2009) – not to study administration, women or peasants; he never named the king.
[64:4:1] - **Hospital:** a **free hospital at Pataliputra**, endowed by citizens – poor patients got doctors, food and medicine (CGPSC 2019, 2020); **Tamralipti** was only his port of departure.
[64:4:2] - **Dates and route:** **c. 399–412 CE** (Chandragupta II); came overland via Central Asia and Gandhara, returned by sea via Tamralipti and **Sri Lanka**; account = **Fo-kwo-ki** ("Record of Buddhist Kingdoms").
[64:4:3] - **What he saw:** mild administration, no spy system, safe roads, capital punishment rare; **20 viharas at Mathura**; decay at Kapilavastu, Gaya, Kushinagar; **chandalas** struck a piece of wood to announce their approach; **cowries** for daily exchange.
[64:4:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Ancient & Medieval 03 p.67, p.70; NextGen Indian History APPSC 03 p.4; app notes 1:64 (sub 0)
